[SECTION] methods

[SECTION] field sampling
We conducted standardized noninvasive capture-recapture surveys of black bears on 43 study areas in the Boreal and Great Lakes-St. Lawrence (GLSL) forest regions (Rowe 1972) of ON, Canada (Fig. 1) during 2006-2009. Different study areas were sampled each year. During spring and early summer, black bears typically occupy stable home ranges and focus their activities within a smaller home range ''core area''; however, they frequently make longdistance excursions from their breeding range when energy rich foods such as berries and nuts become available, typically beginning in mid-July (Rogers 1987;Powell et al. 1997;Schenk et al. 1998;Noyce and Garshelis 2011). We therefore sampled from late May through June (the latest any samples were collected was 06 July) in order to meet the SECR assumptions of demographic closure and static home range center locations (Efford 2004). Most study areas had been established previously for population monitoring by bait-station index lines in habitat representative of the respective management unit (McLaren et al. 2005). On each study area, we snagged bear hair at 20-25 barbed wire hair corrals (Woods et al. 1999), except on three study areas where 15, 17, and 18 corrals were used. Corrals were spaced approximately 2 km apart in curvilinear arrays along secondary roads, 20-200 m from the road itself. We baited corrals with 3 partially-opened tins of sardines in oil suspended from a board nailed 2.5 m high on a tree [2 m from any point along the wire. We collected samples and re-baited corrals one week later, and repeated this for a total of 5 sampling occasions on 36 study areas; bears were sampled on only 4 occasions on 4 study areas, and on six occasions on 3 other study areas. We air dried hair samples in paper envelopes and stored them at room temperature until DNA extraction.

[SECTION] dna analysis
We did not attempt to extract DNA from samples with fewer than 5 guard hairs with visible roots; [90 % of samples were processed using 10-15 hairs to minimize technical artifacts from low template DNA. When the number of samples exceeded what we could analyze with available resources, we excluded samples collected from adjacent barbs at the same trap on the same occasion. Individuals were identified from their microsatellite genotypes at 10-15 polymorphic loci (Paetkau and Strobeck 1994;Paetkau et al. 1995;Taberlet et al. 1997;Kitahara et al. 2000), and sex was determined from amplification of a region of the Amelogenin gene (Ennis and Gallagher 1994). For more detailed DNA extraction, amplification, and profiling methods and criteria for ascribing samples to individuals see Obbard et al. (2010) and Pelletier et al. (2012).
Fig. 1 Map of the greater study area in ON, Canada. The Great Lakes are shaded dark grey. Trap locations are marked with black dots; at this scale traps arrays appear as thick black lines surrounded by gray shading which depicts 10 km buffers around all traps within each study area. Rowe's (1972) Forest region boundary between Boreal and Great Lakes-St. Lawrence Forests is depicted as a 20 km-thick light grey line. Thinner, darker grey lines show Ecoprovince boundaries between the Mid-Boreal Shield in the north, and each of the Lake of the Woods and Southern Boreal Shield to the south (Marshall et al. 1998) We excluded males from statistical analyses because we were concerned that our study areas might be too small to estimate densities of male bears reliably as the size of their home ranges could approach or exceed that of our study areas (Alt et al. 1980;Koehler and Pierce 2003;Efford 2011;Marques et al. 2011). We assumed that the height of the barbed wire strand (*50 cm) would exclude cubs and yearlings from the sample (Woods et al. 1999).
We generated study area-specific integration meshes (see Borchers andEfford 2008, Efford et al. 2009) that extended 10 km around all traps on each study area and excluded points that would have fallen in lakes. Mesh points were spaced 0.8-1.0 km apart. We verified that the extent and resolution of our integration meshes were sufficient to avoid bias by fitting SECR models to data from two study areas with [25 recaptures and movement rate estimates near the minimum and maximum across study areas, while varying the extent of the mask and the spacing of mask points. Extents ranged from 5-15 km in increments of 2.5 km; the spacing of points ranged from 0.4-1.2 km in increments of 0.2 km. Density estimates and their coefficients of variation were insensitive to increases in the extent of the mesh beyond 10 km, or with reductions in point spacing below 1.0 km.
We analyzed data from all study areas simultaneously. In cases where study areas were \20 km apart, we verified that no individuals were detected on [1 study area. Study areas were modeled as groups or ''sessions'' in a multisession analysis that allowed data to be pooled across study areas to estimate g 0 and r (Efford et al. 2009). We assumed the total number of individuals was binomially-distributed on each study area. We estimated g 0 and r by maximizing the conditional likelihood for proximity detectors, and estimated density as a derived parameter using a Horvitz-Thompson-like estimator (see Borchers and Efford 2008;Efford et al. 2009). We used the half-normal form of the detection function, which we suspected would reasonably approximate the above-described home range characteristics of female black bears.
We defined a set of candidate models of variation in g 0 and r based on previously published information about the probabilities of detection, home ranges, and movements of black bears (Garshelis and Pelton 1980;Rogers 1987;Powell et al. 1997;Noyce et al. 2001;Koehler and Pierce 2003;Mowat et al. 2005;Obbard et al. 2010). We used the smallsample corrected version of Akaike's Information Criterion (AIC c ; Hurvitch and Tsai 1989) to identify the most parsimonious models in the candidate set. We assessed support for general and trap-specific responses to prior detection affecting g 0 , (hereafter denoted b and bk, respectively) and differences in g 0 among individuals (h), years, and study areas. For r, we considered differences among individuals, sampling occasions (t), years, study areas, and 4 different patterns of variation among habitat types. Individual heterogeneity was modeled using two-point finite mixture distributions (Pledger 2000;Borchers and Efford 2008). Three of the habitat type covariates used Rowe's (1972) Forest Regions to ascribe study areas to different habitat types; the fourth used Ecoprovince boundaries (''ECOP''; Marshall et al. 1998; see Fig. 1). Habitat productivity for black bears is superior in eastern GLSL than Boreal Forests (Rowe 1972;Kolenosky 1990;Obbard and Howe 2008). We hypothesized that r would be smaller in GLSL than Boreal Forest Regions, and might also vary between eastern and western GLSL Forests, and that bears in the Lake of the Woods and Southern Boreal Shield Ecoprovinces might have lower r than those in the Mid-Boreal Shield. The simplest habitat covariate (FR2) had two levels, and discriminated only between Boreal and GLSL Forests. FR3 further separated eastern from western GLSL forests. FR3I combined eastern and western GLSL forests, but included a separate ''intermediate'' level for study areas that fell within 10 km of the Forest Region boundary. We fit a total of 76 models. The most constrained models in the candidate set were the null model and models with each form of variation in isolation. The most general model had 173 parameters and allowed for study area-specific g 0 and r, and study area-specific differences among individuals (equivalent to fitting a model with h affecting g 0 and r to each study area-specific data set). The most general additive model included differences in g 0 among individuals, after initial detection, and among study areas, and differences in r among sampling occasions, individuals and study areas. Model fitting was prohibitively time-consuming on a stand-alone desktop computer. To reduce the total number of models, we initially emphasized the simplest habitat covariate, and later crossed other habitat covariates with the bestsupported models of variation among individuals, years, sampling occasions, and in response to initial detection. We used the facilities of the high performance computing network ''SHARCNET'' (http://www.sharcnet.ca) to fit many models simultaneously. Integration meshes were generated using program DENSITY (version 4.4.5.1; Efford et al. 2004;Efford 2010); all other analyses were performed in the R programming environment version 2.15 (R Development Core Team 2012) using the ''secr'' package version 2.4.0 (Efford 2012).

[SECTION] field sampling and dna analysis
The number of hair samples collected on each study area ranged from 104 to 860, from which we obtained 38 to 352 genetic detections (including multiple detections of the same individual at the same trap and occasion; Table 1). The number of unique females detected on each study area ranged from 6 to 34, and the total number of detections of females included in spatially explicit encounter histories (i.e., excluding multiple detections of the same individual at the same trap and occasion) ranged from 13 to 93 (Table 1). The mean of maximum distances moved among traps ranged from 881 to 5459 m, and the mean distance between successive detection locations ranged from 352 to 2677 m (Table 1).

[SECTION] data analysis
Models of detection heterogeneity that minimized AIC c included a trap-specific response to initial detection and differences among individuals and years affecting g 0 , and differences in r among individuals, years, sampling occasions, and habitat types (Table 2). Model selection uncertainty was limited to whether r differed among years, and which habitat type covariate best approximated variation in r among study areas (Table 2). Models with study area specific g 0 and r were not supported (Table 2). The top-ranked model that excluded h in either parameter (DAIC c = 108) had the same structure otherwise as the top-ranked model. The most general model, with study area-specific g 0 , r, and effects of h, had DAIC c = 409. Variance calculation failed when this model was fit, and parameter estimates for some study areas were not identifiable or were at a boundary. The null model ranked last (DAIC c = 439).
Densities estimated from the top 8 AIC c -ranked models (Rw i = 1.00) were similar in magnitude (mean D across study areas estimated from 1st-8th ranked models, respectively = 11.9, 12.2, 11.2, 11.0, 9.8, 9.4, 12.1, and 11.3), precision (mean CV across study areas = 0.27 from all 4 models that included differences in r among years, and = 0.26 from models that did not), and the pattern of variation among study areas (Spearman's rank correlation coefficients from pairwise comparisons of D ranged from 0.903 to 0.986). Correlations among estimates from different models were strongest, ranging from 0.976 to 0.986, for the top 4 AIC c -ranked models (Rw i = 0.94). D from supported models ranged from 3 to 30 females aged [1 year/100 km 2 and was generally higher in more productive habitat, but variable in eastern GLSL forests (Fig. 2).
Densities estimated from high-ranking models were similar because these models all had a similar structure. However, D varied when different forms of variation in g 0 and r were modeled (Table 3). Individual heterogeneity increased D and reduced its precision, but the effect size was smaller where other forms of variation were also included in the estimating model (Table 3). Forest region and year effects altered the pattern of variation in D among study areas. For example, lower r in GLSL Forests than in Boreal Forests was associated with higher D in the former (Tables 3,4). Differences in g 0 among years reduced D on study areas sampled in all years other than 2006, and differences in r among years increased D in 2006 relative to estimates from models without year effects (Table 3). Models with study area effects yielded density estimates which differed considerably from estimates from supported models in some cases (Table 3), and were relatively imprecise (mean CV across study areas from the highestranking model with study area effects on either parameter = 0.39). Effects of initial detection on g 0 , and variation in r among sampling occasions had little effect on D here (Table 3).
Parameter estimates from high-ranking models showed that g 0 increased in response to initial detection at the same trap (Table 4). Animals traveled farther to encounter traps in Boreal than GLSL forests; bears on study areas within 10 km of the forest region boundary had intermediate r (Table 4). Parameter estimates from the highest-ranked models with ECOP and FR3 covariates indicated that r was lower in the Lake of the Woods Ecoprovince than in the Southern Boreal Shield, and in Western than Eastern GLSL Forests (b SBS = 0.089, SE 0.061, b MBS = 0.335, SE 0.086; b GLSL E = -0.069, SE 0.063, b GLSL W = -0.187, SE 0.078). Bears also traveled farther on successive sampling occasions during the first 5 weeks of sampling (the estimate of r on occasion 6 was based on data from only 3 study areas and was imprecisely estimated; Table 4). Models with differences in r among years indicated that bears did not travel as far to encounter traps in 2006 as in other years (Table 4) Year effects indicated and that g 0 was highest in 2008 and lowest in 2006 (Table 3). Year effects were imprecise except in the case of lower g 0 in 2006 (Table 4).
Approximately 13 % of individuals were assigned to the 2nd mixture of individuals with higher g 0 and r than other individuals (Table 4). Point estimates of g 0 from the top AIC c -ranked model for the first mixture of individuals were 0.29 in 2008 and 0.10 in 2006, but increased to 0.52 and 0.23 respectively after initial detection (Table 4). Estimates of the same parameters for the second mixture of individuals were 0.64 in 2008 and 0.34 in 2006, and 0.82 and 0.56 after initial detection. Point estimates of r on occasion 5 in 2008 for the first mixture of individuals were 1395 m in GLSL forests, 1876 m in Boreal forests, and 1539 m on study areas within 10 km of the Forest Region boundary; concurrent estimates for the second mixture were 2040, 2743, and 2250 m (Table 3).

[SECTION] material and methods

[SECTION] study sites
Otter faeces (spraints) and data on fish stocks were collected along two salmonid streams in the province of Lower Austria: a) Kleiner Kamp and b) Große Ysper (Fig. 1). The studied area covered 18.3 km of Kleiner Kamp and 21.5 km of Große Ysper (Fig. 1,   1). As studies on otter distribution indicate both sites are representing riverine habitats, which have been repopulated by otters for more than 20 years (Kranz, 1995;Kranz et al., 2001;Kranz and Poledník, 2009). Furthermore, both study sites are situated within the siliceous Bohemian mountains and have similar stream widths and flow regimes (Table 1) (Fink et al., 2000;Haunschmid and Weiss, 2005). Existence of surrounding water bodies, notably fishponds, is comparable between the study sites, both in number and density. According to the longitudinal zonation of running waters (Illies, 1961) and the ichthyological classification, the river stretches investigated belong to the epi-and metarhithral. Thus, the native fish fauna is dominated by brown trout (Salmo trutta) and bullhead (Cottus gobio).
Besides considering hydromorphological comparability as described above, these two study sites were chosen because of differences in fisheries management practices. Kleiner Kamp undergoes a sustainable, ecologically oriented management including the abandonment of stocking fish and harvest regulations considering natural productivity (annual average fish harvest about 0.3 kg/km (G. Unfer, personal observation, 2014). In the fishing beats of Große Ysper hatchery fish are stocked periodically during the fishing season from April to September. Usually brown trout, rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) and brook trout (Salvelinus fontinalis) in catchable sizes (>250 mm total length) are released. All three species are stocked in equal proportions and the total annual amount of stocked fish ranges from 25 to 45 kg/km, the average fish harvest, i.e. fish caught by angling, is about 3 kg/km (A. Pöcksteiner, personal communication, 2011).
Brown trout as the dominant species in our study sites particularly requires structures along the riverbanks, which provide shelter and hardly frequent open water zones in streams (Armstrong et al., 2003;Klemetsen et al., 2003). Accordingly, to supply their needs otters have to adapt the shape of home ranges to given habitat conditions (Ó Néill et al., 2009). Therefore, we chose to present otter densities and fish biomass in oligotrophic salmonid streams per stream kilometre.

[SECTION] sample collection and dna extraction
Otter spraints were collected along the watercourse on sand banks, rocks, tributary outfalls or banks under bridges. Sampling points were defined considering an equal spatial distribution along the investigated river sections, and finally recorded using a global positioning system unit. We visited these points during three sampling periods for each study site between February and mid April 2011. One sampling period consisted of five consecutive days and all sampling points of one study site were checked daily for fresh spraints from the previous night. To minimise DNA degradation and to maximise DNA amplification success, sampling was carried out mainly during morning hours in cold months (Coxon et al. 1999;Nsubuga et al. 2004;Hájková et al., 2006;Lampa et al., 2008). To avoid cross-contamination only spraints that had no physical contact with other spraints were collected. Samples were stored in plastic tubes with 30 ml of a nucleic acid stabilising reagent (3.53 M ammonium sulphate, 13.3 mM EDTA, 16.6 mM sodium citrate, adjusted to pH 5.2 with 1 M sulphuric acid) and frozen at -20 • C.
DNA extraction was carried out subsequently after every study period. Faecal DNA was extracted using the QIAmp DNA Stool Mini Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) following the manufacturer's protocol with slight modifications: increase of final incubation time to 5 min before elution of the DNA extract.

[SECTION] dna quantification, identification of otter individuals and pedigree analysis
To ensure cost-and time-effectiveness as well as data quality we rejected genotyping error-prone samples by exclusion of samples containing target DNA in very low concentrations. Therefore we quantified target DNA in the extracts applying quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) using a SYBR Greenbased assay in a LightCycler 1.0 Instrument (Roche Applied Science, Mannheim, Germany) and the primer system LutRT2, following the protocol of Hausknecht et al. (2010). An absolute quantification was performed with an external calibration curve obtained from three-fold quantification of 17 standards with known DNA concentrations of the target species. Subsequently we determined the DNA concentration of extracts using the equation in Morin et al. (2001) and excluded samples containing <5 pg/L DNA in the extract from further analyses.
Samples were genotyped at 11 microsatellite loci established by Dallas and Piertney (1998) : Lut435, Lut457, Lut615, Lut701, Lut717,  Lut833 (set 1) andLut453, Lut604, Lut715, Lut733, Lut832 (set  2). All amplifications were performed in 15 L reactions containing 7.5 L 2× Qiagen Multiplex PCR Master Mix (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany), 0.04 g/L bovine serum albumin (Fermentas, St. Leon-Rot, Germany), 0.2 pmol/L of each primer and 2.5 L template DNA. Microsatellites were amplified in two multiplex PCRs using the following protocol: initial denaturation for 15 min at 95 • C followed by 40 cycles (30 s at 94 • C, 90 s at 55 • C (set 1)/56 • C (set 2), 60 s at 72 • C) and a final extension step for 30 min at 60 • C. Forward primers were labelled with a fluorescent dye (6-FAM, HEX or TAMRA). Fragment length analysis was performed on an ABI Prism ® 377 DNA sequencer (Perkin Elmer, Rodgau, Germany). Genotyping data were analysed using GENESCAN 3.1.2 and GENOTYPER 2.5 software (Applied Biosystems ® , Foster City, USA).
Initially the selected samples were amplified independently in triplicates for all loci and up to 6 additional PCR reactions were performed to determine a sample's consensus genotype if necessary. We accepted a heterozygote genotype when each of both alleles was recorded in at least two independent PCRs and a homozygote genotype after at least three independent observations of a single allele. Accordingly we based the quantification of genotyping errors on consensus genotypes obtained from repeated genotyping. Frequency of allelic dropout (ADO) and false alleles (FA) were computed using the equations in Broquet and Petit (2004) and rates for PCR amplification success, ADO and FA were calculated for each locus across all samples and for each sample across all loci. The probability of identity (P ID ) and probability of identity for siblings (P IDsibs ), which is a more conservative upper bound for the probability of identity (Taberlet and Luikart, 1999;Waits et al., 2001), were calculated using the software GIMLET (Valière, 2002). We used the software GenAlEx 6.5 (Peakall andSmouse, 2006, 2012) to characterise genetic variation within the study sites providing  2).
For sex identification we amplified a part of the SRY locus (Dallas et al., 2000) and the microsatellite Lut832 as a positive PCR control for female samples in a multiplex PCR. A 15 L reaction was performed consisting of 1.5 L PCR buffer, 0.2 mM dNTPs, 3 mM MgCl 2 , 0.04 g/L bovine serum albumin, 0.08 U/L FIREPol ® DNA Polymerase (Solis Biodyne, Tartu, Estonia), 0.2 pmol/L of the microsatellite locus primers, 0.4 pmol/L for Lut-SRY primers and 2 L of template DNA. The PCR programme used: initial denaturation for 3 min at 94 • C, 40 cycles (30 s at 94 • C, 90 s at 53 • C, 30 s at 72 • C) and a final extension step for 3 min at 72 • C.
Individuals defined by assigning a unique multilocus genotype derived from microsatellite and SRY analysis were tested for possible parent-offspring combinations by the complete exclusion method based on Mendelian rules of inheritance. We compared multilocus genotypes to each other and parent-offspring combinations were rejected if a candidate parent does not share at least one allele with the offspring at any locus under consideration (Jones et al., 2010).
We additionally estimated population sizes by capture-markrecapture (CMR) analysis using the programme CAPWIRE (Miller et al., 2005) to evaluate if the detected otter individuals represent the populations adequately in both study sites. This software takes into account multiple capture events per sampling occasion. Otter population size was calculated separately for each study site. A "recapture" was recorded whenever an identical genotype was found in another DNA sample. A likelihood ratio test (p < 0.05) was used to choose between two models concerning capture heterogeneity: the even capture probability model (ECM) and the two innate rates model (TIRM). Confidence intervals were estimated using a parametric bootstrap procedure.

[SECTION] prey fish populations
Size and composition of prey fish populations were estimated based on electrofishing data obtained for stream sections at Kleiner Kamp between 2006 and 2011 and at Große Ysper between 2003 and 2008 (Fig. 1). Although the data sets cover different time periods a comparison is legitimate because in both streams fisheries management did not change throughout the whole period investigated. Sampling stretches (lengths range from 80 to 198 m) were selected to be representative according to habitat distribution. By weighting a representative amount of fish individuals of every length cohort a length-weight relationship formula was created for body mass calculation. All data on fish originated from autumn samplings. For each data set fish biomass was estimated according to DeLury (1951) or Seber and Le Cren (1967), depending on the number of electrofishing runs per stretch. By exploratory data analysis we compared the fish biomass between the studied streams to ascertain tendencies of differences in food availability for otters caused by stocking and tested for differences applying a Mann-Whitney-U-test. Moreover we show length frequency distribution for the dominant species brown trout to analyse population structure for both studied streams.

[SECTION] quality of samples and characteristics of genetic markers
DNA was extracted from a total of 164 otter spraints (68 samples from the study site Kleiner Kamp, 96 from Große Ysper). 77 samples (46.9%) were excluded after DNA quantification as they contained <5 pg/L target DNA. 81 of the samples left were genotyped successfully for all microsatellite loci (i.e. 49.4% of all collected faeces): 33 samples for study site Kleiner Kamp and 48 for Große Ysper. Another 6 samples were rejected due to incomplete genotypes.
Overall all microsatellite loci were polymorphic with the number of alleles per locus ranging from 2 to 5. Expected heterozygosity ranged between 0.48 and 0.53 and observed heterozygosity ranged from 0.54 to 0.61 for the two study sites, respectively (Table 2). These values correspond well to those of values of related studies (e.g. Janssens et al., 2008;Hájková et al., 2009;Honnen et al., 2011). Mean PCR success rate across all loci was 92.0%. Mean frequency of ADO per locus varied from 8.3% for Lut435 to 23.3% for Lut833. FA were recorded with a frequency from 0.3% for Lut715 up to 6.5% for Lut435. P ID and P IDsibs for eleven microsatellite markers based on allele frequencies in our data set were 6.45 × 10 -8 and 1.38 × 10 -3 respectively.

[SECTION] otter numbers and sex identification
Successfully genotyped samples revealed 6 different genotypes (K1-K6) for the study site Kleiner Kamp. From these we identified 3 male otters, 2 females, one not specified. At the study site Große Ysper 8 different otter individuals (Y1-Y8) were detected -3 males and 5 females (Fig. 2). The number of genotyped faeces per individual varied from 1 to 17 (Fig. 2), indicating considerable capture heterogeneity among individuals.
Using the likelihood ratio test for capture heterogeneity, for both study sites the TIRM model was selected (with p = 0.031 for Kleiner Kamp and p = 0.00 for Große Ysper). The CAPWIRE point estimate of population size for Kleiner Kamp site was 6 otters with a 95% confidence interval of zero. This perfectly coincides with the number of detected genotypes. For the second study site Große Ysper the population size estimate generated by CAPWIRE was 8 individuals with an upper confidence boundary of 9 otter individuals. The CAPWIRE point estimate as well as the lower confidence boundary corresponds to the number of genotypes obtained.

[SECTION] spatial and social organisation and densities of resident otters
Among the 14 identified otter individuals 11 were detected over the entire sampling time. They were defined as resident animals. Hence, there were 4 resident otters at study site Kleiner Kamp and 7 residents at study site Große Ysper (Fig. 2). Individuals represented only in a single sampling period and not fitting into the pedigree of resident otters were defined as transient animals.
The stream lengths between the outermost detection points represent minimum home ranges for each otter individual. The spatial distribution found suggests a typical spacing pattern for mustelids (Powell, 1979) with hardly overlapping intrasexual territories and territory overlap between sexes. However, we observed high territory overlaps between individuals of the same sex for Y1/Y4 (♂) and Y5/Y6 (♀). Complete exclusion for parentage analysis based on microsatellite data revealed an existing family group with Y1 and Y5 as parents of two offspring, Y4 and Y6.
We determined otter numbers per stream length using the numbers of otter individuals identified within each study site (Table 1). Focusing on the numbers of resident otters, we found a one-third higher otter density for Große Ysper, the study site where intensive fish stocking is carried out.

[SECTION] fish biomass and population status
Population structure of fish sizes of brown trout indicated natural reproduction and no deficits in the year-class abundances (Fig. 3). According to regions of the epi-and metarhithral fish species composition is dominated by brown trout regarding the fish biomass (Kleiner Kamp: mean 81.5%, Große Ysper: mean 95.1%) as well as abundance (data not shown). For the study site Kleiner Kamp other stock building species bullhead, burbot (Lota lota) and grayling (Thymallus thymallus) were recorded, which made up to 49.5% of fish biomass depending on the stream section. At Große Ysper bullheads were registered as second stock building species.
Despite intensive stocking at Große Ysper, specimen of rainbow trout and brook trout were missing completely or were detected only by single captures. Additionally the proportion of catchable sized brown trout did not differ between the streams (U = 38, p = 0.857) and averaged 28.4% of brown trout biomass in Kleiner Kamp and 27.1% in Große Ysper (Table 3). Comparing fish biomass of all fish species and sizes per year a tendency for a higher fish biomass for study site Große Ysper was recorded, which however, cannot be referred to stocking measures of catchable sized fish (see Fig. 3).



====================================================================================================
FILE: American J Primatol - 2015 - Basabose - Estimation of chimpanzee community size and genetic diversity in Kahuzi‐Biega.grobid.tei.xml
====================================================================================================
[SECTION] methods

[SECTION] study area
Kahuzi-Biega is one of the largest national parks of the DRC with an area of 6,000 km 2 . It is divided into two sectors: a lowland sector of approximately 5,400 km 2 , ranging at an altitude between 600 and 1,800 m and covered with lowland moist evergreen forest; and a highland sector of approximately 600 km 2 , with an altitude of 1,800-3,308 m and covered with montane forest. The montane forest is connected to the lowland rain forest through a narrow ecological corridor that is 20 km long and 4 km wide (Fig. 1). This ecological corridor has been permanently encroached upon by illegal farming and ore mining [Yamagiwa et al., 2012], resulting in severe habitat disturbance, which may prevent chimpanzees from moving freely between the two forest blocks.
The study area spreads over approximately 80 km 2 of montane forest along the eastern edge of the highland sector of Kahuzi-Biega at an altitude of 2,050-2,350 m above the sea level (Fig. 1).

[SECTION] focal subjects
The Kaboko chimpanzee community in the highland sector of Kahuzi-Biega National Park has been under continuous study since 1994 without complete habituation [Basabose, 2002[Basabose, , 2004[Basabose, , 2005;;Basabose & Yamagiwa, 1997, 2002].
Based on individual identification during daily monitoring, Basabose [2005] counted 23 individuals, including eight adult and adolescent males, seven adult and adolescent females, and eight immature individuals including three infants, which was assumed to constitute the Kaboko community. Recently, two newborn infants were observed within the community, bringing the estimated population to 25 individuals at the time of beginning this research [Basabose, unpublished data].

[SECTION] ethics
This research adheres to the American Society of Primatologists (ASP) Principles for Ethical Treatment of Non-human Primates. The study complies with the protocols of the National Strategy for the Conservation of Biodiversity in protected areas in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), which is an integral part of the Act No. 11/009 of July 9, 2011 establishing fundamental principles for environment protection in DRC. The study was conducted under the framework of the existing long-term formal collaboration between two Congolese public institutions (the Centre de Recherche en Sciences Naturelles de Lwiro and Kahuzi-Biega National Park).

[SECTION] genetic sampling
Chimpanzee fecal samples were collected in the study area (Fig. 1). Samples were only obtained from nest sites encountered opportunistically when routinely tracking fresh chimpanzee trails between October 2011 and June 2013. At all nest sites, only feces estimated to be 1-2 days old were sampled. Only tree nests confirmed to have been used by chimpanzees (presence of fresh feces) were sampled and only fecal samples found in or beneath a night tree nest were collected. One fresh fecal sample per nest was collected at each nest site. However, fresh smaller dung found within the nest of an older individual (based on larger feces diameter) was sampled separately and recorded as presumptive feces from an unweaned infant who might have shared the nest with the mother.
The surface of the feces was scraped and placed in 2 mL of lysis buffer containing 0.5% SDS, 100 mM EDTA (pH 8.0), 100 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), and 10 mM NaCl before extracting DNA [Hayaishi & Kawamoto, 2006]. In total, 279 fecal samples were collected at 51 different nest sites. The geographic coordinates of each sampled nest site were recorded using a Garmin GPS unit for mapping the nest site locations (Fig. 1).

[SECTION] dna extraction, sex genotyping, and individual identification
We extracted genomic DNA from the fecal samples using the QIAamp DNA Stool Mini Kit (Qiagen, Tokyo, Japan) according to the protocol provided by the manufacturer with minor modifications. DNA extracted from noninvasive samples, and especially from fecal samples, is typically degraded and at a low concentration [Inoue et al., 2007;Morin et al., 2001;Taberlet et al., 1996]. To ensure accurate genotyping, we quantified the amount of DNA per sample using a Thermal Cycler Dice Real Time System (TaKaRa, Shiga, Japan) as described by Inoue et al. [2007]. Only samples with >100 pg/mL of DNA were used because allelic dropout rarely happens when using such templates for autosomal microsatellite analysis [Inoue et al., 2007;Morin et al., 2001].
To confirm the sex of an individual, two to four independent PCR amplifications were performed for a segment of the amelogenin locus, which is located in the X-Y homologous region and checked by capillary electrophoresis [Bradley et al., 2001]. Am. J. Primatol.
We prepared three primer sets for 17 STR markers [Arandjelovic et al., 2011;Bradley et al., 2000;Inoue et al., 2008]: set 1 (D16s2624, D5s1457, D5s1470, D1s2130, D18s851, D12s66, and D4s1627); set 2 (D7s817, D1s550, D10s1432, D14s306 , andD8s1106); andset 3 (D2s1329, D11s2002, D9s910,  D3s2459, andD6s1056) as shown in Table I. PCR amplification of each DNA extract was carried out in 5 mL reactions containing 200 nM of each primer, 2.5 mL of QIAGEN Multiplex PCR Master Mix (Qiagen), and 2 mL of DNA template. After an initial incubation at 95°C for 15 min, PCR amplification was performed for 45 cycles consisting of denaturation at 94°C for 30 s, annealing at 57°C for 30 s, and extension at 72°C for 30 s, and a final extension at 60°C for 30 min. The amplification products were separated by capillary electrophoresis using an ABI 3130xl genetic analyzer (Applied Biosystems, Forest City, CA). Allele sizes were manually determined using Peak Scanner Software v1.0 (Applied Biosystems). Samples with any ambiguous results were excluded from the analysis as a conservative measure to avoid any case of contamination that might have happened before and/or during data collection in the field. Inoue et al. (2007) found a 3% allelic dropout rate for extracts containing >100 pg/mL DNA and we used this rate to calculate the number of repetitions necessary to correctly determine homozygous genotypes with 99% certainty. Using this approach, two replications (0.03) 2 were found to be sufficient for samples with more than 100 pg/mL DNA template. As a precaution, we assigned a sample as homozygous at any STR locus if the same allele was exclusively seen in at least three replicate PCRs, and as heterozygous if seen in at least two replicates.
To discriminate individuals, we performed at least three independent PCR amplifications of all samples that contained >100 pg DNA using primer set 1. Using GenAlEx v6.41 [Peakall & Smouse, 2006], we calculated the probability of identity between sibs (PIsibs) [Waits et al., 2001] in order to evaluate whether primer set 1 was adequate for individual discrimination between close relatives. The number of matched and mismatched loci among all genotypes was calculated using CERVUS software [Marshall et al., 1998]. Genotypes from different samples that mismatched at one or two loci were re-examined for possible genotyping errors and in some samples (see results in detail) additional genotyping using primer set 2 was undertaken to resolve any ambiguities. We performed one independent PCR with all the other samples using primer set 2 to confirm the identification from primer set 1. We then assigned a consensus ID to each genotype.
In order to evaluate genetic diversity, we picked one sample for each consensus ID and performed at least three independent PCRs using primer sets 2 and 3. The number of alleles (Na), expected and observed heterozygosities (H E and H O ), inbreeding coefficient (F IS ), and deviations from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (HWE) were calculated using GenAlEx.
The community size was estimated using a genetic mark-recapture model that assumed a closed population and utilized individual genotypes collected from one or more nest sites. Before estimating community size, we checked that all samples were derived from the same community using a nest network analysis. We assumed that samples collected from the same nest site were from the same community. The network was constructed from data on nest site sharing using UCINET 6 [Borgatti et al., 2002]. This analysis can reveal whether all collected samples are derived from the same community.
Capwire software [Miller et al., 2005] was used to estimate population size with the two-innate rate method (TIRM). We calculated 95% confidence intervals (CIs). TIRM has previously been assumed in similar studies to be a conservative estimator [Arandjelovic et al., 2010[Arandjelovic et al., , 2011;;Puechmaille & Petit, 2007].

[SECTION] y-chromosome microsatellites
We analyzed 11 Y-STR loci in all 13 males [Erler et al., 2004;Eriksson et al., 2006;Gusmão et al., 2002;Langergraber et al., 2007]. Two Y-STR primer sets were prepared: set 1 with a mix of six primers (DYs439, DYs469, DYs533, DYs 562, DYs632, and DYs520) and set 2 with a mix of five primers (DYs588, DYs510, DYs517, DYs612, and DYs630). Three to four PCRs were performed and genotyping procedures were the same as that for autosomal STR loci.

[SECTION] mitochondrial dna
A 455-base pair segment of the mitochondrial hypervariable control (D-loop) region was amplified with PCR using L16041 (5 0 -CTCTGTTCTTTCAT GGGGAAGC-3 0 ) as the forward primer and H16498 (5 0 -CCTGAAGTAGGAACCAGATG-3 0 ) as the reverse primer [Eriksson et al., 2004;Morin et al., 1994]. PCR amplification was carried out in reaction volumes of 15 mL containing a mixture of 150 mM of each dNTP, 200 nM of each primer, 0.5 U Expand High Fidelity enzyme mix (Expand High Fidelity PCR Systems, Roche Diagnostics K.K., Tokyo, Japan), 0.2 mL of T4 gene 32 protein (Nippon Gene, Tokyo, Japan), and 2 mL of template DNA. After an initial incubation at 95°C for 5 min, PCR amplification was performed for 45 cycles consisting of denaturation at 94°C for 30 s, annealing at 50°C for 30 s, and extension at 72°C for 30 s, and a final extension at 72°C for 30 min. The PCR products were purified using ExoSAP-IT (USB Corporation, Cleveland, OH), sequenced using a Big Dye Terminator ver. 3.1 cycle sequencing kit (Applied Biosystems), and then electrophoresed on an Applied Biosystems 3130xl Genetic Analyzer (Applied Biosystems). Accession numbers for the mitochondrial sequences are AB924650-AB924658 in the DNA Data Bank of Japan (DDBJ).

[SECTION] comparison of genetic diversity in eastern chimpanzee populations
We used Arlequin 3.5.1.2 [Excoffier & Lischer, 2010] to calculate both Y-STR and mtDNA D-loop haplotype diversity [H; Nei, 1987]. We also compared diversity in mtDNA D-loops and Y-STRs of the eastern chimpanzee (Pan troglodytes schweinfurthii) populations from four communities in Uganda [Langergraber et al., 2007] and Mahale, Tanzania [Inoue et al., 2013;Inoue, in press]. For Y-STRs, we also included data from Ugalla, Tanzania [Moore & Vigilant, 2014b] and Gishwati, Rwanda [Chancellor et al., 2012]. For STR loci, the number of alleles (Na) and observed heterozygosities (H O ) in this study were compared with the data of Sonso, Uganda [Lukas et al., 2005], Mahale, Tanzania [Inoue et al., 2008], and Ugalla, Tanzania [Moore & Vigilant, 2014b]. We used the four STR loci (D2s1329, D5s1470, D7s817, and D11s2002) that were analyzed in all four regions and compared the averages of the values.

[SECTION] individual identification
In total, 164 samples successfully yielded genotypes using STR primer set 1. The majority of samples (93.3%) were genotyped at all seven loci and the average proportion of loci genotyped was 0.989. Only five (4.9%) and three (1.8%) samples were genotyped at 6 and 5 loci, respectively. From the 164 samples, we identified 32 individuals, comprising 19 females and 13 males.
In cases where genotypes at all examined loci matched, the number of examined loci was 6 in 56 pairs and 7 in 818 pairs. PIsibs values in these cases were less than 5.0 Â 10 À3 . This implies that it is highly likely that these pairs are derived from the same individuals. The number of examined loci was five or fewer in the other 11 cases, including samples C141, C177, and C248 (Table II). In such cases, the genotype of STR set 2 (as indicated in Table II) was determined with at least three additional independent PCRs and the samples were then confirmed to be derived from the same individuals with low PIsibs values (less than 1.0 Â 10 À3 ).
There were four cases where the genotype of STR set 1 was mismatched at 2 of 6 loci. However, in such cases, the genotype of each sample was heterozygous at the two mismatched loci, implying that these mismatches could not be explained by allelic dropout, which is one of the most common genotyping errors. There was one case with genotype mismatching at 2 of 3 loci (C177 and C248, Table II). We genotyped loci of STR set 2 using those two samples and found four other mismatched loci in STR set 2 (Table II). In all other cases, the number of mismatched loci was three or more. In those cases, the samples are confirmed to be derived from different individuals.
The genotype result from one independent PCR using STR set 2 was investigated to confirm the individual discrimination from STR set 1. In all sample pairs that were determined to be derived from different individuals by STR set 1, two or more mismatched loci were found using STR set 2. In sample pairs determined to be derived from the same individuals by STR set 1, there were no mismatched loci from STR set 2, except for the pairs that included samples C121 and C233. In such pairs, one mismatched locus was found, which could be explained by allelic dropout of C121 at locus D1s550 and of C233 at locus D10s1432. Given that a 3% allelic dropout may apply to our samples, these results suggest that our subsequent analyses based on individual discrimination determined by STR set 1 were reliable.

[SECTION] number of individuals in the community
All individuals except one (ID 11) shared at least one nest site, and network analysis based on nest site sharing data showed that all these individuals belonged to the same community (Fig. 2). The fecal sample from ID 11 was found only once in a nest site comprising three nests. Samples from the other two nests within this site had small amounts of DNA (less than 100 pg/mL) and were excluded from the analysis. However, the genotype of one of the excluded samples was determined for 11 of the 12 STR loci (sets 1 and 2) in three independent replicates of the PCR; these genotyped loci gave identical results to individual ID 10 (Fig. 2). If this sample with its small amount of DNA is included in the analysis, then all the genotyped individuals are linked.
The number of individuals detected in the nesting sites varied from one to 12 (mean ¼ 3.6 AE SD 3.2) over the entire sampling period. Throughout the study period, only eight individuals (25%),  Ã For these samples, genotypes of STR set 2 were determined with at least three independent PCR amplifications including the two individuals thought to be infants from their small dung size (diameter <2 cm), were sampled in only one nest site. Using the data on the number of samples, Capwire estimated that the community totaled 36 members (95%CI ¼ 32-42).

[SECTION] autosomal str diversity
Information from 17 STR loci is shown in Table I. With one exception (D10s1432), the loci conformed to the Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. Expected heterozygosity was high (average: 0.756) and F IS was negative on average.

[SECTION] y-str haplotype diversity
Only three polymorphic loci were found among the 11 Y-STR loci examined. Five different haplotypes were found among the 13 males; haplotype A was the most common, being present in nine individuals (Fig. 3). Each of the four other haplotypes was present in only one male. Haplotype diversity was estimated as 0.54 AE SD 0.16.

[SECTION] mitochondrial dna d-loop diversity
The samples from the 32 identified individuals yielded a total of nine unique mtDNA haplotypes. In contrast to the Y-haplotype, no single haplotype dominated, although nine individuals (28%) shared haplotype F (Fig. 3). MtDNA haplotype diversity was estimated as 0.86 AE SD 0.03.

[SECTION] community size estimation
Reliable estimates of population size are vital for conservation and successful management of wild animals [McKechnie et al., 2007;van Schaik et al., 1995]. We used a non-invasive genetic method in the present study and found that the Kaboko chimpanzee community in the montane forest of Kahuzi-Biega National Park comprised at least 32 individuals (19 females and 13 males). A Capwire analysis produced an estimate of 36 individuals (95%CI ¼ 32-42) for the community. The estimate produced by the genetic census was somewhat higher than that from direct observation (about 25 individuals). The estimate by direct observation without complete habituation may be underestimated because chimpanzees live in fission-fusion society [Nishida, 1968] and it is difficult to observe some peripheral females and their infants [Langergraber et al., 2014a]. For the estimate by genetic analysis, we need to consider that 21 months sampling period might violate the assumption of a closed population for Capwire analysis, and thus the number by genetic estimation might be somewhat overestimated although the rate of birth, mortality, immigration, and emigration is relatively low in chimpanzees [Nishida et al., 2003]. However, in comparison with direct observation, the genetic-based estimate might be presumed to provide a realistic assessment of the population size. Moreover, the genetic estimation method provides a true minimum of the number of individuals during the sampling period as it is based on the number of genotypes present in the samples.
We estimated population size of a chimpanzee community with the two-innate rate model (TIRM) which assume a population comprising two groups of individuals with distinct capture probabilities [Miller et al., 2005]. Inoue et al. [2007] reported that it is difficult to collect fecal samples from infant chimpanzees even when following habituated chimpanzees. Our result is consistent with this report. We genotyped two very small dung samples (diameter <2 cm) in our study and consider these individuals to be infants. Samples from these two individuals were encountered only once during the study period. It is also expected to have less chance to collect the samples from some peripheral females [Langergraber et al., 2014a]. These suggest sampling bias in chimpanzee population. Therefore, TIRM might be appropriate for estimating population size of chimpanzee communities.
Here, we used a noninvasive genetic markrecapture method, which assumed a closed population, to estimate with high accuracy the population size of a group-living species. For this approach to be successful, it may be important to consider the group to which genotyped individuals belong. Previous noninvasive genetic studies on chimpanzees were unable to confirm reliably that all collected samples were from individuals belonging to the same community. In a study on chimpanzee populations in Gabon, Arandjelovic et al. [2011] estimated community identity from Y-STR haplotypes and the location of the samples. Although a pattern of male philopatry and female-biased dispersal can enable assignment of an individual to a community on the basis of Y-STRs, there are limitations to this method in some populations. For example, there are normally several Y-STR haplotypes in one community, but some haplotypes are found in only a few males [Langergraber et al., 2007; this study]. In addition, previous studies have observed the transfer of a young male chimpanzee of about 5 years old with his mother in Mahale [Nishida et al., 1985;Takahata & Takahata, 1989]. Y-chromosome haplotype sharing between neighboring chimpanzee communities has been confirmed in Budongo Forest Reserve, Uganda [Langergraber et al., 2014b] and Mahale chimpanzee communities [Inoue, in press]. Consequently, shared Y-STRs may occur between neighboring chimpanzee communities, albeit rarely. These factors indicate the need for some caution when relying on Y-STR haplotypes to define a community.
In the present study, we used information on nest site sharing to identify the community. The nest site sharing analysis showed that all the genotyped individuals are linked if one sample with its small amount of DNA is included in the analysis. This suggests that the identified individuals are members of the same community and this probably leads to the narrow 95%CI of our estimate.

[SECTION] genetic diversity of kahuzi chimpanzees and conservation implications
We found high diversity in mtDNAs and low diversity of Y-chromosome haplotypes. One Y-chromosome haplotype was dominant in the Kaboko community, whereas no dominant haplotype was found for mitochondrial DNA. These results likely reflect male philopatry and female-biased dispersal patterns similar to other chimpanzee communities [Boesch & Boesch-Achermann, 2000;Goodall, 1986;Nishida et al., 1990].
Despite the minor differences observed between sites, Kahuzi chimpanzees have similar genetic diversity as other eastern chimpanzee populations (Table III). Although Y-STR diversity in Kahuzi chimpanzees was slightly lower than the average Y-STR diversity calculated for four chimpanzee communities in Uganda (Table III), the diversity in mitochondrial and autosomal microsatellites is still important for conservation of chimpanzees given that the communities have female-biased dispersal patterns. On the basis of mitochondrial D-loop and autosomal microsatellites, Kahuzi chimpanzees show comparable genetic diversity to their conspecific populations (Table III).
Although the corridor connecting highland and lowland sectors in Kahuzi has been continuously encroached upon in the last three decades by farmers and illegal ore mining concessionaires, the chimpanzees inhabiting the highland sector of Kahuzi-Biega National Park showed a high observed heterozygosity (H O ) and a negative inbreeding coefficient (F IS ). This suggests that the Kaboko community belongs to an outbreeding population. Female chimpanzees in the highland sector may have probably been transferred between communities. Moreover, previous genetic analyses suggested that gorillas may have traversed the corridor and entered into reproductive contact with the gorilla population ranging the lowland sector [Saltonstall et al., 1998]. The genetic diversity results found in this study might reflect the fact that the chimpanzee populations in the highland and lowland sectors have been in reproductive contact in the recent past, in a similar manner as the sympatric gorilla populations. This expectation is consistent with reports that a large part of the corridor that was untouched by poacherswas still used by gorillas and chimpanzees, as evidenced by the observation of their fresh nests prior to large-scale deforestation [Refisch, 1991]. In the Bossou chimpanzee community, where female immigration from other communities is limited, it has been reported that one mitochondrial haplotype is dominant and that the risk of losing mitochondrial diversity is high [Shimada et al., 2009]. Likewise, a chimpanzee population inhabiting the easternmost distribution of the chimpanzee range in dry and open habitat in Ugalla shows extremely low Y-chromosome haplotype diversity [Moore & Vigilant, 2014b] in comparison to other chimpanzee communities (Table III). It has been suggested that this low Ychromosome haplotype diversity could be the first indication of isolation and loss of genetic diversity in this population [Moore & Vigilant, 2014b]. In Kahuzi, genetic diversity is still relatively high and the status of the population is less threatened compared to Bossou and Ugalla chimpanzee populations. However, there has been extensive human activity in the corridor in Kahuzi. In the 1950s, villages were evacuated from the deep forest, but a few human settlements remain within the lowland sector near the park's corridor. Much of the Kahuzi corridor habitat has been subjected to large-scale and lowtechnology ore mining and timber cutting activities since the 1980s [Hall et al., 1998]. Recently, rampant deforestation due to illegal timber cutting, mineral mining, and cutting for agricultural fields has affected about 80% of the corridor, disturbing the movement of large forest dwelling mammals, including elephants and great apes, in and around the corridor. If the current ecological corridor becomes completely deforested, the small isolated chimpanzee population inhabiting the highland sector of Kahuzi will be highly susceptible to inbreeding in the short term and may suffer a limited evolutionary development [Keller & Waller, 2002;Lacy, 1997]. To ensure the long-term survival of Kahuzi chimpanzees, conservation efforts need to focus on restoring the ecological corridor connecting the highland and lowland sectors of the Kahuzi-Biega National Park. Such an effort would enable the continuation of regular reproductive contacts between the chimpanzee populations in the montane and lowland forests and, thereby, preserve viable genetic diversity in both populations.
More genetic studies are needed on the chimpanzee communities adjacent to the Kaboko community and on the chimpanzee population inhabiting the lowland sector of the park to get a more holistic understanding of the genetic structure of chimpanzee populations in the Kahuzi-Biega National Park.

FILE: Aquaculture Research - 2014 - Alonso - Non‐invasive fast real‐time PCR assay for detection of the enteric parasite.grobid.tei.xml
====================================================================================================
[SECTION] materials and methods

[SECTION] sample collection, storage and dna extraction
Whole juvenile turbot, S. maximus, and turbot caecum tissue infected by E. scophthalmi, were provided from a local farm in the north of Galicia (Insu ıña S.L, Spain). In both cases, the parasite was previously identified through ultrastructural studies by experts at the farm (Palenzuela et al. 2002). These samples were preserved and transported under refrigerated conditions until the isolation of the parasite at the laboratory.
Other parasites which can affect S. maximus were provided from the same local farm. Tetramicra brevifilum and Philasterides dicentrarchi were used to support the specificity of the developed methodology. These parasites were microscopically identified by the pathologist of the farm before the DNA extraction. These DNA were frozen at À80°C until used.
Different tissues samples from whole infected fish, such as fin, gills, intestine, kidney, liver, spleen tissues and the mucus obtained by scraping the skin of the fish, were analyzed to evaluate the presence of the parasite. Also, non-invasive samples were taken due to the importance of developing a method that allows detecting the parasite at the farm which does not imply sacrificing the fish. These samples consisted of blood, faeces and rectal swabs. Blood samples were obtained by puncturing the caudal vessels, and faeces samples were obtained from the tanks of the farm directly. To obtain the rectal samples, the fish were anaesthetized with benzocaine and a sterile swab was inserted into the anogenital pore by a slight motion. This procedure was performed assuring that no harm was caused to the fish. After sampling, fish was allowed to recover from the anaesthesia and were monitored in the subsequent days.
Furthermore, different methods of storage [dry, in 95% ethanol and in RNAlater â (Ambion, Life Technologies S.A., Madrid, Spain)], temperatures (at 4°C and À20°C) and shipment times (0, 7 and 21 days) were assessed to determine the cheapest and easiest way (while keeping the appropriate preservation of the sample) of sending samples to be analyzed from the farm to the laboratory. The methods of storing and sending samples are shown in Table 1.
DNA extractions from infected tissues, faeces and rectal swab were performed according to the protocol described by Lago, Herrero, Madriñ an, Vieites and Espiñeira ( 2011) with slight modifications. The modifications are as follows: extractions were carrying out from 500 mg of tissues and faeces, and for rectal samples, the swap tip was cut and directly used. UltraClean BloodSpin DNA isolation kit (MoBio Laboratories, Carlsbad, CA, USA) was employed for the DNA isolation from blood samples.
The quality and quantity of the DNA extractions were determined by measuring the absorbance at 260 nm and at 260/280 and at 234/260 ratios using a NanoDrop TM ND-1000 spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific, Madrid, Spain) (Winfrey, Rott & Wortman 1997). DNA extractions were stored at À80°C for subsequent tasks.
Design of a specific Real-Time PCR method to detect E. scophthalmi From the ssrRNA (18S rRNA) sequences obtained from the NCBI database (National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) 2002) AF411335 (E. scophthalmi), and EF126038 (S. maximus), two internal primers and a probe set specific for E. scophthalmi were designed with the Primer Express v 3.0 software (Applied Biosystems, Life Technologies S.A.): ENTEROMYX F (5′-GGC TTA ATT TGA CTC AAC A-3′), ENTEROMYX R (5′-CTC CAC CAA CTA AGA ACG-3′); and a labelled probe, ENTEROMYX PROBE (5′-6-FAM-CCA TGC ACC ACC AAT CAT TGT ATC AT-BHQ-1 -3′). The same region was selected to be used as an inhibitor control. This DNA extraction control allows the amplification of S. maximus with the same primers and a new probe (CONTROL ROD 1 5′-6-FAM-CAC CAC CAC CCA CAG AAT CG-BHQ-1 -3′) to check the correct extraction and the absence of inhibitor compounds in the sample. This probe was designed in the same way as described above and used with the same primer pair designed for the detection of E. scophthalmi.
For both primers/probe sets designed, PCR was performed in a total reaction volume of 20 lL containing 200 ng DNA template, 10 lL TaqMan Fast Advanced Master Mix (Applied Biosystems), the optimized amount of primers and probe, and molecular biology grade water (Eppendorf, Ib erica, Madrid, Spain) adjusted up to the final volume. Optimal amounts of primers and probe were evaluated by preparing a dilution series to determine the minimum concentrations giving the maximum DRn (normalized reporter, defined as emission intensity of reporter/Emission intensity of passive reference). First, forward and reverse primer concentrations of 50, 300, 500 and 900 nM were evaluated with a constant probe concentration of 50 nM. Following primer optimization, probe optimization was initiated using concentrations of 50-250 nM. The two primers/probe sets, were optimized independently. Independent optimization was necessary because they were used in different reactions.
The reaction was performed in triplicate on DNA samples in MicroAmp Optical 96-well reaction plates (Applied Biosystems) with MicroAmp optical caps (Applied Biosystems) in the ViiA TM 7 Real Time PCR System (Applied Biosystems). Amplification was carried out with the following cycling protocol: 95°C for 20 s, and 40 cycles each of 95°C for 1 s and 60°C for 20 s.

[SECTION] analytical specificity, detection limit (lod) and reproducibility of the real-time pcr assay
Specificity was calculated by testing the specific primers/probe set for E. scophthalmi on DNA extracts from some of the most important parasites affecting turbot (T. brevifilum and P. dicentrarchi) and on its host (S. maximus). Also, phylogenetic analyses were carried out to evaluate relationship between E. scophthalmi and other parasites, determined by 18S rRNA. The analyses included sequences from mixozoan species, typical intestinal parasites in fish (Cryptosporidium) and parasites affecting the turbot. Parasites' sequences used for analysis were obtained from the NCBI database with accession number: AY38260, JX090294, AB643794, AY382606, AY152747, AB553293, AY152750, AY152749, AB710384, AY078428, JX090293, AF414692, AY078429, JX090295, JQ974029, AF378347, AY152748, AB693043, FJ204246, EU440379, HM037787, HM037789, HM037789, FJ848877, AJ581916, DQ851568, U13829, AJ582061, AY688957, JX271832, AF411334, DQ448298, DQ139796, DQ127230, AF001579, DQ301509, and AF411335. The phylogenetic tree was created by the software Mega 4.0 using the Tamura-Nei model to calculate the genetic distances between sequences (Tamura, Dudley, Nei & Kumar 2007). The inference of the phylogenetic tree was carried out with the Neighbour-Joining method (Saitou & Nei 1987). The reliability of the clades formed at the species level in the tree was evaluated by means of a bootstrap test with 2000 replications.
Due to technical limitations that currently exist in purifying the parasite, the calculation of the detection limit of the methodology was carried out from dilutions made by scraping the content of the caecum of infected turbots. The dilutions were made in water and corresponded to 500, 100, 50, 25, 10, 5, 2, 1, 0.5 and 0.1 lL of the scraping of the caecum contents in a final volume of 500 lL. These preparations were mixed by vortex. All the dilutions were done in duplicate, and the methodology developed here was applied to a complete series.
To infer the limit of detection (LOD), parasites from the duplicate of the last tube of the series that tested positive were counted under a microscope using a Neubauer counting chamber. This quantification is necessary because the degree of infestation in the fish is highly variable and will determine the concentration of parasites in the dilutions and therefore the LOD reached by the methodology developed. The parasites were visualized by examination under oil immersion microscopy objective (10009). The number of parasites counted in five squares of the chamber, and the total parasites in the suspension were calculated according to general instructions of Neubauer chamber to recount of microorganisms. This procedure was repeated three times and the data presented as mean AE standard error.
The reproducibility of the RT-PCR assay was evaluated by testing multiple replicates of the standard control material. Each intra-and interassay was performed to evaluate its reproducibility: two analysts; three samples (with two replicates in each assay); three different days. The mean (M), standard deviation (SD), and coefficient of variation (CV) of the cycle threshold values were calculated. The CV values were calculated as the standard deviation (SD) divided by the mean (M) 9 100% (CV = SD/M 9 100%).

[SECTION] application of the developed rt-pcr method in cultured turbot
The method was validated in infected and non infected fish samples provided from a local farm in the north of Spain. All samples were analyzed by means of classical histological techniques carried out by the pathologist of this farm. Subsequently, they were transported to the laboratory under refrigerated conditions (4°C) and were analyzed with the described methodology.

[SECTION] evaluation of sample collection, storage and dna extraction
In this study, different tissue preparation, preservation and shipping methods were evaluated. This evaluation was conducted based on the quantity and quality of the isolated DNA (Table 1), and reflects the real alternatives for tissue storage and transport from the farm to the laboratory. In this sense, RNA later, besides being a reagent for the stabilization of RNA, is used typically as a stabilization reagent to store tissue (Nsubuga, Robbins, Roeder, Morin, Boesch & Vigilant 2004;Bent & Taylor 2010;Michaud & Foran 2011).
All DNA extractions obtained from the different variables showed good results because of the high quantity and quality of DNA obtained, according to spectrophotometric measurements (data not shown). Only dry samples, which were send without any refrigeration or preservation conditions, and in conditions of ordinary dispatch, showed low DNA quality. It is reflected in the low purity of the extractions (< 1.6), probably due to the degree of decomposition of the sample. When samples arrived within a few hours, the quality of extracted DNA was high regardless of the transport method (dry, without refrigeration or preservation). In all these cases, the inhibitor control test was always negative, eliminating the possibility of false-negative results, unlike the method published by Piazzon et al. (Piazzon et al. 2012).
Therefore, we concluded that the best way to send samples to reduce costs would be shipping the samples by ordinary shipment in 95% ethanol, regardless of the time that has elapsed before and during shipment. Thus, some extra costs such as different preservatives as RNAlater â (Ambion), or hiring special shipping conditions such as refrigerated shipping or dry ice, can be avoided.
Regarding the evaluation of the presence of E. scophthalmi in other tissues different from caecum or intestine tissues, it was concluded that the parasite was only present in target tissues such as caecum and intestine tissues, and in the rectal samples obtained by non-lethal sampling by rectal swab (Cq <35). E. scophthalmi was not detected in muscle, fin, gills, kidney, liver, spleen or in the mucus, or in blood and faeces, regardless of the degree of infestation in the analyzed fish.
These results agree with the study of Redondo et al., which showed that, from different areas of infection, parasites were detected in blood and intestine. Only when infection was severe the parasite was observed in other organs as spleen, kidney, pancreas, gills and muscular tissue (Redondo et al. 2004). In this study, the presence of the parasite in blood was tested. But contrary to what Redondo et al. reported in their study, the results for the blood samples from fish infected by the parasite were all negative and their controls were correct, discarding a false-negative result. On the basis of these findings, we highly recommend that the sampling for E. scophthalmi is carried out on the intestine and with rectal swabs to avoid the sacrifice of fish.

[SECTION] design of a specific fast real-time pcr method for the detection of e. scophthalmi
In this study, a specific Fast RT-PCR method for authentication of E. scophthalmi and another probe for detection of S. maximus with the same primer pair were designed. From a selected internal region of the 18S rRNA, these sets generate PCR products of 120 bp in both cases. The design of an inhibitor control was used to indicate the appropriate development of the analytical procedure. The inhibitor control assured a correct DNA extraction at quantity, quality and purity level. Even more, it assured the absence of amplification inhibitors and avoided the diagnosis of false-negative results.
The combination of two probes with the same primers allows testing for parasites and amplification inhibitors in the same sample without the need of designing other primer set in a fast and reliable assay. An inhibitor control to avoid false-negative results and assure the correct DNA extraction process is essential in PCR methodologies. The inhibitor control is a non-target sequence of DNA amplified in the sample and can be an endogenous gene in sample or an incorporated plasmid with a gene control (Arkush, Miller, Leutenegger, Gardner, Packham, Heckeroth, Tenter, Barr & Conrad 2003;Hoorfar et al. 2003Hoorfar et al. , 2004;;Apfalter et al. 2005;Hoffmann et al. 2009). In this case, the selected gene is the same of the parasite, but the signal in the host is provided by the primer/probe specific set from S. maximus.
When the inhibitor control shows absence of amplification, the result is negative. In this case, the complete extraction process should be repeated or, in order to eliminate impurities in the DNA extraction, this could be purified by commercial purification kits (by magnetic systems, e.g. Wizard magnetic DNA purification system-Promega, Madrid, Spain, or by column systems, e.g. Nucleo-Spin tissue Genomic DNA purification system-MACHEREY-NAGEL, D€ uren, Germany).
The optimization of the reaction in terms of specificity, sensitivity, efficiency and reproducibility of the fast real-time PCR for the detection of E. scophthalmi is possible through a mixture of different concentrations of primers and probe. Concentrations of 900 nM for both primers and 250 nM for probe yielded the highest endpoint fluorescence and the lowest threshold cycle. The same optimal concentrations of primers and probe for the control set of S. maximus were obtained.
The specificity of the assay was tested using DNA from some of the most important parasites which affect the turbot (T. brevifilum and P. dicentrarchi) and with its host (S. maximus) to verify the suitability and reliability of the method. A BLAST analysis, specifically the MEGABLAS search with the sequences of the E. scophthalmi primer/probe set was carried out to investigate specificity and non-target affinities with other submissions in the database. Each primer and the probe in separate mode showed an homology of 100% with a lot of species but all three in combination, two primers and the probe, show only 100% of homology with E. scophthalmi. There were no other findings regarding homologies with some other parasite that affects turbot based on the affinity of the primers and the probe.
For the rectal swabs, the negative control test was taken with a sterile swab to avoid collecting material that could interfere with the reaction, giving false-positives. It is important to mention that the inhibition controls have not been tested on other host species. This means that the inhibition controls should be previously tested on other fish species so that the methodology can be applied to these species. If the inhibition control works with the new host species, the test could be used right away, and if it does not work, a new control would have to be designed. No cross-reactivity was observed with any of the tested samples using methodology herein developed.
A methodology for the detection of pathogens must be specific and must be able to differentiate with all security whether the species of interest are present or not. This security is supplied by the specificity of the assay. The application of the developed methodology to different related species, genetically close or that are sharing the same host, must assure the specificity of the method.
The assay described in this manuscript has been designed for specific conditions in which the host is S.maximus and only for application in aquaculture. Within this framework, the specificity evaluation has been reduced to the main parasites in the culture of S. maximus. This renders the evaluation of many parasites obsolete which do not affect the turbot in culture conditions, although they are closely related with the target parasite (E. scophthalmi). It is also unnecessary to evaluate the specificity with other hosts, because the framework is specific for a single host (S. maximus). The only variable that plays a role in specificity is the parasite, and its variability is determined by two constant parameters, the host and farm cultivation conditions. In this study, the specificity was tested empirically for species host-related to avoid interferences or crossreactivity by the presence of different parasites.
Also, phylogenetic analyses have been performed to evaluate the relation, determined by 18S rRNA, between E. scophthalmi and other related parasites (host-related, taxonomic-related and locationrelated). Figure 1 shows the phylogenetic tree obtained where all the sequences belonging to individuals of the same species were grouped in the same cluster, allowing their identification. The bootstrap method can be used to obtain the support of the different groups obtained in the phylogenetic tree. It has been calculated that bootstrap values higher or equal to 70 usually correspond to a probability higher or equal to 95% that the corresponding cluster is real (Hillis & Bull 1993), giving a quantitative measurement of the certainty of the assignment of a sample to a particular species.
The phylogenetic tree shows that E. scophthalmi is differentiated from all parasites with bootstrap values higher than 90. This shows that the variable positions inside the selected fragment of 120 bp allows the differentiation of the parasites included in the analysis. There is a noticeable and clear differentiation between E. leei and E. scophthalmi, which are included in two separated clades strongly supported and based on this DNA sequence. For all these reasons, we conclude that the selected fragment provides the necessary information to develop this molecular tool with high specificity and robustness.
The threshold cycle (Cq) is a basic parameter of the RT-PCR and it is an essential component that produces accurate and reproducible data. It is defined as the fractional PCR cycle number at which the reporter fluorescence is greater than the threshold. The Cq depends on the starting template copy number, the efficiency of PCR amplification, the efficiency of separation or hybridization of the fluorogenic probe and the sensitivity of detection (Bustin 2004;Bustin et al. 2009). The aim of the data analysis is to determinate when the target amplification is sufficiently above the background signal, by facilitating more accurate measurement of fluorescence.
In all samples analyzed, when 200 ng of template were used, the Cq values obtained were <35 and 17 AE 2, for E. scophthalmi and S. maximus primer/probe sets respectively.
For E. scophthalmi primer/probe set, a particular Cq cannot be determined. It depends on the degree of infection of the fish in question. The DNA added to the reaction (200 ng) contains DNA from both the turbot and the parasite. For this reason, the concentration was determined by manual cell counting using a Neubauer chamber. The LOD, regardless of the degree of infection, was two parasites for 500 lL. This limit was obtained with DNA extractions from real contaminated fish, in contrast with Piazzon, who obtained a very low limit from an ideal situation with pure DNA from E. scophthalmi (Piazzon et al. 2012). The real situation in turbot aquaculture is that the DNA extraction from infected fish contains a mixture of turbot and parasite DNA, or only turbot DNA in DNA extraction from non-infected fish. For this reason, a low LOD from pure DNA of the parasite, although it is a signal of a sensitive methodology, is not a real indicator of the limit reach in detection of the pathology.
The sensitivity obtained is very important at the moment of the detection because sensitivity allows detection of the presence of E. scophthalmi at early stages of infection, when the infection intensity is low, and regardless of the life cycle stage of the parasite. The method allows the adoption of early control measures and the avoidance of propagation of the pathogen.
For the E. scophthalmi primer/probe set, UND (undetected) results corresponded to the values of non-target species (the most important parasites affecting the turbot) and negative controls. Also, in the cross-reactivity analysis, no false positive results have been observed under the most severe conditions used in the test.
The accuracy of the fast real-time PCR is highly dependent on the PCR efficiency. In the developed method, it was calculated based on the slope of the standard curve obtained using DNA serial dilutions with a template of known concentration (from 250 ng to 25 pg) as templates for RT-PCR. The efficiency (E) of the reaction was calculated according to the equation E = (10 (À1/slope) À 1) 9 100 (Bustin 2004) (Fig. 2a).
The amplification plot of the experiment with the primer/probe set E. scophthalmi and S. maximus generated a slope of À3.38 and À3.35, an efficiency of 97% and 99%, and a correlation coefficient of 0.999 and 0.998 respectively (Fig. 2b). These values of Cq and efficiency have demonstrated the utility of the fast real-time PCR system to detect E. scophthalmi and S. maximus, which is used for the control of the methodology developed, where the efficiency is nearly 100%.
Moreover, within the reproducibility of the assay, intra-assay variation (CV) was 3.18%, while inter-assay variation (CV) was 4.21%, thereby indicating that the RT-PCR was highly reproducible (data not shown). This confirms that RT-PCR is a robust methodology to detect the presence of E. scophthalmi in cultured turbot.

[SECTION] application of the developed real-time pcr in cultured turbot
Extracted DNA showed a good yield and optimal purity in all products analyzed (data not shown). Both molecular and classical histological techniques showed concordant results for the detection of E. scophthalmi in the analyzed samples.
This concordance in the result indicates the reliability of the methodology; the results are in accord with histological results. In addition, it is applicable in early stages of infection, and shows high specificity, efficiency and reliability.
