[SECTION] materials and methods

[SECTION] study area
The study area was located in the Lu í s Ant ô nio municipality, in the northeast region of S ã o Paulo State ( Figure 1 ). This region is a transition zone between Cerrado and semideciduous vegetation and includes a protected area, the Jata í Ecological Station (JES; 21 ° 35 ′ S-47 ° 48 ′ W), which covers 9010 ha and represents the largest protected area in the state with continuous Cerrado vegetation. This area is surrounded by sugarcane crops, cattle ranches, eucalyptus plantations, dirt roads, and highways.

[SECTION] sample collection
Between October 2008 and December 2009, we conducted 2-day field expeditions once per month inside and surrounding the JES. This protected area is intersected by dirt roads throughout its extent. Therefore, during each expedition, we looked for feces on the dirt roads inside and surrounding the JES, covering approximately 200 km of roads. All of the fieldwork was conducted by two researchers. On the basis of tracks and feces diameter/ morphology ( Dalponte 1997, Chame 2003 ), we collected 41 distinct maned wolf fecal samples and recorded the coordinates of all collection points using a Global Positioning System. The samples were stored in sterile preservativefree plastic tubes without any preservative solution and were kept at -22 ° C in the laboratory until DNA extraction was performed.

[SECTION] dna extraction
We extracted fecal DNA using either the QIAmp DNA Stool Mini Kit (Qiagen, GmBH, Hilden, Germany) or PSP Spin Stool DNA Kit (Invitek, Regensburg, Germany), according to the manufacturer ' s recommendations. For the extraction of blood DNA to be used as reference sequences in the genetic analysis, we followed the phenol/chloroform/ isoamylic alcohol protocol proposed by Sambrook et al. (1989) . Blood samples (two) were kindly provided by the Americana Municipality Zoo and CENAP/IBAMA.

[SECTION] fecal sample individualization and genetic analyses
To individualize each fecal sample, we amplified a set of seven tetranucleotide microsatellite loci with primers that were initially designed by Francisco et al. (1996) for Canis familiaris (Linnaeus 1758) and successfully characterized for Chrysocyon brachyurus by Fontoura- Rodrigues et al. (2008Rodrigues et al. ( ) : loci 2001Rodrigues et al. ( , 2018Rodrigues et al. ( , 2054Rodrigues et al. ( , 2088Rodrigues et al. ( , 2132Rodrigues et al. ( , 2137Rodrigues et al. ( , and 2140. PCR was performed using a three-primer labeling system ( Schuelke 2000 ). Each amplification (15 μ l) included 7.5 μ l of GoTaq Master Mix (Promega; 1 × buffer, 1.5 m m MgCl 2 , 0.2 m m dNTPs, and 1u Taq polymerase ), 8 pmol of the reverse primer, 2 pmol of the forward primer, 8 pmol of the M13 sequence tagged with the 6-FAM fluorophore, and 150 μ g/ml of bovine serum albumin. The remaining volume of the 15 μ l reaction consisted of the sample DNA. We performed the amplifications in a PTC-100 Thermocycler (MJ Research Inc.), according to the following program (for all  We genotyped homozygous samples in three to five independent PCR assays and heterozygous samples two times to prevent genotyping errors that are frequently associated with non-invasive genetic analyses ( Taberlet et al. 1996 ). Only samples that were successfully genotyped for at least five loci were included in the fecal individualization analysis, and only loci that were genotyped for at least 70% of the samples were included in the analyses.
We conducted individual identification of genotypes with Gimlet version 1.3.3 ( Vali è re 2002 ). We determined the probability of identity (p (ID) ), i.e., the probability of two individuals in the population randomly sharing identical genotypes for all of the analyzed loci ( Paetkau et al. 1998, Waits et al. 2001 ), to quantify the discriminatory power of the microsatellite dataset among all of the individualized samples. The p (ID) values were calculated for each locus using Gimlet and then multiplied among the loci to obtain the total p (ID) ( Paetkau et al. 1998 ). We also estimated the probability of identity assuming siblings (p (ID)sib ) ( Waits et al. 2001 ).
We determined the total and per-locus genotyping error rates (allelic dropout) by dividing the number of detected errors by the number of cases in which an error might have been detected (i.e., the total number of heterozygous genotyping reactions; see Broquet and Petit 2004 ). We investigated the occurrence of null alleles with Micro-Checker 2.2.3 ( Van Oosterhout et al. 2004 ). We used Genepop 3.4 ( Raymond and Rousset 1995 ) to estimate the expected (H E ) and observed (H O ) heterozygosity, and to test each locus for linkage disequilibrium and deviations from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (HWE) proportions (Markov chain exact test; Guo and Thompson 1992 ), with all of these analyses including 10,000 dememorizations, 1000 batches, and 10,000 interactions per batch. Using FStat 2.9.3 ( Goudet 1995 ), we estimated the allelic richness and the F IS coefficient ( Weir and Cockerham 1984 ) as a measure of the inbreeding level in the population.
Bottleneck 1.2.02 ( Piry et al. 1999 ) was used to test heterozygosity excess as a consequence of a recent bottleneck event using a " Wilcoxon test " . We assumed a two-phase mutation model incorporating 10%, 20%, and 30% of infinite allele mutation model (IAM), with 10,000 iterations. The test was also repeated assuming IAM and the stepwise mutation model.
We estimated the genetic relationships between individualized maned wolves using ML-Relate ( Kalinowski et al. 2006 ). The maximum likelihood estimate of relatedness (r) ( Blouin 2003 ) was employed to discriminate four common pedigree relationships: unrelated (U), half siblings (HS), full siblings (FS), and parent-offspring (PO). When the estimated putative relationships between individual pairs differed from unrelated relationships, we used the same software to assess the uncertainty (p-values) of these estimates by testing two a priori hypotheses: a putative relationship with a higher likelihood (HS, FS, or PO) against an alternative hypothesis (the " unrelated " relationship). When the pair comparisons exhibited a low p-value ( < 0.05), we excluded the alternative hypothesis and accepted the relationship with the maximum likelihood (HS, FS, or PO). Because we had no control group of samples with known relationships to calibrate the analysis, the goal of this analysis was to verify the existence of related animals in the study area, rather than defining exact categories of kinship.

[SECTION] discrimination of individuals and genetic variability
We successfully extracted DNA from and genotyped the 41 collected samples. Of the seven microsatellite loci that were initially tested, only five displayed an amplification success > 70%; therefore, we excluded loci 2132 and 2137 from further analyses. Among the 41 fecal samples, we identified 13 distinct maned wolves (Figure 1), and 9 (69.2%) of these individuals were sampled at least twice. The probability of identity estimated for the five analyzed loci indicated that our microsatellite panel was efficient in discriminating individuals within the entire dataset (p (ID) = 0.1 × 10 -19 and p (ID)sib = 0.8 × 10 -6 ). Values < 0.001 may be considered satisfactory ( Waits et al. 2001 ). The observed allelic frequencies for the seven analyzed loci are presented in Table 1 . Our data displayed no evidence of null alleles.
Genetic variability analysis indicated mean values of 0.52 and 0.72 for H O and H E , respectively. The number of alleles per locus ranged from 3 (locus 2088) to 8 (locus 2140), with a mean of 5.4 alleles per locus. The range size, number of alleles, allelic richness, observed and expected heterozygosity, and allelic dropout rates for the analyzed loci are presented in Table 2 .
No linkage disequilibrium was detected among the seven analyzed loci; however, we observed significant deviations from the HWE for two loci (2054 and 2140; Bonferroni correction p < 0.00714) ( Table 3 ). The estimated total F IS coefficient was significant (F IS = 0.324; p < 0.01), indicating a heterozygote deficit in the sampled population.
Testing for the recent occurrence of a bottleneck event in this maned wolf population resulted in no significant values based on all of the tested mutation models. Investigation of the patterns of the genetic relationships between all possible pair combinations indicated significant r values for the PO, FS, and HS pedigree categories (p < 0.05), which reveals the existence of related individuals in the   protected area. Theoretically, the r values for the FS and PO relationships are distributed around a mean of 0.5, and those for HS around a mean of 0.25 ( Blouin et al. 1996 ). The significant values of r ranged from 0.000 to 0.5253.

FILE: American J Primatol - 2013 - Barelli - Extra‐pair paternity confirmed in wild white‐handed gibbons.grobid.tei.xml
====================================================================================================
[SECTION] methods

[SECTION] study site
The study was carried out on the wild Mo Singto-Klong E-Tau white-handed gibbon population (H. lar) close to the headquarter of Khao Yai National Park (2,168 km 2 ; 14°26'N, 101°22'E; $150 km NE of Bangkok). The park consists of a sandstone plateau and is covered by seasonal evergreen rain forest ranging in elevation between 600 and 1,000 m above sea level [Lynam et al., 2006]. The study site covers approximately 8.5 km 2 of hilly terrain with continuous forest cover.
All individuals included in this study are subjects of ongoing socioecology and behavioral studies since the early 1990s [e.g., Barelli et al., 2007Barelli et al., , 2008Barelli et al., , 2011;;Reichard, 2003;Reichard et al., 2012]. Accurate birth and demographic records of the population are available, which allowed us to run paternity tests.

[SECTION] social organization and social mating system
Although gibbons are still thought to live in pairs [Bartlett, 2007], at Khao Yai National Park group compositions and the social mating system are more flexible [Barelli et al., 2007[Barelli et al., , 2008;;Reichard, 2009]. Similar flexibility has also been observed in other hylobatid populations [Kenyon et al., 2011;Lappan, 2007]. During annual census walks over 16 years (from 1992 to 2007) on average 76.9% of social units observed lived in pairs, consisting of a single adult male, a single adult female and up to four offspring, whereas 21.2% lived in multi-male/one-female groups with more than one adult male unrelated to the resident female, and 1.9% consisted of one-male/ multi-female groups [Reichard & Barelli, 2008]. The white-handed gibbon density at the site is high with 4.0 groups and 15.9 individuals/km 2 [Barelli et al., 2007], but it is not exceptional compared to other gibbon populations [Leighton, 1987;Mitani, 1990;Reichard, 2009;Yanuar, 2009]. Following previous studies [Barelli et al., 2007[Barelli et al., , 2008]], we differentiated adult males into three categories based on status and involvement with a resident female: (i) primary males, (ii) secondary male partners and (iii) neighboring males. Primary males were either the single male in pair-living groups or the male in multi-male groups who engaged in singing duets and the majority of copulations with the adult female [Barelli et al., 2008]. Secondary males were the remaining males in multi-male units [Barelli et al., 2008], while neighboring males were considered separately as a female's potential extra-pair partners.
We recently demonstrated [Barelli et al., 2008] that although the majority of mating is skewed towards primary males, half of the females living in multi-male units also copulated with secondary males. Copulating with both primary and secondary males occurred throughout female menstrual cycles and continued during pregnancy when conception was impossible. Irrespective of alternative functions copulations may serve (i.e., social bonding and reducing male aggression toward a female) in addition to achieving conception, female mating behavior strongly contrasts with the common view that white-handed gibbon females are socio-sexually monoandrous and suggests that female gibbons are more precisely characterized as sexually polyandrous [Barelli et al., 2008;Reichard, 2009].

[SECTION] subjects and sample collection
A total of 89 gibbons, for which social histories were available [Reichard & Barelli, 2008;Reichard et al., 2012], were examined in this study, which at one point in time belonged to either of 14 habituated groups (A, B, C, D, E, H, J, M, N, R, S, T, W, and NOS) or to one of three neighboring groups (G, ER, and  (1996-2005 and 2010-2011), Khao Yai National Park, Thailand
( ), three surrounding groups which were not habituated to human presence; [ ], individuals for which mtDNA analysis was available but no STR was possible.
a
Male not belonging to any other group.
NER), and one adult male was considered solitary (Table I).
We collected about 10 g of feces from target animals using disposable gloves directly after an individual had defecated. Between 1996 and 2005, UR, CB and colleagues collected 656 feces preserved in 70% ethanol [Kohn et al., 1995] or RNAlater (Ambion) [Nsubuga et al., 2004], or dried in silica gel beads [Wasser et al., 1997]. These feces were kept frozen at the Max-Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology, Germany, until they were generously provided to us to complement this study sample. Feces stored in ethanol were desiccated by silica gel beads prior to DNA extraction. In addition, between 2010 and 2011, K.M. collected 320 feces using the two-step storage method [Matsudaira et al., 2013;Nsubuga et al., 2004]. All fecal samples were stored at ambient temperature on site and at 4°C in the laboratories.

[SECTION] dna extraction
DNA was extracted using a QIAamp® DNA Stool Mini Kit (Qiagen, Germany). In order to maximize the amount of DNA extracted, we followed the modified protocols proposed by Nsubuga et al. [2004]. For desiccated feces, a specimen (approximately 100-150 mg) was scraped from the surface of feces and suspended in 1.6 ml Buffer ASL (Qiagen). For feces collected in RNAlater, 2 ml of the mixture was centrifuged for 15 min at 3,000g and the supernatant was removed. The specimen was centrifuged a second time for 15 min at 500g and the supernatant was also removed. The feces were resuspended in 1.6 ml Buffer ASL. The specimens in Buffer ASL were vortexed and incubated overnight at room temperature prior to DNA extraction steps. In addition, at the final step of extraction, DNA was incubated with 200 ml Buffer AE (Qiagen) for 20 min before centrifugation.

[SECTION] dna quantification
In order to avoid genotyping errors derived from allelic drop outs [Morin et al., 2001;Navidi et al., 1992;Taberlet et al., 1996], we repeated PCR based on the quantity of DNA as in previous studies [Morin et al., 2001]. DNA derived from subjects was quantified by Real-Time PCR using TaqMan® probe assay performed with a StepOnePlus™ Real-Time PCR System (Applied Biosystems, USA). We used probe and primers which had been designed for c-myc gene: c-myc 105 assay combination [Smith et al., 2002]. Real-Time PCR was carried out in a 20 ml cocktail containing 2 ml DNA template, TaqMan® Fast Advanced Master Mix (Applied Biosystems), 250 nM probe and 900 nM of each primer. Cycle conditions were as follows: pre-incubation at 95°C for 2 sec, followed by 45 cycles of 95°C for 1 sec, 60°C for 20 sec. Triplicate sets of standards of known DNA amount were included in each analysis: DNA extracted from immortalized B-cell line of a whitehanded gibbon was quantified by spectrophotometer and diluted to 20 ng, 5 ng, 1.25 ng, 312 pg, 78.1 pg and 19.5 pg per 2 ml for the standards. Analysis and calculations were performed using StepOne Software v2.1 (Applied Biosystems).

[SECTION] str genotyping
STR genotyping was done for a total of 12 loci with tetra-nucleotide repeat motif originally designed for humans (Table II), the utility of which has been already reported, at least for some loci, in the same population of white-handed gibbons: D1S548, D1S1656, D2S1329G, D3S1766, D3S1768, D4S243, D5S1457, D6S501, D10S1432, D11S2002G, D13S321, and D20S206 [Chambers et al., 2004]. Sequences of primers were cited from UniSTS database of the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) website (http://www.nubi.nlm.nih.gov/). However, for loci D2S1329G and D11S2002G, reverse primers were redesigned because of poor amplification. The 5'-end of the forward primer of each locus was labeled by one of four fluorescent markers: 6-FAM, VIC, NED, or PET. PCR amplifications were carried out in a 20 ml PCR cocktail containing 2 (or 3) ml DNA template, PCR Buffer II for AmpliTaq Gold®, 3 mM Mg 2þ , 200 mM each dNTP, 50 mg BSA, 200 nM each primer and 0.5 unit AmpliTaq Gold® (Applied Biosystems). Cycle conditions were as follows: pre-incubation at 95°C for 5 min, followed by 45-50 cycles (depending on the locus, Table II) of 95°C for 30 sec, 48-55°C (depending on the locus, Table II) for 30 sec and 72°C for 30 sec, and a final extension at 72°C for 30 min followed by 4°C for 5 min. One to three PCR product (s) labeled by different fluorescent colors were separated by electrophoresis at once on an ABI PRISM® 3100-Avant Genetic Analyzer (Applied Biosystems) with size standard, Genescan™ 600 LIZ (Applied Biosystems), and were sized using GeneMapper ID v3.2 (Applied Biosystems). Two to seven independent PCR cycles were repeated for each locus depending on the quantity of DNA produced [Morin et al., 2001]. CERVUS 3.0 [Kalinowski et al., 2007] was used to calculate observed and expected heterozygosities, to test deviation from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (HWE), and to estimate a null allele frequency for each locus. GENA-LEX 6.4 [Peakall & Smouse, 2006] was used to calculate the probability of identity.

[SECTION] mitochondrial dna
To confirm mother-offspring relationships, we determined the 631 or 632-base sequences of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) including the hyper variable segment I (HVSI) [Matsudaira et al., 2013]. This was particularly effective in three cases (two cases in group D and one case in group E) where the STR genotypes of mothers could not be confirmed. In addition, the confirmation allowed us to minimize the potential effect of errors in the sample collection.

[SECTION] paternity tests
Among 82 individuals whose STR genotypes were determined, 44 individuals were born during the study period of the Khao Yai Gibbon long-term Project. For only two offspring, the resident adult male at the time of conception (i.e., 7 months prior to the offspring's birth date) was not genotyped because no sample was available. Thus, we excluded these two offspring and analyzed the paternity of the remaining 42 offspring. Of the 42 offspring, 27 were conceived in pair-living groups and 15 in multi-male groups. In multi-male group D, all three offspring were conceived while the same two adult males were present, but no genotype for the secondary male was available.
We considered as potential sires adult males of 8 years or older age and 7-year-old subadult males [Reichard, 2003] in cases where sub-adult males were living in the same group as the offspring (but when the offspring's mother was not the sub-adult's mother) or were residents in a neighboring group of the offspring at the time of conception. Due to a lack of reports of mother-son copulations in the wild, we excluded sub-adult males residing with their mother at the time of conception as potential sires. The complete number of potential sires in neighboring groups was not known for some non-habituated groups. In such case, we assumed the presence of one potential sire for each non-habituated group. For the 42 offspring tested, the average number of potential sires and the number of potential sires sampled were 8.17 (AE1.95 SD) and 5.81 (AE1.90 SD), respectively.
Based on STR genotypes, paternity was assigned via CERVUS 3.0 [Kalinowski et al., 2007]. This program compares likelihood ratios of two most-likely candidate sires, and assigns paternity using statistical criteria generated by computer simulation. The algorithm of the program takes genotyping errors into account, as well as the presence of close relatives in the study population [Marshall et al., 1998; but see Jones & Ardren, 2003], which was the case in our study. For the paternity simulation in CERVUS, we were able to use 71% of the entire possible sampling subjects and up to eight potential sires per offspring. To further protect results against false paternity identification we conservatively also considered 1% genotyping error and 10,000 simulation cycles. The confidence levels of analysis were set at 95% for relaxed level and at 99% for strict level. Because 2 of the 12 loci deviated from HWE, 2 data sets, 1 with 12 and 1 with 10 loci were used during analysis. We considered cases of EPP when a neighboring male was assigned as sire, or when none of the primary and secondary males were assigned as sire. Though paternity was assigned based on the likelihoods, we counted the number of allelic mismatches between the paternal alleles of offspring and the alleles of potential sires via CERVUS in order to detect cases where no mismatches were observed with more than one male.
To compare the reproductive output of pair-living males and primary males of multi-male groups, we carried out two-tailed Fisher's exact test in R [ R Core Team, 2012].
We detected some unnoticed dispersal events in the population and were able to confirm and correct individual migrations through careful examination of genotypic data. In the few cases where observational data and genetic data disagreed, we used genotypic identities in our analyses.

[SECTION] ethical standard
We conducted the study without direct contact or interaction with the gibbons and under permission of the National Research Council of Thailand (NRCT) and the Department of National Parks, Wildlife and Plant Conservation (DNP) of Thailand. Our data collection procedure adhered to the American Society of Primatologists principles for the ethical treatment of primates, and complied with the laws governing wildlife research in Thailand.

[SECTION] genotypes and identity of individuals
We determined STR genotypes for 82 individuals out of 89 sampled individuals. For 69.5% of samples (N ¼ 57), STR genotypes were confirmed from two or more independent feces. In addition, among the 89 individuals genotyped through mtDNA, we found 11 haplotypes [Matsudaira et al., 2013]. Since two of the 82 individuals (from which STR genotypes were determined) were collected during an early stage of group habituation, their identities were ambiguous. However, we included them into the analyses because the genotypes clearly showed the presence of both individuals in the respective groups. The number of alleles per locus varied between 5 and 14. Observed heterozygosities ranged from 0.585 to 0.878 and expected heterozygosities ranged from 0.584 to 0.893. Two loci showed significant deviation from HWE after Bonferroni correction (D3S1768: P ¼ 0.003 and D11S2002G: P ¼ 0.004, Table III). However, since we did not detect any allelic mismatches between 41 mother-offspring relationships for all 12 loci, including the two which deviated from HWE, and estimated null allele frequencies of the two loci were low (0.044 and 0.040, respectively, Table III), we considered such deficiencies deriving from sampling of a kin structured population. The expected probability of identity estimated over 12 loci was 6.8 Â 10 À13 suggesting that the chance that two randomly taken individuals from this population have the same genotype at multiple loci is unlikely. Although the presence of close relatives among subjects might potentially lead to underestimating the probability of identifying individuals, we did not detect a single pair of individuals with the exact same genotype.

[SECTION] paternity
Paternity assignment using both 12 and 10 loci gave similar results, except for one case in which paternity was assigned to different males (i.e., M-F1, Table IV). However, since the difference found was minor, we only present results from the analysis of 12 loci. Paternity based on CERVUS at a confidence level of 99% could be assigned to a total of 41 individuals (97.6% of total paternity tests). For the majority of the offspring (N ¼ 38), paternity was assigned to primary males (90.5% of total paternity tests) while in two cases, offspring were sired by known adult males from a neighboring group (4.8%). In one case, both a primary and a neighboring male revealed no allelic mismatch with the offspring (i.e., N-AF2, Table IV). This case of paternity was considered "inconclusive." In one remaining case, where paternity could not be assigned to any potential sire sampled (including the resident male present at the time of conception), we considered this as an additional EPP event. However, to indicate the indirect assessment, we labeled it "inferred EPP" (Table IV).
When separating the paternity data by social organization, among the 27 offspring born in pairliving groups, 23 offspring (85.2%) were sired by a primary male, three offspring (11.1%) were sired by extra-pair males (two "confirmed EPP" cases; one "inferred EPP" case) and one paternity case we considered inconclusive (Table IV). In the 15 offspring born in multi-male groups, 14 offspring (93.3%) were sired by primary males and one offspring (6.7%) was sired by a secondary male (Table IV). For two offspring born in multi-male group D, the genotype of the mother and the secondary male were    unavailable, thus although the primary male was assigned as the father, the possibility that the secondary male could theoretically also have sired the offspring could not be rejected (Table IV). Ratios of reproductive monopolization by pair-living primary males (23:3) and primary males in multi-male groups (14:1) did not differ statistically (Fisher's exact test, P ¼ 1.00). Thus, primary males living in multi-male groups were as successfully reproducing as primary males living in pairs.

[SECTION] reproductive skew in multi-male groups
Interestingly, in multi-male groups, paternity was highly skewed towards primary males, in fact only one secondary male could be confirmed as a sire, despite the fact that secondary males have been observed to occasionally copulate with females also during a female's fertile period [Barelli et al., 2008]. On the other hand, the finding is also in line with observational data that demonstrated that copulations during the female's fertile phase were also skewed towards the female's primary male partner [Barelli et al., 2008]. The predominance of primary male sires in our study is interesting. For these males, it suggests that the risk, that is, the reproductive cost, of sharing a home range and socio-sexual access to a breeding female with a secondary male may be lower than expected from observations of polyandrous mating. Moreover, the cost may be outweighed by a potential benefit from joint forces of two or more males in repelling neighboring individuals from exploiting home range resources and/or from philandering males in search of EPC opportunities. Thus, a low potential reproductive cost to primary males could well explain the relatively widespread occurrence of multi-male groups in Khao Yai white-handed gibbons and provide an explanation as to why immigrant males do not always oust a resident male during a takeover, but tolerate a former sole resident male as a secondary male [Barelli et al., 2008;Reichard, 2003Reichard, , 2009]].
Primary males in multi-male groups may be able to dominate secondary males and effectively suppress a secondary male's sexual activity with the female when conception is most likely. Indeed, primary males have most frequent access to females during their fertile phase [Barelli et al., 2008]. Alternatively, it could be speculated that the higher reproductive success of primary males compared to secondary males (despite copulation activity of the latter during a female's fertile phase) may be related to individual variation in sperm quality and that primary males produce sperm that is more successful in sperm competition [Gomendio et al., 1998;Møller, 1988]. Gibbons' testes are relatively large for their small body weight [Harcourt et al., 1995] suggesting mild sperm competition, and primary and secondary males in multi-male groups have been observed to copulate with a female within hours [UR pers. obs.], thus raising the possibility for sperm competition in the female reproductive tract. Indirect support for speculating about variation in sperm quality among males comes also from our observation of one female copulating with her pair mate for many years without conceiving but giving birth again after a male immigration had occurred. However, no firm evidence yet exists for variation in sperm quality and the extent of sperm competition in white-handed gibbons.
In contrast, the very limited reproductive success of secondary males is even more surprising when viewed from their own perspective. A predicted benefit for a male who has lost the primary position to an immigrant and accepts a secondary status (as we have often observed in this population [Reichard et al., 2012]) is the potential for sharing paternities with the more dominant primary male group member. Although our sample size is small, we nevertheless suggest that the chances for reproduction by secondary males must be generally low and that, by inference, secondary males do not benefit from a multi-male situation in terms of increased reproductive chances. Alternatively we propose that staying in a multi-male group must be associated with other, more direct benefits for secondary males, such as staying on a familiar home range and avoiding a potentially costly transfer into another group or reducing the risk of predation compared to solitary living. This is especially relevant where primary and secondary males are relatives, for example father and son, which this study was now able to confirm in a few cases. However, since this is beyond the scope of our analyses, future studies are needed to clarify effects of relatedness on behavioral and genetic levels of the gibbon social system and, for example, examine potential benefits of males accepting secondary status. It must also be remembered that despite apparently low chances of successful reproduction, any chance of siring an offspring (i.e., a probability of >0) may be sufficient for a secondary male to stay in a multi-male group.

[SECTION] benefits of epcs and epp for females
Females may also benefit directly and/or indirectly from EPCs and EPP [Akçay & Roughgarden, 2007;Cohas & Allainé, 2009;Jennions & Petrie, 2000]. Among the direct benefits mammalian females may gain by performing EPCs, confusing paternity might be a more important benefit as it helps to reduce potential aggressive behavior, such as infanticide and sexual harassment, by neighboring males [Wolff & Macdonald, 2004]. However, firm evidence of sexually selected male infanticide in the Khao Yai white-handed gibbon population is still lacking.
Alternatively, females may copulate with an extra-pair male to obtain indirect, genetic benefits for the female's offspring, assuming that extra-pair males have superior genetic quality compared to those with which the female maintains a constant pair-bond. For nearly two decades this has been a popular explanation of female EPC behavior, however, this idea has more recently come under criticism for its weak empirical support [Akçay & Roughgarden, 2007;Arnqvist & Rowe, 2005;Westneat & Stewart, 2003], at least in birds. Indeed, the small amount of EPP observed in this study population, also questions the presence of "attractive males" in the Khao Yai gibbons.
Instead, the observed EPP suggests that females may compensate sterility of pair-mates by EPCs. Two of the three EPP occurred in the same group and during the residence of the same male in pair-living group N. Although the mating pattern of this particular female was not well known, she conceived two successive offspring with extra-pair partners. Thus, it may be speculated that the primary male was sterile, and it is likely that the female could be fertilized only by EPCs.
Other possible direct benefits include material benefits or paternal care a female may receive from an extra-pair partner, although the latter seems not very likely in white-handed gibbons since observations suggest that females raise young without direct assistance from males.
In summary, this study provides the first comprehensive genetic evidence showing that EPCs in female gibbons result in EPP. This extends and supports previous findings from demographic and behavioral observations suggesting that the mating system of the white-handed gibbon is more flexible than traditionally believed. Overall, our data highlight the importance of genetic paternity analysis for characterizing a species' mating system and their consequences in terms of reproductive output. Such data can ultimately help towards improving our understanding of the evolution of social and mating systems in primate species and mammals more broadly.

FILE: BiffiWilliams2017.grobid.tei.xml
====================================================================================================
[SECTION] material and methods

[SECTION] study sites
We searched for marine otter feces in two regions along the coast of Peru separated by ∼730 km. The central region was located in the Department of Lima and had two sampling localities and the southern region included the Departments of Moquegua and Tacna and encompassed five localities (Fig. 1, Table 1). A total of 18.14 km of coastline was searched regularly for spraints (Table 1).
In the central region, Pucusana Bay (PU) is an artisanal fishing port and yacht club. There is constant traffic in the bay by fishing and recreational boats. The bay is composed of rocky shores alternating with small patches of sandy beaches. We collected feces inside the recreational boats anchored in front of the club. The second site in the central region is Punta Corrientes (PC) located 60 km south of PU and is a summer residential site. It has a 450 m sandy beach surrounded by rocky shores. There is a low cave with easy access where feces were collected.
The Southern Ilo site (SI) was made up of three localities, the pier of the thermal power plant of Enersur, and the rocky shores of La Higuera and Chorrillos. The first section is a 100 m stretch of tetrapods (concrete structures used in breakwaters) located at the beginning of the pier, a 1.5 km extension of sandy beach with rocky patches, and an area of shallow rocky shores. Feces were collected in all three sites but due to their proximity (less than 5 km apart) we merged the sites in this area since Medina-Vogel et al. (2007) determined the home ranges of marine otters were from 1.4 to 4.1 km of seashore. Punta Picata (PP) is 5 km south of SI and is a 4 km rocky shore where feces were found and is located between 5 km of sandy beach on its north end and shallow rocky shores to the south. Puerto Grau (PG) is 28 km south of PP. PG is an artisanal fishing port and feces were located mainly along a man-made breakwater of large rocks. To the north of this area were rocky shores and to the south were low rocky shores where no otters or feces were seen. Quebrada Burros (QB) is 7 km south of PG and is composed of nearly 3 km where feces were found. Vila Vila (VV), the southernmost site, is a fishing village located 11 km south of QB. This site was composed of two man-made water breaks composed of large rocks and the rocky shore of Canepa, a beach located north of the village. Feces were found in both water breaks and along the rocky shore. To the south of this site were ∼ 10 km of low rocky shores and then a 40 km sandy beach extending to Chile.
Marine otters are patchily distributed along the coast of Peru and Chile depending on the presence of suitable rocky shores (Medina-Vogel et al., 2008;Valqui, 2012). Long stretches of sandy beach appear to limit otter movement. The two sites in the north are separated by six sandy beach areas that range from 1.2 to 7.8 km in length (Fig. 1). In the south there are fewer long stretches of sandy beach between the sites. The longest stretch (14 km) is located between PP and PG which is the zone of the artificial Ite wetlands (Fig. 1). Between PG and QB there are no extensive stretches of beach.

[SECTION] sample collection
We collected fresh marine otter spraints (∼1 day old) and discarded older ones for every visit. GPS coordinates were taken for all feces collected. Two sampling periods were conducted in each region between June -August 2012 separated by ∼10 days. During each sample period, each location was visited a first time and then a second time three days later. Using surgical gloves, a small part from the surface of the feces was extracted with a straw and immediately placed in a vial with 1 ml 8 M urea preservative buffer (10 mM Tris pH 7.5, 125 mM of NaCl, 10 mM EDTA pH 8.0, 1% SDS and 8 M urea) (Asahida et al., 1996).

[SECTION] genetic analysis

[SECTION] dna extraction
DNA was extracted using the QIAamp DNA Stool Mini-kit (Qiagen Genomics, Valencia, CA). We followed the manufacturer's protocols with the following modifications: at the beginning of the extraction we spun the vial with the sample, removed the supernatant and added 1.6 ml of Buffer ASL. Negative DNA extraction controls were included in each extraction batch to test for contamination of reagents. Extractions were conducted in an extraction dedicated AirClean
® 600 PCR workstation.

[SECTION] microsatellite marker development
We selected 16 microsatellite loci developed for L. longicaudis (Beheler et al., 2005), Pteronura brasiliensis (Ribas et al., 2011), and L. lutra, (Dallas and Piertney, 1998;Huang et al., 2005) to be tested on fecal samples of marine otters. Nine markers either did not amplify or were monomorphic: Lut435, Lut453, Lut701, Lut782, Pbra21, Rio06, Rio12, Rio16 and 04OT02. Seven microsatellite loci amplified and were polymorphic in marine otters: 04OT17, Pbra01, Pbra02, Pbra24, Rio11, Rio13, and Rio18 (Table 2). PCR products for all seven loci were gel purified using the Wizard ® SV Gel and PCR Clean-Up System (Promega, USA). PCR products were cloned with the pGEM-T Easy Vector System (Promega, USA). We sequenced clones using ABI Big Dye Terminator Cycle Sequencing v 3.1 chemistry (Applied Biosystems, USA) using pGEM vector primers.
Sequences were electrophoresed on an ABI 3130XL Genetic Analyzer (Applied Biosystems, USA). Sequences were trimmed and edited using Sequencher v. 5.0. We verified the sequences contained the expected microsatellite region and then used Primer3 (Rozen and Skaletsky, 2000), for five of the seven loci to redesign primers flanking the microsatellite region in order to amplify fragments less than 200 bp. We did not redesign primers for Rio11 and Rio18 because these were in the appropriate size range and there was not sufficient sequence flanking the microsatellite repeat to design high quality primers. Each locus was fluorescently labeled with one of four dyes (Table 2).

[SECTION] genotyping
Sets of 16 samples were amplified at each single locus with three to nine PCR replicates each (1178 total PCR reactions). PCR reactions were conducted in a separate room from DNA extractions in a PCR     3). One microliter of each coload was added to 10 l of Hi-Di formamide and 0.1 l of GS500 LIZ size standard (Life Technologies) and then electrophoresed on an ABI 3130XL Genetic Analyzer (Life Technologies). Genotypes were scored using GENEMAPPER 5.0 (Life Technologies). We initially ran three replicates of all samples. We then used the comparative method (Frantz et al., 2003;Hansen et al., 2008;Hájková et al., 2009) to create consensus genotypes. A genotype at a locus was scored as a homozygote if a single allele occurred >2 times across replicates and a heterozygote was scored if more than one allele was scored ≥2 times across replicates. Consensus genotypes were constructed manually for each individual. If a sample had a consensus genotype with fewer than five loci we then ran three more replicates up to a total of nine replicates. Genotypes were then discarded if the consensus still had four or fewer loci. Genotypes were considered identical when they matched at all loci or all but one locus. We used the multilocus analysis in GenAlEx v 6.5 (Peakall and Smouse, 2012) to find genotyping matches.
We used GIMLET v. 1.3.2 (Valière, 2002) to determine error rates for each locus including the proportion of successful PCRs across all replicates, the proportion of allele dropout (ADO) which occurs when an allele of a heterozygous individual does not amplify in a PCR that is positive for the other allele, and the incidence of false alleles (FA) which occurs when a homozygote from the consensus genotype is typed as a heterozygote from repeated genotypes (Broquet and Petit, 2004). Using GIMLET v. 1.3.2, we also calculated the probability of identity (PI) and probability of identity for siblings (PI sibs ). PI is the probability that two individuals drawn at random from a population will have identical multilocus genotypes. The PI sibs is the probability that a parent or offspring of a particular individual or their siblings would have the same genotype.
We calculated the number of alleles, observed heterozygosity, expected heterozygosity and the inbreeding coefficient F IS using the unique consensus genotypes in GenAlEx v6.5. We tested for Hardy-Weinberg and genotypic linkage equilibrium using GENEPOP v4.2 (Rousset, 2008).
The number of otters at a site was estimated using the number of unique genotypes and using the program CAPWIRE that utilizes multiple observations of individuals within a sampling session to estimate population size (Miller et al., 2005). This program also accounts for potential capture heterogeneity (i.e. some individuals are captured more easily than others). We used the two innate rates model (TIRM) for all analyses. We analyzed data for each sampling session separately and across all sampling sessions. We then standardized all sites by the number of kilometers searched and used regression models (with intercept set at 0) to test whether the density of scats predicted the density of otters at a site estimated from the genetic data and from CAPWIRE. Samples with consensus genotypes were sexed using the male specific SRY primers SRY2F: 5 -GAGAATCCCCAAATGCAAAA-3 and SRY2R: 5 -CTGTATTCTCTGCGCCTCCT-3 developed by Mowry et al. (2011). These primers were originally designed to amplify a 111base pair fragment in male Nearctic river otters. Cloning of several PCR products (methods as above for microsatellite loci) indicated that these primers also amplify a portion of the SRY gene in marine otters. PCR conditions were the same as for the microsatellite loci except the annealing temperature was 55 • C and 40 cycles were used. We assigned samples as male when ≥3 amplifications had the PCR product and as female when ≥3 amplifications were blank.

[SECTION] genotyping
We collected 240 samples (68% fresh feces, 18% anal jelly [anal sac secretions], and 14% feces with anal jelly) which represented 45% of all feces present. A total of 133 samples (55%) were successfully amplified at five to seven loci (Online Appendix A). The remaining 107 samples were discarded, since they amplified at fewer than five loci. The genotyping success rate of anal jelly was higher (74% of 43) than that of feces with jelly (61% of 36) and feces (50% of 161) (X 2 = 7.98, df = 2, P = 0.02).
The seven loci were moderately polymorphic with an average of nine alleles (range 7-11) and an average observed heterozygosity of 0.55 (range 0.392-0.788) (Table 3). When all sites were analyzed as a single population, Rio18 and Pbra01Lf exhibited significant heterozygote deficits (P < 0.001) and Rio13Lf had a significant heterozygote excess (P = 0.003). None of the pairs of loci exhibited genotypic linkage disequilibrium. When analyzing each sampling site separately, Rio18 exhibited a significant heterozygote deficit only in SI (P = 0.001) and Pbra01Lf and Rio13Lf no longer exhibited deficits or excesses so we kept these loci in the consensus genotypes. The presence of a possible null allele in Rio18 may have reduced our ability to differentiate some individuals if they had the null allele present.
PCR success rate at a locus averaged 45% and ranged from a minimum of 19.5% for Pbra01 to a maximum of 60% for Rio13 (Table 4). Allelic dropout was high, averaging 34% and ranging from 22 to 48% while the incidence of false alleles was only 1.5% (Table 4). The probability of identity (PI) was 0.000048 for all sites combined and ranged from 0.00004-0.00160 across sites for genotypes with all seven loci and ranged from 0.021-0.002 for genotypes with only five loci (Table 5). The probability of discerning full siblings from each other (PI sibs ) was not very high, averaging 0.024 (range 0.01-0.05) across the seven sites for genotypes with seven loci. For

[SECTION] table 5
The probability of identity (PI) and probability of identity for full siblings (PI sibs ) for increasing number of typed loci at each sampling site (5 loci -O4OT17Lf, Pbra01Lf, Pbra02Lf, Pbra24Lf, Rio11, 6 loci previous five plus Rio13Lf, and 7 loci previous six plus Rio18). genotypes with only five loci there was no ability to differentiate siblings at a site with an average PI sibs of 0.10 (Table 5).

[SECTION] site

[SECTION] population estimation
A total of 80 individuals were identified across all sites and visits, ranging from four otters in PU to 16 otters in PC (Table 6). Of the 80 individuals identified, 41 were typed at all seven loci, 25 were typed at six loci, and 14 were typed at five loci. Overall, the number of unique individuals at a site does not stabilize by four visits although the sampling curve suggests the addition of new individuals is reduced by the fourth visit and may stabilize with several more visits to each site (Fig. 2). New individuals were identified during every visit, with the second visit having the highest number of individuals being detected for the first time. Most individuals (N = 63) were sampled only a single time whereas 17 individuals were sampled multiple times either during the same visit or across multiple visits. The average number of samples found for these individuals was 4.1 ± 0.70 SE (range 2-14). For these 17 individuals, distances between samples of the same individual ranged from less than a meter up to 6.4 km apart. Most (90.9%) of these samples were within 150 m of each other (159 of 175 pairwise distances within sites).
The sex ratio across sites was close to 1:1 with 39 females and 41 males. Within sites, the numbers of males and females were also similar (Table 6). Most of the individuals that were sampled multiple times were male (13 males, four females), although the individual with the greatest number of samples (N = 14) was a female. Overall, there was no difference in the number of samples collected from males and from females (58 female samples and 75 male samples, X 2 = 1.19, df = 1, P = 0.28) All of the individuals that were detected at distances greater than 200 m apart were male (N = four individuals). One male was at PP (520 m), one at QB (240 m) and two were from SI and ranged from 1.64-6.4 km apart.
We were able to estimate population size using CAPWIRE for 14 site visits that had recaptures during the same visit (Online Appendix B). For the remaining 14 site visits, all individuals were sampled only a single time during a visit or no samples were collected (Online Resources 2). We also estimated the total population size at a site by combining all data for the four visits. For most sites, the CAPWIRE point estimate of N was greater than the minimum estimated from the genetic data and was considerably higher than previous estimates based on sightings (Apaza and Romero, 2012;Valqui, 2012) (Table 6). The confidence intervals (95%) often included the minimum estimate from the genetic data but were fairly wide for most estimates, reflecting the high incidence of single captures in the data as evidenced by an average recapture of individuals of less than two during most visits with recaptures (Online Appendix B, Table 6). Our minimum estimate from the genetic data (80 individuals) was similar to visual estimates, about 1.3 fold greater than Apaza and Romero's (2012) visual estimate (31 individuals) and 0.95 fold greater than Valqui's (2012) visual estimate (35 individuals, excluding SI). Estimates of density ranged from 4.4 otters per km using only the minimum genetic estimate (N = 80 otters) to 12.6 otters per km when using all CAPWIRE estimates for each site across all four visits (N = 231 otters).
Both PU and especially PC had very high numbers of otters detected in a small area (Table 6). We removed these data points from most of the following regression analyses because they strongly influenced the overall results. There was a strong positive relationship between the minimum number of otters estimated from the genetic data across all four visits, even after both PC and PU were removed from the analysis (n = 5, y = 0.231x + 0, R 2 = 0.93, F 1,4 = 52.77, P = 0.005). Adding PU into the analysis gives a similar relationship (n = 6, y = 0.186x + 0, R 2 = 0.98, F 1,5 = 300.05, P = 0.00006) (Fig. 3a). The relationship based on estimates from CAPWIRE across all four visits was non-linear when both PC and PU were removed (n = 5, y = 0.024X 2 + 1.261X + 2.92, R 2 = 0.36) (Fig. 3b) and strongly linear (y = 0.376x + 0, R 2 = 0.75) when PU was included although this data point has high leverage in the regression model.

[SECTION] materials and methods

[SECTION] study area
Our work was conducted in the Nakai-Nam Theun (NNT) National Protected Area (NPA; 3532 km 2 ) and adjoining areas, especially the Nakai Plateau, of Laos (Fig. 1). In and around the NNT NPA, elephants occur on the Nakai Plateau (1250 km 2 ) and range into the lower NNT NPA and the Nakai-Nam Theun-Phou Hin Poun (NNT-PHP) Corridor (738 km 2 ) that links the NNT NPA with the Phou Hin Poun NPA. The NNT NPA is dominated by dry broadleaved evergreen forest from 500-1800 m asl; the Nakai Plateau by a mosaic of pine/semi-evergreen forest, scrub, and cultivation at 500-600 m. Rainfall in the plateau area is highly seasonal, with a wet season between May and September and typical annual precipitation of c. 2400 mm.

[SECTION] dung-count based surveys
Dung count-based surveys were conducted to CITES Monitoring the Illegal Killing of Elephants (MIKE) Programme standards (Hedges and Lawson, 2006). From September 2004 to August 2005, we conducted a pilot survey to estimate dung-pile encounter rates using 'recce transects', in which teams walked on a compass bearing counting all dung-piles seen but without measuring the distance from the survey line to the dung-pile (Walsh and White, 1999). These pilot survey data were used to define two strata (low-and high-density) within the line transect survey area (Fig. 1). From 17 February to 6 May 2006, we used line transect methods to determine elephant dung-pile density (Buckland et al., 2001;Hedges and Lawson, 2006). The 1.5 km long transects were arranged in clusters along short baselines, with the clusters randomly located within strata and the line transects perpendicular to the Nam Theun river; there were 13 clusters in the high-density stratum and five clusters in the low-density stratum, and each cluster had eight line transects (Fig. 2).
Estimating elephant density from the dung-pile density requires data on rates of elephant defecation and dung-pile decay. Following Hedges and Lawson (2006), we used a mean defecation rate of 18.07 defecations per 24 h with standard error 0.0698; these data were derived from a study of free-ranging elephants in Indonesia (Hedges et al., 2005). We calculated dung decay rate using the method of Laing et al., (2003), which entails locating cohorts of fresh dung-piles prior to the line transect survey and then revisiting the marked dung-piles half-way through the line transect survey to establish whether they have decayed. We used logistic regression to characterize the probability of decay as a function of time, and estimated the mean time to decay from this function. We analyzed transect data using the program Distance (Thomas et al., 2010), which integrates information from the three parameters of interest (dung density, defecation rate, dung decay rate). Following Barnes (2001), we used PCCL, the ratio of the confidence limit (CL) to the estimate (N), expressed as a percentage (i.e. PCCL = (CL/N) Â 100) as a measure of precision.

[SECTION] fecal dna-based cmr surveys
From 16 September 2004 to 3 March 2005, we conducted a pilot survey to (1) assess whether fresh dung-piles could be found in adequate numbers; (2) determine whether sample preservation techniques were appropriate; (3) select loci likely to be informative for this population; and (4) help us design the CMR survey.
The  (Hedges and Lawson, 2006), we aimed to maximize capture rates by focusing on areas in which elephants are likely to be found ('hotspots' such as salt licks and waterholes) while also spacing sample collection so that every elephant's home range would contain at least 2-3 collection locations. Hedges and Lawson (2006) note that the distance between sample collection locations must be small if home ranges are expected to be small; if home ranges are large, the distance between sample collection locations can also be relatively large. For CMR sampling of tiger (Panthera tigris) populations using camera traps, Karanth and Nichols (2002) suggest deploying camera traps (which can be thought of as sample collection sites) 5-10 km apart for tigers with home ranges of 200-500 km 2 ; these broad guidelines are also appropriate for forest elephants -indeed, they are likely to be conservative as many elephant's home ranges will be larger (Hedges and Lawson, 2006). We identified 16 sample-collection blocks, each 2-8 km 2 (Fig. 2) and containing one or more 'hotspots' none of which were more than 10 km apart, with no part of the study area >10 km from a 'hotspot'. Thus, the study design provided full spatial coverage of the survey area in each sampling occasion, ensuring exposure of all elephants present to potential 'captures' and (2) equivalent areas of the Nakai Plateau were covered by both the fecal DNAand dung-count-based survey methods. Blocks were sampled at approximately 4-week intervals. All dung-piles sampled were destroyed afterwards to prevent accidental re-sampling. For each sample, approximately 10 g of dung was placed in a 40 ml polypropylene tube, boiled for 15 min, and preserved in Queen's College Buffer [20% DMSO, 100 mM Tris pH 7.5, 0.25 M EDTA, saturated with NaCl]. Samples were stored in the dark at room temperature before shipment to the laboratory under USDA permit number 48529.

[SECTION] determination of population age structure
Elephant size (a proxy for age) can be estimated from dung bolus size (e.g. Jachmann and Bell, 1984;Reilly, 2002;Tyson et al., 2002). Following Tyson et al. (2002), for each dung-pile sampled during the CMR survey, we measured (to the nearest cm) the maximum circumferences of the three largest intact boli, or all intact boli if <3 were present, and calculated a mean circumference. We then assigned age classes thus: mean circumference 6 30 cm = neonate/juvenile; 30 cm < mean circumference 6 42 cm = sub-adult; mean circumference > 42 cm = adult.

[SECTION] laboratory protocols
Total genomic DNA was extracted using the guanidine thiocyanate/silica protocol of Eggert et al. (2005). Simple tandem repeat, or microsatellite, loci were used to distinguish individuals by genotype and to estimate the level of genetic variability. We used several loci designed for the African elephant (Loxodonta africana), as well as nine dinucleotide loci characterized in the Asian elephant (Kongrit et al., 2008): EMU04, EMU07, EMU10, EMU12, EMU14, EMU15, EMU17, and EMU23. In addition, primers were redesigned for FH94 (Eggert et al., 2008), an African elephant locus that was found to be polymorphic in Asian elephants.
To test the power of these markers to distinguish individuals, genotyping results from the first subset of samples were analyzed using the Prob-id5 program (Waits et al., 2001). This program computes P(ID)random, the power to differentiate between randomly chosen individuals, as well as a more conservative measure, P(ID)sib, the power to differentiate between siblings. The results of the more conservative test were used to test the power of the loci used in this study (Waits et al., 2001).
Genotyping and genetic sexing methods are outlined in Ahlering et al. (2011). Final genotypes that contained at least six loci were retained in the study, while those with five or fewer were not included in the CMR analysis. Although these samples might have represented recaptures or unique individuals, the results of the P(ID)sib test indicated that with only five loci scored, there was a 0.007 probability that two siblings would be misidentified as the same individual, and with only four loci scored, that probability increased to 0.017. The best way to avoid this 'shadow effect', in which different individuals with similar genotypes are mistakenly counted as a single individual (Mills et al., 2000), is to genotype a sufficient number of highly polymorphic loci for all individuals in the study.
Genotypes were compared in Microsatellite Toolkit (Park, 2001) to identify those that differed at four or fewer alleles: each of these genotypes were rechecked for accuracy. We considered samples that differed at two or fewer alleles but matched in sex and had very similar bolus circumferences to be the same individual (Ahlering et al., 2011). Including erroneous genotypes as captures in the CMR analysis could have positively biased the estimate of population size (Creel et al., 2003).
Genotypes for the individuals detected were analyzed in Gene-Pop 3.1c (Raymond and Rousset, 1995) for departures from expectations under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium and for linkage disequilibrium. We then compiled capture histories for each unique genotype, which were analyzed using the program CAPTURE (Otis et al., 1978). Once again, we used PCCL as a measure of the precision of the resulting estimates.

[SECTION] dung-count based survey

[SECTION] dung decay rate estimation
A total of 1051 dung-piles were found throughout the study area, and monitored from September 2004 to March 2006. Logistic regression indicated a mean time to decay of 150.28 days (se = 2.77).

[SECTION] line transect-based survey
During the line transect-based survey, we found a total of 545 elephant dung-piles along 116 transects with total length 183.45 km in the high density stratum, but only one dung-pile along 56.63 km in the low density stratum (Fig. 1). Elephants appeared to be restricted to the high-density stratum and so a density estimate was not calculated for the low-density stratum. Moreover, our data (especially from the recce-and line-transects) and other data (Boonratana, 2000;Johnson and Johnston, 2007;Khounboline, 2002) indicated that our high-density stratum encompassed the entire dry season range of the Nakai elephant population. Applying a mean defecation rate of 18.07 (se = 0.0698) defecations per 24-h, we estimated elephant population density as 0.142 elephants/km 2 for the high-density stratum and population size as 141 (95% CI = [95,208]) elephants in the 989 km 2 this represented.

[SECTION] fecal dna-based survey and population structure
Because of the short survey duration (70 days), we could reasonably assume demographic closure (Karanth and Nichols, 1998). As already noted, our data (especially from the recce-and line-transects) plus others' data (Boonratana, 2000;Johnson and Johnston, 2007;Khounboline, 2002) all indicate that our high-density stratum survey area encompassed the entire dry season range of the Nakai elephant population, so we could also assume geographic closure. We analyzed 267 dung samples, of which 215 (81%) yielded sufficient genotypic information for analysis. However, only 19 samples were found in the third sampling session, so for the CMR analyses we treated these as extra-study samples and restricted the primary sampling period to the first two sessions, further strengthening the assumption of population closure. Within these two sampling sessions, 94 unique genotypes were detected; a further eight unique genotypes were detected during the extra study sessions. Of the recaptures, 27 were duplicate captures during the first session, 60 more were duplicate recaptures of the same individuals in the second session, and five were recaptures during the extra-study sessions. Thus, the CMR analysis was performed using 94 genotypes (40 in session one plus 54 in session two), with 20 of the individuals detected in the first session having been recaptured in the second session.
Population size estimation using model M(h) in CAPTURE suggests that there were 132 (se = 7.55; 95% CI = [120,149]) elephants in the Nakai Plateau population. There were an additional eight individuals detected in the extra-survey samples; these are included in the analysis of sex ratio and age structure (Tables 1 and2).
The 94 individuals identified comprised 27 males and 67 females, 17 (18%) juveniles, 29 (31%) sub-adults, 37 (39%) adults, and 11 (12%) undetermined (Tables 1 and2).

[SECTION] precision
Our dung survey estimate of 141 (95% CI = [95,208]) elephants yields a PCCL of 80.14% and our DNA CMR estimate of 132 (95% CI = [120,149]) elephants yields a PCCL of 21.97%.

[SECTION] costs incurred
Table 3 shows the costs incurred in conducting the two surveys and the estimated costs of repeating them at 2011 rates. The costs of the line transect survey comprise maintaining staff in the field to monitor dung decay rate prior to the line transect survey, and to conduct the line transect survey itself, and the necessary equipment. The costs associated with a fecal DNA CMR survey comprise maintaining sample collection teams in the field, field equipment, and laboratory analyses.

[SECTION] estimation of abundance from the two surveys
Our surveys were the first in mainland Southeast Asia to be conducted to MIKE standards. We estimated the size of the Nakai population as 141 (95% CI = [95, 208]) elephants using the dung count method and 132 (95% CI = [120,149]) elephants using the DNAbased CMR method. Although the two point estimates are similar, the DNA-based survey provided a much greater precision (PCCL 21.97% vs. 80.14%), at lower cost, more rapidly, and with additional information on population structure.
It is not possible to assess the accuracy of our population estimates, since the actual size of the surveyed elephant population is unknown. However, since (1) our simultaneously-conducted surveys returned two very similar estimates of the size of the Nakai elephant population with the confidence interval of the more precise CMR estimate contained completely within the confidence interval of the dung density based estimate and (2) the methods used have no assumptions in common and were conducted according to internationally-agreed standards for best practice (Hedges and Lawson, 2006), it seems likely that the survey results reflect the true abundance of elephants in the Nakai population.
The precision of our DNA-based survey compared well with that of other elephant surveys reviewed by Barnes (2001): for surveys returning an estimate of <1000 elephants median PCCL was 113% for aerial sample surveys (n = 38) and 45% for dung density surveys (n = 9). The relatively poor precision of our dung density based estimate probably reflects the very small population size, and the contribution of variance in three parameters -dung density, dung decay rate, and defecation rate (Plumptre, 2000).
We were only able to use the first two secondary sampling periods of the CMR survey because too few fresh dung piles were found in the third period. Although we were able to produce a population estimate using a CMR analysis, it is desirable to have at least five secondary sampling periods to facilitate the use of more refined models for data analysis (Otis et al., 1978;Williams et al., 2002).

[SECTION] comparison with photographic cmr methods
CMR methods are well developed with a solid statistical underpinning (Otis et al., 1978;Williams et al., 2002), and photographic CMR methods have become a standard tool for estimating the size and dynamics of animal populations (Karanth and Nichols, 1998;  Silver et al., 2004;Soisalo and Cavalcanti, 2006), including elephants (Goswami et al., 2007;Morley and van Aarde, 2007). However, CMR methods using either camera-traps or direct-sightings do not work for species in which individuals cannot easily be uniquely identified, and can be undermined by low detection rates where animals are wary or live at low densities. Camera trap-based CMR methods also require large numbers of camera traps, which are vulnerable to theft, damage, and high humidity (Mondol et al., 2009).

[SECTION] other evaluations of fecal dna-based cmr methods
There have been very few direct comparisons of the results of fecal DNA based CMR surveys and other independent surveys of the same population. For a review see Waits (2004); for specific examples involving coyotes (Canis latrans) see Kohn et al., (1999), for badgers (Meles meles) see Frantz et al., (2003), and for tigers see Mondol et al., (2009). In addition, Creel et al. (2003) used a wolf (Canis lupus) population of known size (41) to assess the impact of genotyping error on population size estimates from a census based on genetic analysis of feces and were able to tally 39 individuals (i.e. within 5% of the true population size). However, while this is obviously encouraging the study was not designed to assess the relative merits of non-invasive genetic and other survey methods, and did not use the CMR based methods which are likely to be preferred for most non-invasive population monitoring applications. Eggert et al. (2003) compared two genetic methods (rarefaction analysis and CMR) with a dung density based method to estimate the size of a population of African elephants, and while the results were encouragingly similar the dung count was not conducted simultaneously with the genetic sampling and the genetic sampling design was acknowledged to be suboptimal. Nevertheless, despite the cautionary remarks about the last two examples, it is clear that there are a growing number of fecal DNA-based CMR studies -including this one -which demonstrate that the combination of appropriate study design, rigorous sample collection and handling techniques, and the application of error-detection protocols produce accurate and precise population estimates.

[SECTION] advantages of fecal dna-based cmr methods for population estimation and monitoring relative to dung density-based methods
The methods evaluated here -dung counts using line transects and fecal DNA-based CMR surveys -are those typically recommended for estimating population size for elephants in forested areas (Hedges and Lawson, 2006) and are also appropriate for other species, such as ungulates and macropods. Dung density surveys are primarily suitable for relatively small areas because, before each survey can be conducted, a survey-specific dung decay rate needs to be estimated by monitoring a spatially representative sample of fresh dung piles across the survey area for long-enough that >90% of the first cohort of dung piles will have decayed by the time of the transect survey. This estimation is logistically challenging and time-consuming (e.g. P6 months in this study) but is vital because dung decay rates vary substantially in space and time, and using unrepresentative estimates would introduce biases of unknown magnitude (Hedges, 2012a;Hedges and Lawson, 2006;Kuehl et al., 2007;Laing et al., 2003). Elephant survey work in Asia has shown that such methods are feasible for survey areas of up to c. 5000 km 2 (Hedges, 2012b). For larger areas, the logistic challenges and cost become prohibitive; indeed, they are daunting even for considerably smaller areas. By contrast, fecal DNA-based CMR methods like those used in this study are much easier to implement because sample collection can focus on areas in which elephants (or other species) are likely to be found. Thus, DNA CMR methods can be used when estimating animal population size from dung density is not feasible. Moreover, the DNA CMR methods are quicker to implement than dung density-based methods. Indeed, CMR surveys should be completed as quickly as possible (typically over a 63-month period) to minimize the impacts of births, deaths, immigration, and emigration on the population estimate.
Our finding that the DNA CMR method provided a more precise estimate than the dung density methods is unsurprising, because the latter integrates estimates of dung density, dung decay rate, and detection rate, and the last two parameters are often highly variable (Hedges, 2012a;Kuehl et al., 2007;Plumptre, 2000). In addition, the DNA CMR method is expected to be, in general, more accurate because it avoids the problems of estimating a representative survey-specific dung decay rate: i.e. the difficulty of finding spatially representative samples of fresh dung piles across even relatively small survey areas (<5000 km 2 ) raises the possibility of using unrepresentative dung piles and thus inaccurate decay rates (Hedges, 2012a;Kuehl et al., 2007;Laing et al., 2003;Walsh and White, 2005).
Finally, the combination of genetic methods and CMR statistics provides researchers and wildlife managers with a much more informative means of monitoring populations than that provided by dung density-based methods since, in addition to population size, it becomes possible to assess population sex-structure, fecundity, genetic diversity, gene flow, and other parameters without needing to see an animal. Moreover, if the DNA CMR surveys are repeated it also becomes possible to study population dynamics, including survival and recruitment rates.

[SECTION] cost implications
The cost-effectiveness of a survey method is clearly an important consideration. Advances in sequencing technologies and the development of multiplex protocols have reduced the costs of genotyping fecal samples over the last decade (Beja-Pereira et al., 2009;Eggert pers obs.;Schwartz et al., 2007), but the perception remains that DNA-based methods are prohibitively expensive. It is therefore useful to compare the typical costs of conducting a DNA-based CMR and a dung density based survey. Let the cost of a DNA CMR survey be represented by C + L and the cost of a dung density-based survey be represented by D + T, where C = CMR field survey costs, L = laboratory costs, D = dung decay rate monitoring costs, and T = line transect field survey costs. In most cases, T % C, because a similar number of people is needed in the field for a similar length of time. Hence, the relative costs of DNA-based CMR and dung count-based methods can be assessed by comparing D with L. In this study, D and L were approximately equal in 2006 but L was significantly lower than D at 2011 rates (Table 3). More generally, D will often exceed L because the time needed to estimate dung decay can easily be 3-12 months depending on local conditions and significant manpower and other resources will always be required if dung decay rates are to be estimated in a spatially unbiased manner (Section 4.4).

[SECTION] application of dna-based cmr methods to surveys of large areas
Despite the strengths of fecal DNA-based methods, there are practical limitations which currently preclude their use for population surveys over very large areas such as those occupied by elephants in Central Africa or Southern India. For example, Lukacs and Burnham (2005, p. 3914) suggest that fecal DNA-based methods are only likely to be appropriate when elephant population size is smaller than 'a few thousand individuals', because otherwise a very large number of samples would have to be collected and analyzed making the cost prohibitive. So, how can we estimate and monitor elephant population size reliably in large forested landscapes containing large populations?
Recent advances in occupancy survey methods (Hines et al., 2010;Mackenzie et al., 2009;Nichols et al., 2008) and especially the integration of population estimation at two geographic scales -occupancy across large landscapes and abundance in selected areas within those landscapes (e.g. Conroy et al., 2008) -present what is probably the most reliable currently-available method for estimating the abundance of elephants (and other species) in large landscapes. Adapting the approach of Conroy et al. (2008) for use in estimating the abundance of elephants across a large landscape would involve, in a first phase, estimating occupancy from surveys to detect elephant sign (dung piles) in all selected sites in the landscape (where selection would be of all sites available (if possible), or a random sample of sites (if not)). In a second phase, if a detection threshold had been achieved in the first phase, fecal DNAbased CMR sampling would be conducted to estimate elephant abundance. Alternatively, following Conroy et al. (2008), in landscapes where the elephant population is likely to be highly overdispersed, CMR sampling would be conducted in a randomly selected set of sites (from which detection samples are also taken). In addition, population-size constraints might need to be applied to the definition of sites to keep population size per site below a few thousand elephants. Detection and CMR data would then be used in a joint likelihood approach to model probability of detection in the occupancy sample via an abundance-detection model. Capture-recapture modeling would then be used to estimate abundance for the abundance-detection relationship, which could be used to predict abundance at the remaining sites, where only detection data were collected. Practical evaluations of this approach are needed but it appears to be a promising way of extending the power of the DNA-based CMR methods demonstrated in this study to those very large areas for which there are currently no appropriate methods for estimating elephant abundance.

[SECTION] other constraints on the use of fecal dna-based methods
Fecal samples are not covered by CITES' restrictions but a number of countries do not allow the export of fecal samples for intellectual property related reasons. In such cases, the laboratory work would have to be done in country. Unfortunately, there are still relatively few laboratories able to analyze fecal DNA samples to the necessary standard and this can pose a significant constraint on the use of these methods. Nevertheless, the number of suitable laboratories is growing and the authors of this paper, the CITES MIKE programme's Technical Advisory Group, and the IUCN/SSC elephant specialist groups can provide advice on suitable laboratories.
