[SECTION] materials and methods

[SECTION] study area
We carried out this study in the Białowieża Primeval Forest (BPF, 52º30'-53º00' N, 23º30'-24º15' E), located in Eastern Poland on the Polish-Belarussian border. The BPF is a temperate mixedlowland forest, characterized by a high percentage of natural stands (Faliński 1986). It constitutes a relatively well distinguished patch of forest habitat within the matrix of human-dominated land (Fig. 1). The total area of the forest is 1500 km 2 , but only 600 km 2 is on the Polish side. The Polish part of the forest consists of fragments under various protection regimes, including the Białowieża National Park (BNP, 100 km 2 ) with a 50 km 2 of a strictly protected zone, a network of nature reserves covering nearly 180 km 2 and the remaining part managed by the state forestry. The area is flat and easily accessible for vehicles by a dense network of dirt roads that usually follow a regular grid of square forest compartments (approx. 1 x 1 km). The average temperature during the study was -3.9º C in the winter (December-March) and 19.1º C in the summer (June-September). Snow cover persisted for an average of 96 days per year from November to March.
In 1994, the lynx population in the Polish part of BPF was estimated by snow-and radiotracking at 29 individuals (Jędrzejewski et al. 1996). However, despite being fully protected since 1995 the population apparently decreased by about 30-35% in 200330-35% in -200630-35% in (Schmidt 2008)). Due to an isolated character of the BPF and high reliance of lynx on the forest cover (Podgórski et al. 2008), this population comprises a relatively isolated entity, which is sharply genetically distinct from neighboring populations (Schmidt et al. 2009;Ratkiewicz et al., 2012).

[SECTION] monitoring the spatial distribution of lynx individuals
We collected data on lynx spatial distribution by two supplementary methods: live-trapping for the telemetry monitoring and genotyping of hair samples obtained by hair-trapping (Schmidt & Kowalczyk 2006;Davoli et al. 2013). For this study we used spatial data on a total of 28 individuals: 11 live-trapped and 17 hair-trapped (see Appendix 1).

[SECTION] telemetry
Five male and six female lynx were live-trapped using either foot-snare traps (Breitenmoser 1989) set at fresh ungulate kills or wooden box-traps (Kolbe et al. 2003) and monitored with telemetry in 2004 -2011. The traps were equipped with radio-alarm systems (Wagener Telemetrieanlagen HF-NF Technik, Köln, Germany and Abratronik, Wrocław, Poland) that allowed us to remotely control trapping and minimize the time animals spent in the traps. Lynx were immobilized by a mixture of ketamine hydrochloride (5 mg/kg of body weight) and xylazine hydrochloride (6 mg/kg of body weight). The effect of xylazine was reversed with atipamezole hydrochloride (0.5 mg/kg). The age of live trapped lynx was estimated at the time of capture by a method based on canine gum recession developed for mountain lions (Puma concolor) (Laundré et al. 2000). To estimate the rate of growth of lynx teeth we used the canine measurements of a lynx male (not genotyped for this study) twice captured in BPF (in 2004 and2011;authors' unpublished data).
Ten lynx were equipped with VHF radio-collars (Wagener Telemetrieanlagen, Germany) and one male (Lly28) was fitted with a GPS collar (Vectronic, Germany). The collars weighed approximately 230-280 g (1-2% of the lynx body mass). Blood samples (1 ml) for genetic analyses were drawn from a radial vein with an EDTA vacutainer, and stored frozen at -20°C.
All collared lynx, except Lly28, were radio-tracked with standard VHF telemetry. We aimed to obtain one location during the day and one at late evening every day, however, approximately 20% of searches failed due to the large size of a lynx home range. Locations taken by triangulation were superimposed onto topographic maps with a 1 : 50000 scale, and recorded to the nearest 50 m. The only GPS collar (Lly28) was set to obtain four locations per day (three during the most active time from 21:00 to 03:00 and one at midday). In total, 2579 telemetry locations were collected with an average of 247 per individual. Lynx were radio-tracked from 1 to 27 months with an average of 14.9 months per individual. Six radio-tracked lynx were also monitored genetically by hair-sampling, with four of them recorded by this means already before the radio-tracking period. This increased their total monitoring time to 4-6 years (Appendix 1). From among the remaining five radio-tracked lynx that were not recorded by hair-sampling, four individuals were trapped two years after terminating the hair-trapping study (although based on their age at least three of them could have potentially existed in the population during hair-trapping) and one was a female kitten (11 months old) that died one month after trapping.The license for lynx live-trapping and blood sampling was obtained from the National Ethics Committee for Animal Experiments (no: DB/KKE/PL -110/2001) and the Local Ethics Committee for Animal Experiments at the Medical University of Białystok (no: 52/2007).

[SECTION] non-invasive sampling
Hair-trapping was conducted in 2004-2006 using a hair-sampling system developed for Canada lynx (McDaniel et al. 2000) and modified for the Eurasian lynx, as described in detail by Schmidt and Kowalczyk (2006). We placed hair-traps (8 x 8 cm pieces of carpet supplied with 10 nails) directly on the objects identified by snow-tracking as being scent-marked by lynx. The hairtrapping sites were spaced at 1-2 km intervals and distributed along forest roads in the entire Polish part of BPF (Fig. 1). To evoke cheek-rubbing in lynx we applied to each trap a mixture of beaver castoreum and catnip oil (Schmidt & Kowalczyk 2006). We conducted the surveys in 2004-2006, at different times of year and in sessions lasting 7-13 weeks, with 36-113 (mean ± SD = 85.2 ± 29.0) scent-stations per session, but the majority of samples (73%) were collected in winter-spring months (December -April). As this period includes the mating season in lynx (Schmidt et al. 1997) it warrants highest probability of detecting both males and females widely ranging during this time.
Considering the average size of lynx home ranges in BPF, there were approximately 30 traps distributed per home range. We attempted to check and re-bait hair-traps every 10-14 days though the actual range of intervals was 1-23 days. Hairs were dried at a temperature 30-40ºC and stored in paper envelopes at room temperature, in plastic boxes with silica gel (following Wasser et al. 1997;Roon et al. 2003).

[SECTION] genotyping methodology
In total, 349 lynx-hair samples were collected during the study. However, only 170 samples provided enough (>10) hairs with roots for genetic analyses. We analysed 11 blood samples collected from live-trapped lynx. The DNA extraction and amplification were undertaken following the protocol described by Davoli et al. (2013). Individuals were genotyped using 12 autosomal microsatellite loci, which were originally described in the domestic cat (Menotti-Raymond et al. 1999). See Appendix 2 for details of the genetic protocols. The PCR products were obtained for 96 hair samples of which 85.4% provided reliable genotypes. Twenty four reliable hair-genotypes were determined from among all the hair-samples, but we excluded from spatial analyses the unsexed individual. The hair-determined genotypes were resampled on average 3.9 times (range: 1 -14).
More than half of the genotypes (14/24) were re-sampled 3-14 times, whilst the others were sampled only once.

[SECTION] spatial analyses
To minimize a bias potentially resulting from small sample size we adopted two approaches for the spatial analyses: 1) calculation of the degree (%) of overlap between home ranges and 2) measurement of distances between the centers of home ranges or locations of single-sample hair genotypes. With this double-checking we aimed at ensuring higher certainty of obtained results with a maximum use of collected data. The spatial analyses were done with the Biotas TM software.
To estimate the overlap between home ranges we combined data from the telemetry and hair-trapped genotypes. According to our previous study, although the hair-trapping does not allow for reliable estimation of the actual home range size, the problem of low sample size can be partly compensated by its simultaneous use with other methods, such as telemetry (Davoli et al. 2013). Thus, we applied following additional procedure to minimize possible underestimation of home range size with hair sampling: 1) we considered only the hair-trapped genotypes represented by minimum 4 samples; 2) we excluded from the overlap analyses two genotypes which were recorded within an area smaller than 10 km 2 despite being represented by more than 4 samples; 3) in result of this selection only three hair-genotyped lynx individuals (whose home ranges were estimated at 49.1, 129.8 and 184.6 km 2 ) were used for overlap analyses. The number of locations considered for home range estimation in the case of lynx monitored with telemetry ranged from 10 (a single female kitten that died during dispersal one month after trapping) to 453. We estimated home range sizes using the 100% Minimum Convex Polygon method. We calculated an average overlap for each lynx pair according to following formula: (Ov/hr1+Ov/hr2)/2 x 100, where hr1 and hr2 are the home range sizes and Ov is the area of overlap between the ranges. We analyzed the association between the home range overlap (between both radio-tracked and hair-sampled individuals) and relatedness for a total of 14 individuals, but only 57 lynx pairs provided sufficient data for analyses due the procedure of data selection as mentioned above.
To measure distances between lynx we used two sets of data. Firstly, we calculated the harmonic mean centers of home ranges using the Biotas TM software (for both the radio-tracked and multi-sample, hair-trapped individuals). Secondly, we used the locations of single-sampled hairgenotypes and considered them as the centers of their home ranges. As we were aware that single location may incidentally occur at the edge of the home range, and thus potentially introducing a bias for the true distances between the home range centers we tested for the effect of sample size on the pair-wise distances. We compared three sets of distances data: 1) between pairs of lynx including at least one individual sampled at single location (mean ± SD = 14.89 ± 8.73 km, n = 95); 2) between pairs including at least one individual sampled at 3 to 10 locations (15.34 ± 8.72 km, n = 77) and 3) between pairs sampled at > 10 locations (17.46 ± 8.12 km, n = 52) with ANOVA and found no significant differences (F (2, 221) = 1.57, p>0.2,). We additionally selected a fourth set of distances data for those pairs including both single-sampled lynx (mean ± SD = 13.46 ± 8.46 km, n = 18) and ran ANOVA for all four groups of pair-wise distances and again obtained no significant differences (F = 1.41, p>0.2, df = 3). Therefore, we pooled both sets of data and measured the Euclidean distance between both types of points using the Biotas TM . We examined the relationship between distances and relatedness for a total of 225 pairs of lynx (28 individuals).
During the spatial analyses we used pairs of individuals or genotypes monitored in the same years, with the exception of pairs Lly02-Lly08 and Lly12-Lly31. The former case involved a likely father (a hair-trapped and radio-tracked male in 2005-2009) and son (the only hair-trapped male in 2004) with disjunctive home ranges. Based on the estimated age of Lly02 and his likely paternal bonds with Lly08, we assumed that he was also present in BPF during 2004 (Appendix 1). We undertook a similar assumption in the case of the Lly12-Lly31 pair -a likely mother (radio-tracked and hair-trapped in [2004][2005] and her daughter (radio-tracked in 2009-2010).

[SECTION] statistical analyses
We calculated basic genetic data (allelic frequencies, observed and expected unbiased heterozygosity, mean number of alleles per locus, departures from the Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium and probability of identities) using the software GenAlEx 6.5b5 (Peakall & Smouse 2006: http://biology.anu.edu.au/GenAlEx). We calculated Wright's inbreeding estimator (F IS ) and pairwise linkage equilibrium (LD) using the software Genetix 4.05 (Belkhir et al.1996(Belkhir et al. -2004: : http://kimura.univ-montp2.fr/genetix).
To account for possible bias related to inferring the relatedness between genotypes of lynx we used different software to analyze the relationship between individuals in the population. We estimated pair-wise coefficients of relatedness based on the Lynch and Ritland (1999) method on the GenAlEx software and the maximum likelihood relatedness on the ML-Relate software (Kalinowski et al. 2006). The ML-relate procedure uses Milligan's (2003) maximum likelihood estimator. It calculates the probabilities that the given genotypes are observed on the assumption that the two individuals are parent-offspring/full-sibs/half-sibs/nonrelatives and these four relationships are evenly distributed in the population. However, it must be noted that the a'priori distribution of the four relationships is unknown and there is actually more than four possible relationships. Therefore, the inferred relationships should be treated with caution. The pedigree was reconstructed from the individual genotypes analysis using both Colony v. 2.0.5.0 (Jones & Wang 2009) and FRANz v. 2.0.0 (Riester et al. 2009). The FRANz reconstructed pedigree was drawn using Graphviz v. 2.34.
We tested the correlation between the relatedness coefficient (Lynch & Ritland 1999) and spatial distribution (both the degree of overlap and distance) in four sets of data: female-female, male-male, male-female and all lynx pooled. We performed the Mantel test (Mantel 1967) using the "zt" software (Bonnet & Van de Peer 2002) with the randomization of 100,000 iterations for all comparisons (with  set at 0.0005, adjusted to the number of iterations as suggested by the software). We used bootstrapping method (with1000 replications) to test for significance of differences in average relatedness between sex dyads with the COANCESTRY software v. 1.0.1.5 (Wang 2011). The differences in pair-wise distances and pair-wise overlap between the gender and kinship classes were tested with Kruskal-Wallis ANOVA. Both, GLM and ANOVA were conducted on the Statistica v. 9.1 software (StatSoft Inc.).
We also performed a spatial autocorrelation using the GenAlEx software with the "Single Pop" method, assuming a single population using a single genetic distance matrix. We assumed significance of the heterogeneity tests at the level of p<0.01, following Banks and Peakall (2012).

[SECTION] individual identifications and relatedness in the lynx population
We identified twenty eight lynx individuals (15 males and 13 females) by genotyping either the live-captured and radio-tracked lynx (in 2004 -2011) or hair-trapped samples (in 2004 -2006).
The 12 autosomal microsatellites amplified reliably either in blood and or hair-trapped samples with the average allelic drop out (ADO) and false allele (FA) rates 0.034 and 0.000 for invasive samples and 0.207 and 0.003 for non-invasive ones. Individual genotype reliability values ranged from 0.9 to 1.0. All microsatellites except of one (Fca023) were polymorphic, showing from 2 to 7 alleles per locus. The average observed and unbiased expected heterozygosity were H o = 0.540 (SE 0.073) and UH e = 0.506 (SE 0.062). All loci were in HWE at threshold p = 0.01. The individual genotypes differed by minimum 2 or more alleles, but only three genotype pairs (Lly03-Lly24, Lly13-Lly27 and Lly21-Lly31) differed at two loci and only one genotype pair (Lly12-Lly21) differed at three loci. The cumulative probability of identity values with 11 loci (the monomorphic locus Fca023 was excluded) were PID = 2.5 x 10 -7 and PID sibs = 1.1 x 10 -3 , suggesting that a "shadow effect" was unlikely. The 28 genotypes were used for analyses of relatedness and the spatial relationships between individuals.
Of these, 11 lynx (5M, 6F) were live trapped and radio-tracked. The period of monitoring these particular individuals, by combination of radio-tracking and hair-trapping, was from one to six years (mean 2.0 years). Average (±SD) relatedness (Lynch & Ritland 1999 estimator ranging from -∞ to +1) in the lynx population of Białowieża Primeval Forest for all pairs of individuals monitored in the same years (N = 225) was relatively low (-0.03±0.23; Table 1). The relatedness between females (0.05±0.23) was, however, significantly higher than between males and females (-0.06±0.25) (bootstrapping method: difference between means: 0.108; (95% CI: -0.077-0.095); p<0.05) (Table 1). There was no difference in average relatedness between other sex dyads (female-female : male-male difference: 0.076 (95% CI: -0.089 -0.097); male-female : male-male difference: 0.032 (95% CI: -0.065 -0.071); p>0.05).

[SECTION] pedigree analysis
From among 225 pairwise estimates of relatedness calculated with the ML-Relate software, 76.4% were found to be unrelated (Table 2). Only 10.7% of lynx pairs were identified as having parent-offspring relationships. Full siblings were identified in 4.4% of cases and half-siblings in 8.4% of cases. Among the 28 genotypes four groups of individuals interconnected by direct parentoffspring relationships were distinguished (Fig. 2). However, the majority of the population was dominated by only two of the parental-lines with one, originating from a pair MLly03-FLly12, being most numerous (35.7% of all genotypes). Within the largest parental line, mating occurred with different partners both in the case of male and female lynx (e.g. male MLly03 sired offspring with female FLly12, but he was also the father of two kittens with another unidentified female; female FLly12 except a kitten sired with MLly03 had three more offspring with another unsampled male Fig.

[SECTION] 2).
The parental relationships determined by FRANz (Fig. 2) were confirmed in five cases by Colony software (Fig. 2) and in ten cases by ML-Relate (Appendix 3). Colony identified three fathers and five mothers among all the possible pair-wise combinations of the 28 lynx genotypes (Fig. 1). On the other hand, the ML-Relate program failed to detect an evident mother-daughter relationship between the lynx Lly12 and Lly21, which were blood-sampled and radio-tracked simultaneously for a period of 50 days (Fig. 1 and2). It was, however, confirmed by both the FRANz and Colony software.

[SECTION] relationship between pair-wise relatedness and spatial distribution of lynx individuals
The average (±SD) distance between the centers of the harmonic mean home ranges of lynx pairs or the points of single-hair sampling was 15.7±8.6 km, while the home ranges overlapped on average by 20.9±23.5% for all pair-wise comparisons (Table 1). No differences between kinship classes (parent-offspring, full sibling, half sibling and unrelated) within sex groups (the same sex and male-female group) were found, neither in distance nor home range overlap (Table 2). There were also no differences between sex groups within particular kinship classes in either of the spatial indices.
The distribution of lynx pairs identified as parent-offspring within Białowieża Forest showed a random character, with some pairs occupying close locations and others distantly spaced regardless of the sex (Fig. 1). A slight, and insignificant, negative correlation between pair-wise distances and kinship was revealed by the Mantel test (Table 1) for all pairs of lynx. Interestingly, a negative, significant correlation between the pair-wise distance and relatedness was revealed in the case of male-female pairs (R=-0.27, p<0.00001, Table 1, cf. Fig. 3). This suggests that male and female lynx tend to stay closer to each other if they are closely related. On the other hand, no significant relationship between either the distance or the overlap and the relatedness was found in the remaining comparisons within the same sex or different sex subsamples (Table 1). Analysis of the spatial autocorrelation in GenAlEx has confirmed an insignificant relationship between the genetic relatedness and the pair-wise distance between lynx (Fig. 4).

[SECTION] figure captions
The multiple-tubes genotyping protocol
We used the multiple-tubes procedure to test for amplification errors and genotyping hair samples according to following steps: 1) A screening step was designed to identify and remove lowquality DNA samples. All samples were amplified four times at two loci (Fca008 and Fca149) selected for their good amplification rates and reliability; samples showing <= 50% positive PCR (PCR+) were removed. 2) All samples which passed the screening were further processed to obtain four additional PCR replicates per locus. Multilocus genotypes were analysed with software RELIOTYPE (Miller, Joyce and Waits 2002), which computes the maximum-likelihood of each genotype in the sampled population (reliability score R), and estimates the number of additional replicates needed for each locus to obtain a reliable genotype (see step 3). Maximum-likelihood estimates are obtained assuming that allele frequencies of the sampled population are known. Reference allele frequencies were estimated from the genotypes of 11 individual blood samples collected from captured lynx. We used RELIOTYPE with the default settings. A sample was accepted as reliable if R > 0.95. Each allele was accepted as "true" if it has been seen at least twice in PCR replicates at putative heterozygous loci, or at least three times at putative homozygous loci. 3) Samples with low amplification success and R < 0.95 were further replicated four times. A final reliability analysis led to definitive genotype acceptance (if R > 0.95) or rejection. Reliable genotypes were used to identify the consensus genotypes, using GIMLET 1.3.3 (Valière, 2002) with the threshold method: an allele was retained in the consensus genotype if it was scored at least two times. The consensus genotypes were used as "true" reference genotypes to compute the frequency of PCR errors. The blood samples were replicated twice using the same multiple-tubes protocol.
PCR errors are expressed per-genotype as the observed number of erroneous genotypes divided by the number of genotypes in which an error could have been observed (Broquet and Petit, 2004). Allelic dropout (ADO) was counted as the proportion of alleles which did not amplify per each heterozygous locus. False alleles (FA) were identified as follows: 1) alleles originating from nonspecific amplifications were identified by their molecular weight which was outside the range detected in the reference genotypes; all those FA were easily identified and not recorded; 2) alleles originating from cross-sample laboratory contaminations during PCR processing: alleles showing the molecular weight of true alleles were defined as FA if they were detected only once at least in seven replicated PCRs; accepting these alleles could have led to define false heterozygotes (Taberlet et al. 1996; 3) alleles originating from mixed samples, that is from DNA extracted from samples containing hair from more than one individual (Roon et al. 2005). In these cases, three or four distinct alleles could be detected at some polymorphic loci. Only the last two kinds of FA were recorded.

[SECTION] materials and methods

[SECTION] sampling
Sampling was performed in the continental part of Croatia from colonies in Ćošak Šume (Kopački Rit Nature Park, 45°38.15′N, 18°50.76′E) and at the Jelas fishpond (near the Sava River, 45°08.27′N, 17°48.08′E) during regular monitoring and ringing in 2015. We sampled three species: the Great Egret (Ardea alba), the Purple Heron (Ardea purpurea), and the Grey Heron (Ardea cinerea) (Table ). We collected noninvasive samples of contour (molted) feathers and eggshells; these were harvested around nests of the Great Egret and the Grey Heron. Only contour (molted) feathers with transparent calamus and intact barbs on the vane were collected. The Purple Heron and the Great Egret were sampled during ringing; from each nestling of the Great Egret and Purple Heron, two pin (blood) feathers were plucked (Table ). The samples were stored in paper envelopes at room temperature and kept separately to avoid cross-contamination.

[SECTION] isolation of genomic dna
Isolation of DNA from each sample type was performed twice; the DNA was placed in two separate tubes and then used in two different extraction protocols. In detail, the tips of the pin feathers (two from each nestling) were cut into pieces of 3 to 5 mm long. The calamus of the contour feather (molted) was cut in half and placed into two separate tubes. From the eggshell, a piece of vascularized membrane was excised and cut into smaller fragments. From the same eggshells, the external surface was swabbed as described by Schmaltz et al. (2006) by using cotton tips. To avoid cross-contamination with nestling DNA, swabs were taken only from eggshells that did not have blood smears (which could have come from the mother) on the surface. A similar amount of each sample was used for both DNA extraction protocols.
We used two methods to extract DNA from noninvasive samples (Table ). Genomic DNA was isolated using the DNeasy Blood and Tissue Kit (QIAGEN, Germany) and a standard protocol for DNA isolation according to De Volo et al. (2008). For DNA isolation with the DNeasy Blood and Tissue Kit, manufacturer instructions were followed. De Volo et al. 's protocol was modified as follows: samples were incubated in 360 µL of extraction buffer containing 10 mM Tris-Cl (pH 8.0), 10 mM EDTA, 100 mM NaCl, 2% sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS, Carl Roth GmbH, Germany), 40 mM dithiothreitol (DTT, Carl Roth GmbH), and 2 mg/mL proteinase K (Carl Roth GmbH) in final concentrations. Furthermore, after overnight incubation at 56 °C, keratin, vascularized membranes, and cotton tips were precipitated with 300 µL of 3 M sodium acetate (Carl Roth GmbH). Samples were vortexed, incubated on ice, and centrifuged at 4 °C and 16,000 × g for 10 min. Genomic DNA in the supernatant was precipitated at -20 °C for 30 min with the addition of 1:1 isopropanol (v/v). Samples were centrifuged again, and the pellet was washed with 70% ethanol. After centrifugation, DNA was air-dried and dissolved in 40 µL of nuclease-free water (Promega, USA). DNA quantity (concentration) and quality (A 260 / A 280 ) were quantified using a NanoPhotometer (Implen GmBH, Germany).

[SECTION] the chd-based molecular sexing protocol
Sex-specific fragments of the CHD gene were amplified with primer pair 2550F/2718R (Fridolfsson and Ellegren, 1999) in a total volume of 20 µL. The PCR reaction contained 10 µL of Takara Emerald Mix (Clontech, USA), 2 µM of each primer, and 30-50 ng of genomic DNA. The  ). We were unable to extract DNA from one contour feather of Great Egret using the commercial kit as opposed to isolation with the standard protocol. When the two isolation protocols were compared, results showed that the highest DNA yield was obtained from pin feathers and the lowest yield from contour feathers (Table ). Isolation procedure did not influence DNA quality (ratio A 260 /A 280 ) in feathers (contour and pin) or eggshells. All samples had relatively good DNA quality (1.8-2.0) except for swabs and one eggshell, and these two samples had a lower DNA quality (0.610-1.639).
The primer set 2550F and 2718R was efficient in heron sex identification for both extraction protocols (Figure 1). In subsequent sex-typing of ringed birds, we used the modified standard protocol for DNA extraction. Results of molecular sexing based on DNA obtained from pin feathers of Grey Egret and Purple Heron nestlings are presented in Figure 2. PCR bands were clearly visible in all tested samples, showing a size of 450 bp for the W-chromosome and 600 bp for the Z-chromosome. All the Purple Heron nestlings were males, whereas nestlings of the Great Egret were females.
For the Grey Heron, amplification of the CHD gene was successful only for three eggshells; it indicated two males and one female. Of three swab samples taken from the aforementioned eggshells, only one sample was successfully amplified, showing the CHD-Z fragment indicating a male. Amplification failed for the other seven collected samples even though they did not have a lower DNA concentration (19-23 ng/µL) than those with successful amplification (23-50 ng/µL).

FILE: Wildlife Society Bulletin - 2015 - Lonsinger - Evaluating the reliability of field identification and morphometric.grobid.tei.xml
====================================================================================================
[SECTION] (no title)
The development of sound and effective management and conservation strategies for wildlife populations requires reliable and accurate information on species distributions and population trends. For carnivores, invasive monitoring methods requiring capture and handling of animals can be challenging and costly, often limiting their utility for large spatial extents or long-term monitoring (Gese 2001, MacKenzie 2005, Gompper et al. 2006). Noninvasive surveys (Long et al. 2008, Kelly et al. 2012) are an appealing alternative for monitoring populations because they are simple, cost-efficient, and facilitate multispecies monitoring (Gompper et al. 2006). For many elusive or rare species, such as carnivores, scats are often the most conspicuous indication of their presence and therefore noninvasive scat surveys are a widely used means of monitoring populations (e.g., Prugh and Ritland 2005, Gompper et al. 2006, Harrington et al. 2010, Long et al. 2011). Scat surveys are frequently employed to delineate distributions (Kozlowski et al. 2012), assess relative abundances (Schauster et al. 2002, Cunningham et al. 2006, Kamler et al. 2013), develop models of resource selection (Vynne et al. 2011, Dempsey 2013), and evaluate occupancy patterns (Long et al. 2011, Schooley et al. 2012). Scat surveys can provide additional information on diet (Kozlowski et al. 2008, Marucco et al. 2008), resource partitioning (Vanak andGompper 2009, Kamler et al. 2012), and parasitology (Kohn and Wayne 1997). In addition, scat collections afford researchers the opportunity to obtain fecal DNA to assess measures of population genetics (Waits and Paetkau 2005), social and spatial ecology (Kitchen et al. 2005), and breeding strategies (Kitchen et al. 2006).
Correct inferences from scat surveys depend on accurate species identification, and misclassifications could bias results and potentially reduce the effectiveness of management strategies (Marucco et al. 2008, Harrington et al. 2010). Commonly, field-based species identification (hereafter, field identification) is determined through inspection of scat morphology including color, odor, overall size, and physical appearance (Vanak andGompper 2009, Kamler et al. 2012); this is often coupled with auxiliary information, such as presence of tracks, dietary content, or distance from a den, to improve field identification confidence (Green and Flinders 1981, Prugh and Ritland 2005, Harrington et al. 2010, Kozlowski et al. 2012, Schooley et al. 2012). However, sympatric carnivores may produce scats with overlapping sizes (Green and Flinders 1981, Danner and Dodd 1982, Farrell et al. 2000, Reed et al. 2004, Gompper et al. 2006), and auxiliary information may be lacking, misleading, or uninformative. For example, counter-marking is common among conspecifics (Ferkin and Pierce 2007) and may produce confounding sign; and dietary content may not contribute to improving field identification for species with high dietary overlap (Onorato et al. 2006, Foran et al. 1997). Consequently, carnivore scats can be difficult to discriminate and confidence in field identifications can be misleading or completely erroneous (Foran et al. 1997, Paxinos et al. 1997, Farrell et al. 2000, Davison et al. 2002, Harrington et al. 2010).
Molecular species identification (hereafter, molecular identification) provides a reliable alternative to field identification (Foran et al. 1997, Kohn and Wayne 1997, Farrell et al. 2000, Dalen et al. 2004, Prugh and Ritland 2005). Comparisons of field and molecular identifications have yielded contrasting results. Coyote (Canis latrans) scats could be distinguished from sympatric carnivores in Alaska, USA, with high accuracy using field identification (Prugh and Ritland 2005), whereas pine marten (Martes martes) and red fox (Vulpes vulpes) scats could not be confidently discriminated in Britain (Davison et al. 2002), and experienced researchers failed to successfully identify American mink (Neovison vison) scats in Scotland et al. 2010). Despite the challenges and ambiguity associated with field identification, many wildlife managers and researchers still rely on field identification, likely because of the increased costs associated with molecular identification. Conservation and management programs often suffer from limited funding and the number of imperiled species continues to rise, increasing the need to improve and evaluate cost-effective monitoring strategies (Gese 2001). We used molecular identification to evaluate the accuracy of field identification for scats of 2 sympatric carnivores, coyotes and kit foxes (V. macrotis), in the Great Basin desert of western Utah, USA. Coyote populations have increased notably over the past several decades at this site, where they are now the most abundant carnivore (Arjo et al. 2007). The kit fox is a species of conservation concern; kit foxes are significantly smaller than coyotes and have been experiencing population declines that have been contributed, in part, to increased competition with and predation by coyotes (Arjo et al. 2007). Consequently, multiple studies have been conducted in western Utah to investigate kit fox and coyote populations, some of which have employed scat surveys (Kozlowski et al. 2008(Kozlowski et al. , 2012;;Dempsey 2013;Dempsey et al. 2014). To evaluate alternative classifications to field and molecular identification, we explored 2 common nonparametric classification approaches-k-nearest neighbors and classification trees-based on morphometric measurements as objective, quantitative alternatives for discriminating scats. The k-nearest neighbor approach is among the simplest supervised classification algorithms and assigns an unknown observation to a class based on class majority of the k closest training observations within the parameter space (Cover andHart 1967, Hastie et al. 2001). Classification-tree analysis, or recursive partitioning, searches all possible binary splits of the predictor variables to identify splits that optimize classification (i.e., prediction of the species) and produces a decision tree that provides clear classification rules and information on variable importance (Breiman et al. 1984). Both k-nearest neighbor and classification-tree analyses require sufficiently large samples sizes, though, to develop training data sets. Consequently, using these approaches may restrict analyses to species with sufficient representation (i.e., adequate sample sizes to characterize the population), whereas field identification and molecular identification do not have this requirement. Focusing on 2 target carnivore species, we hypothesized that field identification would be more reliable for the abundant species (coyotes) than for the rarer species (kit foxes) as observed in other systems (Davison et al. 2002, Prugh andRitland 2005). We further hypothesized that scat diameters of the 2 species would overlap (e.g., Green andFlinders 1981, Danner andDodd 1982), but that inclusion of additional morphometric measurements (i.e., length and no. of disjoint segments) into nonparametric classification methods would provide a more accurate and objective method of identifying scats than would field identification.

[SECTION] study area
The study was centered on the eastern portion of the U.S. Army's Dugway Proving Ground, Utah, and extended to surrounding federal lands managed by the U.S. Bureau of Land Management (Fig. 1). Elevations across this Great Basin Desert site ranged from 1,228 m to 2,154 m (Arjo et al. 2007). Winters were cold ðJan: x high ¼ 48C; x low ¼ À108CÞ and summers were moderate ðJul: x high ¼ 368C; x low ¼ 158CÞ, with the majority of precipitation accumulating in the spring and autumn ( x annual precipitation approx. 20 cm; Arjo et al. 2007). The site was characterized at low elevations by cold desert playa (dominated by Allenrolfea occidentalis), cold desert chenopod shrubland (dominated by Atriplex confertifolia and Kochia americana) and vegetated dunes, along with nonnative invasive grasslands (Bromus tectorum), which dominated in disturbed areas. Higher elevations supported arid shrubland (e.g., Artemisia spp., Chrysothamnus viscidiflorus) and open woodland (Juniperus osteosperma) complexes. Sarcobatus vermiculatus shrubland was distributed across the elevational gradient of the site but found more often at moderate to higher elevations.

[SECTION] methods
Field sampling and identification of carnivore scats.-We conducted surveys for carnivore scats in the winter and summer of 2013 along transects that followed 2-track or gravel roads. We surveyed 30 transects (5 km each; including 15 transects previously utilized to develop a resource selection function for kit foxes (Dempsey 2013), evaluate survey methods for kit foxes (Dempsey et al. 2014), and to evaluate scat-deposition rates for kit foxes and coyotes (Lonsinger et al. 2015), and 15 additional random transects (Fig. 1). We conducted 3-4 surveys on each 5 km transect within each season. Additionally, we selected 240 shorter random transects (500 m each) that were surveyed once in each season (Fig. 1). Nine researchers participated in the surveys and were responsible for identifying and sampling scats. We surveyed each transect with 2 researchers, each searching half of the transect width for carnivore scats. When a carnivore scat was encountered, we determined field identification by inspecting the scat's morphology, including color, odor, overall size, and physical appearance (Kozlowski et al. 2012). We then collected a fecal DNA sample (approx. 0.7 mL) from the side of the scat (Stenglein et al. 2010), which was stored in 1.4 mL of DET buffer (20% DMSO, 0.25 M EDTA, 100 mM Tris, pH 7.5, and NaCl to saturation; Seutin et al. 1991). For a subset of scats sampled, we measured the diameter at widest point and total length with a sterilized digital caliper (resolution ¼ 0.1 mm; Mitutoyo America Corporation, Aurora, IL) and recorded the number of disjoint segments, prior to fecal DNA sample collection. When scats consisted of multiple disjoint segments, the total length was determined by summing the lengths of the segments. Scats that lacked the typical physical structure (e.g., soft piles for which accurate measurements could not be obtained) were not measured and were excluded from subsequent analyses. Mitochondrial DNA species confirmation.-We conducted fecal DNA extraction and mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) polymerase-chain reaction (PCR) amplification in a laboratory dedicated to low-quality and low-quantity samples such as fecal samples. We randomized samples and extracted fecal DNA using QIAamp DNA Stool Mini Kits (Qiagen, Inc., Valencia, CA) with negative controls to monitor for contamination (Taberlet et al. 1999, Beja-Pereira et al. 2009). We performed mtDNA species identification tests by amplifying fragments of the control region using established protocols and including negative controls to monitor for contamination (De Barba et al. 2014). Qiagen Master Mix (1 Â concentration), Q solution (0.5 Â concentration), and 1 mL of DNA extract were combined with species identification primers into a 7 mL (total vol) multiplex. The PCR conditions for each primer were as follows: 0.29 mM SIDL, 0.20 mM H16145, 0.10 mM H3R, 0.13 mM FelidID F, 0.03 mM LRuf F, and 0.03 mM PCon R. The PCR thermal profile had an initial denaturation of 958 C for 15 min, 35 cycles of 948 C for 30 sec (denaturation), 468 C for 90 sec and 728 C for 60 sec (elongation), and a final elongation stage of 608 C for 30 min. We conducted PCR on a BioRad Tetrad thermocycler (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA) and included negative and positive controls. We visualized results using a 3130xl DNA Analyzer (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA) and scored allele sizes with Genemapper 3.7 (Applied Biosystems). Species-specific PCR product lengths were 335-337 base-pairs (bp) for kit foxes and 115-120 bp and 359-363 bp for coyotes. For samples that failed to amplify for mtDNA, we repeated the species identification test once to minimize sporadic effects (e.g., pipetting errors; Murphy et al. 2007). We classified samples that contained DNA from multiple species as mixed and removed these samples and any samples that failed from subsequent analyses. We calculated the proportion of samples that were misclassified (hereafter, misclassification rate) based on field identification, including an overall misclassification rate and species-specific misclassification rates.
Statistical classification of scats.-Six species were identified with molecular identification (see Results) but only coyotes and kit foxes had sample sizes sufficient to evaluate speciesspecific classification techniques. Initially, we restricted classification of scats to samples that 1) were confirmed through molecular identification to have originated from coyotes or kit foxes, and 2) had morphometric measurements collected. For coyote and kit fox samples, we evaluated 3 predictor variables, including diameter, length, and number of segments, for normality with Shapiro-Wilk tests (Zar 1996, Razali andWah 2011). We tested for predictor variable differences between coyote and kit fox scat using Mann-Whitney U-tests (Zar 1996).
To explore the ability of statistical classification algorithms to improve classification over field identification, we used 2 nonparametric classifiers, k-nearest neighbors and classification trees, to classify scats based on measurements. Differences in the distribution of all 3 predictors suggested that each may contribute to discriminating species, so we included all 3 predictors in classification models. The k-nearest neighbor classifier can be sensitive to the k selected and the structure of the training data set. Consequently, we evaluated classification success for values of k from 1 to 20. For each k, we randomly selected a training data set of 100 kit fox and 100 coyote scats and then used the remaining samples for model validation. To minimize the influence of the local structure, or configuration in parameter space of a single random training data set, we repeated this procedure 500 times for each k and calculated the mean misclassification rate for each k. We then identified the k with the lowest mean misclassification rate for each species and overall. Classification trees may utilize predictor variables in >1 split. To account for over-fitting (i.e., branches resulting from noise or that provide limited contribution to classification), we used 10-fold cross-validation to generate an error rate for each split. We then pruned the tree back to the split corresponding to the lowest cross-validation error (Breiman et al. 1984, Therneau et al. 2014). Based on the pruned tree, we estimated variable importance, a measure of each variable's relative contribution (scaled to sum to 100) to the classification across splits (Therneau et al. 2014). We compared the performance of k-nearest neighbor and classification-tree models with one another and to field identification based on the misclassification rate. We used the "class" (Venables and Ripley 2002) and "rpart" (Therneau et al. 2014) packages in R (R Core Team 2014) to conduct k-nearest neighbor and classification-tree analyses, respectively. We conducted additional classification-tree analyses to further assess the influence of each predictor (i.e., diam, length, and no. of segments) and explore misclassification rates by season. Using the same procedures as above, we built classification-tree models for all possible combinations of the 3 predictor variables contained in the full model and evaluated the change in misclassification rates. Seasonal variation in misclassification rates may result from differences in juvenile body size or dietary changes. Using the model with the lowest misclassification rate overall (i.e., the full model), we evaluated differences in winter and summer misclassification rates. Finally, samples from nontarget, sympatric carnivores may occur relatively infrequently in our study system, and inclusion of these species in classification approaches may increase misclassification rates of target species. To evaluate the potential influence of additional sympatric carnivores, we conducted a classification-tree analysis focusing on kit foxes. We conducted this analysis in the same fashion as reported above, but evaluated the classification success of kit fox scats versus all other scats. We limited these additional analyses to classification trees because this approach provided the lowest overall misclassification rate when comparing misclassifications of kit foxes and coyotes (see Results).

[SECTION] field identification

[SECTION] coyote
Less than 4% of samples were determined by molecular identification to be from carnivores other than coyotes or kit foxes. Classification-tree analysis for kit foxes versus nontarget species (i.e., all other carnivores including coyotes) resulted in a decision tree with 7 terminal nodes, which was pruned to 5 terminal nodes following cross-validation (Fig. 5). Relative to considering only kit foxes and coyotes, misclassifications of kit foxes increased to 9.6% when considering all observed carnivore species, but was still substantially lower than misclassifications from field identification. Decision rules were similar to those generated when considering only coyotes and kit foxes. Scats with diameters !15.55 mm or lengths !81.10 mm were classified as nontarget carnivores, as were scats with diameters <15.55 mm that were !63.75 mm in length. All other scats were classified as kit foxes (Fig. 5).

FILE: Journal of Fish Biology - 2013 - Janse - Paternity testing using the poisonous sting in captive white‐spotted eagle rays.grobid.tei.xml
====================================================================================================
[SECTION] (no title)
has been used to identify species (Shivji et al ., 2003), to understand parthenogenesis (Chapman et al ., 2007) and to trace the origin of captive specimens (Heist & Feldheim, 2004). Recently, an extensive review on the application of molecular techniques in elasmobranches has been done by Dudgeon et al . (2012).
This study describes paternity research within a captive breeding programme of A. narinari . A group of six young A. narinari (two males and four females) from the waters around the Maldives arrived 10 years ago at Burgers' Zoo, Arnhem, The Netherlands. The group has since produced 20 offspring (10 males and 10 females). To obtain their DNA, poisonous sting samples were used. The sting of Myliobatiformes has an epidermal tissue from which DNA can be extracted. Because lost stings easily grow back, the use of stings for genetic research is an ideal non-invasive and animal-friendly sampling method.
The sting from each fish was incubated for 1 h at 56 • C in 200 μl lysis buffer containing 10 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8•0, 10 mM EDTA, pH 8•0, 100 mM NaCl, 40 mM dithiothreitol (DTT) and 1 mg ml -1 proteinase K. Genomic DNA was isolated from the extract using a QIAamp DNA Mini Kit (QIAGEN; www.qiagen.com). The amount of genomic DNA isolated from one sting varied from 9 up to 70 μg depending on the size of the sample, with an average mass of 33 μg.
Eight microsatellite markers, originally isolated from A. narinari (Ser61, Ser27, Ser453 and Ser92) (Sellas et al ., 2011) and longheaded eagle ray Aetobatus flagellum (Bloch & Schneider 1801) (Aefl01, Aefl05, Aefl06 and Aefl07) (Yagishita & Yamaguchi, 2009), were amplified in the genomic DNA of the 20 A. narinari . For each locus, the PCR was carried out in a thermal controller (Eppendorf; www.eppendorf.co.uk) using the following PCR profile: an initial denaturing step of 95 C for 5 min, followed by 10 cycles of 30 s at 95 • C, 30 s at 50 • C and 1 min at 72 • C, followed by 30 cycles of 30 s at 94 • C, 30 s at 52 • C and 1 min at 72 • C and finally 10 min at 72 • C. Each 10 μl reaction contained 0•25 U of Taq polymerase (5 PRIME; www.5prime.com), 1× manufacturer-supplied buffer, 200 μM of each deoxynucleotide triphosphate (dNTP), 5 pmol of each primer and 20 ng of genomic DNA. Forward primers were 5 -end labelled with 6-carboxyfluorescein (FAM) or VIC (Applied Biosystems; www.appliedbiosystems.com) fluorescent dyes. Amplified fragments were sized on an ABI Prism 3130 Genetic Analyzer using GeneScan 500 LIZ size standard and scored using GeneMapper 4.0 (Applied Biosystems). Observed and expected heterozygosities were calculated using Arlequin (Schneider et al ., 2000).
In all the 20 A. narinari individuals, the entire eight loci were polymorphic with the number of alleles ranging from three to eight in the five adults. Observed heterozygosities ranged from 0•711 to 1•000 (Table I). None of the loci was found to be out of Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium and no significant linkage disequilibrium was detected. The microsatellites used in this study show high levels of heterozygosity and are therefore valuable tools for investigating parentage and for monitoring genetic variation in breeding programmes of A. narinari .
Of interest was the successful use of microsatellite loci from A. flagellum on A. narinari . This may suggest close relation between the two species. This is in agreement with the current scientific discussion on the genus Aetobatus, where A. narinari might not be one species but a species complex of three closely related species, including A. flagellum (Richards et al ., 2009;White & Last, 2012).
Phylogenetic analyses on A. narinari identified three well-supported, reciprocally monophyletic lineages each restricted to the western and central Pacific Ocean,    eastern Pacific Ocean and central Atlantic Ocean regions, respectively (Richards et al ., 2009). The microsatellite loci used from the study of Sellas et al . (2011) are from A. narinari originating from the eastern Gulf of Mexico and therefore from a different region than the adults in this study.
Because A. narinari is an ovoviviparous species, the mother and offspring relationships are known. Therefore, the father could be identified easily from the microsatellite data. The microsatellite genotypes unambiguously identified male number 1 as the father of five young, and male number 6 as the father of the other 15 young A. narinari , showing that both adult males are reproductively active. One male was more successful than the other possibly because of dominance difference. Litter size averaged 1•7 (n = 20), with a maximum of two young per litter. In one twin, multiple paternity was found, being the first case of multipaternity within this species. Multipaternity has up to now only been described in one other ray species, R. clavata (Chevolot et al ., 2007).
Results of this study show that using stings works efficiently for DNA sampling in A. narinari . This technique could easily be applied for all ray species belonging to the families Urolophidae, Hexatrygonidae, Gymnuridae, Dasyatidae, Rhinopteridae, Mobulidae, Myliobatidae and Potamotrygonidae.

FILE: Wildlife Society Bulletin - 2015 - Miles - A paired comparison of scat‐collecting versus scat‐swabbing methods for.grobid.tei.xml
====================================================================================================
[SECTION] (no title)
Noninvasive fecal sampling and genetic analyses of scats are used increasingly in wildlife research (e.g., Waits and Paetkau 2005, Vynne et al. 2011, DeMatteo et al. 2014a, Gulsby et al. 2015, Lounsberry et al. 2015). The value of this approach for estimating abundance, occupancy, individual longevity, home range, habitat use, gene flow, and social structure without the need to capture or handle individual animals presents tremendous potential, but applications are often limited by challenges in adequately preserving samples for subsequent DNA extraction and analyses (e.g., Schwartz et al. 2007).
Although many variables (e.g., diet, environmental conditions, time since deposition, DNA extraction method) can affect the success of DNA acquisition from scats (Waits and Paetkau 2005), the single most influential factor in control of most field biologists is how samples are collected and stored prior to transfer to a laboratory. A variety of storage methods have been used and tested for efficacy, including desiccation, freezing, or storage in buffers or ethanol. In most studies, pure ethanol (i.e., 95-100%) works similarly to or better than other methods for shorter storage periods and can substantially outperform them during extended storage periods (Murphy et al. 2002, Frantz et al. 2003, Piggott and Taylor 2003, Beja-Pereira et al. 2009, Panasci et al. 2011, Tende et al. 2014). However, acquiring, storing, and transporting sufficient quantities of ethanol for sample storage can be difficult in remote field conditions. Sample transport following collection and storage can also pose an issue because ethanol is volatile, highly flammable, and is subject to various shipping and travel restrictions (Beja-Pereira et al. 2009). One alternative has been to use dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO)-based buffers such as DET (e.g., Panasci et al. 2011, Vynne et al. 2011), but this method has a limited shelf-life relative to ethanol (e.g., Murphy et al. 2002).
Another method that has become increasingly popular, and is even required by some service laboratories, involves the use of a cotton swab to collect the epithelial cells themselves from the mucous layer of scats in the field (Ball et al. 2007, Rutledge et al. 2009, DeMatteo et al. 2014a, b). The accessibility of the mucous layer, however, likely depends on time in the environment, ambient conditions, and various other factors. In general, fecal swabs are likely to be most successful when scats are sufficiently fresh that the mucous layer containing the epithelial cells remains moist, also enabling separation from the fecal matrix, which typically contains polymerase chain reaction (PCR) inhibitors (Ball et al. 2007, Rutledge et al. 2009). Depending on the purpose of a study, however, reliance solely on freshly deposited scats may not be feasible, such as in studies of rare species (e.g., Stenglein et al. 2010, Sacks et al. 2011, Statham et al. 2012, DeMatteo et al. 2014a, b). Therefore, it is of interest to know how methods of fecal collection and preservation are likely to perform relative to one another under more variable field conditions. In such cases, the mucous layer may not be as readily separated from the external scat via swabbing.
Unfortunately, it is difficult to evaluate the efficacy of swabs used on nonfresh scats based on the existing literature because few studies have reported their success in terms of DNA quantity (but see Ball et al. 2007, Rutledge et al. 2009), which, along with PCR inhibition, ultimately determines all measures of downstream success. Comparisons based solely on the downstream success measures themselves, such as proportion of scats that yield species types, are complicated by differences among study protocols. This problem is particularly significant for nuclear DNA (nDNA) amplification, which can be highly sensitive to particular species, markers, amplification protocols, and the authors' criteria for success (e.g., number of loci amplifying, differences in numbers of replication attempts, etc.). For these reasons, paired comparisons are crucial. We are aware of only one such study (i.e., using scats of unknown and variable ages), which compared extractions from swabs of scats preserved by freezing (i.e., swabbed in the laboratory at the time of extraction) to those from subsamples of the same scats preserved in DMSO buffer (Vynne et al. 2011). The study reported a 73% success rate in mitochondrial amplification of the swab extracts, which was higher than the comparably low 53% success they achieved for the DMSO-based extracts. Nevertheless, genotyping success from those swab samples identified in the first step to be from the target species was relatively high (82%). However, this study was conducted in a semitropical climate, which potentially preserves the moisture in the mucous layer for a greater period of time. We are aware of no study that has compared swabbing directly to ethanol-preserved scats or which has explored the efficacy of swabbing in an arid environment. In the present study, we used a paired design to directly compare the performance of methods involving fecal swabs versus ethanol-preserved fecal material using mesocarnivore scats collected from an arid, Mediterranean climate zone, and ranging up to 3 weeks old. We compared approaches both in terms of mitochondrial DNA sequencing, which is commonly used for species identification, and, for a subset of scats that were shown to be canine, nuclear (e.g., microsatellite) genotyping, which is used for individual and sex identification. Importantly, we also directly quantified the amount of target-species DNA in extracts, which will facilitate future comparisons to studies in other environments.

[SECTION] study area
We collected scats for this study from California's Sacramento Valley (USA), in elevations <150 m, latitudes ranging from 39.368N to 40.408N, and longitudes ranging from 122.258W to 121.438W. The landscape was composed primarily of agricultural lands, including flooded rice agriculture, dry cropland, vineyards, and orchards. Remnant grasslands remained where livestock were grazed. The study area was hot (highs ranged from 328 C to 408 C) and experienced almost no precipitation during the summer, and mild (highs ranged from 88 C to 248 C), with very little precipitation during the particular winter during which sampling for this study was conducted.

[SECTION] methods
We collected 104 putative mesocarnivore scats for this study during May-September 2013 (n ¼ 79) and January-February 2015 (n ¼ 25). We resampled transects every 2-3 weeks, collecting all mesocarnivore scats encountered. The 104 scats used for this study excluded those collected on the first run of transects and, therefore, were presumed to have been collected 21 days since deposition. In the field, we collected scats in individually labeled paper sacks and recorded whether scats appeared fresh (<2 days old), moderate-aged (2-4 days old), or older (>4 days). Within 12 hr of collection, we transferred a portion of each scat (approx. 2 g) into >4 parts (approx. 8-12 mL) 95-100% ethanol in a 15-mL tube and swabbed the unsampled portion of the same scat. Specifically, we used Q-tips 1 cotton-tipped swabs to sample the external surface area of approximately half of each scat on all sides. We first moistened swabs with 95-100% ethanol to help free cells from the scat surface (except for 3 scats that were so fresh there was no need to premoisten swabs; Rutledge et al. 2009). We allowed swabs to air dry and then stored them in manila coin envelopes. We stored all samples at room temperature (20-258 C) until DNA extraction. The average time between collection in the field and DNA extraction was 9.3 days (SD ¼ 7.7 days). Note: we chose ethanol as the moistening agent because it evaporates quickly. However, because other studies have moistened swabs with salt solutions, such as phosphate-buffered saline (PBS; e.g., DeMatteo et al. 2014a, b), we swabbed a subset of 25 scats with both PBS and ethanol; we found no significant differences (Supporting Information 1). We also used a subset of samples to test our primary storage method (i.e., dried in manila envelopes) to storage of swabs in ethanol to control for the preservation versus the celltransfer aspect of swabbing and, again, found no qualitative differences in terms of DNA yield, inhibition, or performance (Supporting Information 2).
For DNA extraction directly from the ethanol-preserved scat samples, we used a QIAmp Stool Mini Kit (Qiagen, Valencia, CA) to extract DNA from approximately 200 mg of the outer surface of scats, following the manufacturer's protocol, except that DNA was eluted in 100 mL of elution buffer. For swab samples, we extracted DNA using a DNeasy Blood and Tissue Kit (Qiagen). We transferred swabs from envelopes directly into 2-mL microcentrifuge tubes with reagents for digestion: 700 mL PBS, 200 mL of Buffer AL, and 25 mL of Proteinase K. To remove swabs from the digestion tubes, we vortexed samples for 5-10 s, centrifuged them for 1 min at 14,000 rpm, and pressed swabs against the sides of the tubes to remove any remaining liquid before discarding. All subsequent steps followed manufacturer's instructions. Hereafter, we use the terms "direct" and "swab" to differentiate the DNA extracted directly from scat preserved in ethanol versus from swabs, respectively. We first attempted to amplify and sequence a 402-bp fragment of the mammalian mitochondrial cytochrome b gene using primers (Perrine et al. 2007) and procedures (Aubry et al. 2009) described previously. Although use of a shorter fragment, such as by other studies (e.g., Vynne et al. 2011;DeMatteo et al. 2014a, b), would likely have produced higher species-typing success, we chose the longer fragment for purposes specific to various ongoing research projects in our laboratory. Because the direct method typically incorporates some fecal matrix in the extraction procedure, these extracts were likely to contain PCR inhibitors. Therefore, for direct-method extracts failing to amplify in the first step, we performed 10-fold dilutions to reduce the concentration of any PCR inhibitors and attempted a second time to amplify them at the cytochrome b fragment (Beja-Pereira et al. 2009). (We did not sequence the samples that amplified after dilution, which resulted in 4 samples that amplified but which we did not species-type or, therefore, use in subsequent analyses.) We evaluated sequences to determine species using the Basic Local Alignment Search Tool (BLAST) in the nucleotide database in Genbank.
From the scats that assigned to coyote (Canis latrans), gray fox (Urocyon cinereoargenteus), or red fox (Vulpes vulpes) for !1 of the 2 preservation methods in the previous step, we selected all but 10 samples (set aside for unrelated purposes) to attempt nDNA amplification. Specifically, we attempted to amplify 7 canine nuclear DNA microsatellite loci that amplify in all canid species in our study area (AHT137, AHT142, CXX-279, CXX-374, INU055, REN162C04, REN169O18; primer sequences provided by Moore et al. 2010). Because nuclear DNA occurs in much lower copy-number than mitochondrial DNA, we used only the undiluted (i.e., original) extracts, along with the Qiagen Multiplex PCR Kit reagents and manufacturer's protocol using Q-solution (Sacks et al. 2011). We used STRand software to call alleles (Toonen and Hughes 2001). Because we were primarily interested in gross performance, we did not attempt to quantify allelic dropout, which would have required replications, but instead report numbers of loci amplified and, for purposes of quantifying success discretely, considered genotyping successful when !6 loci were successfully amplified for at least one allele in the single attempt. Elsewhere, we have reported allelic dropout rates for the same study system using the direct-method approach (Sacks et al. 2010(Sacks et al. , 2011)).
Lastly, we performed a quantitative PCR (qPCR) analysis of a subset of 35 pairs of the undiluted extracts on which we attempted genotyping. The reduced subset was necessary to complete the quantitation assay on a single 96-well plate, which also included 12 internal positive control (IPC) standards, 12 extracts used in the supplementary swab-storage comparison (Supporting Information 2), and 2 blanks. We estimated concentration of canine genomic DNA based on canine Melanocortin-1 receptor gene copies and incorporated the IPC (a synthetic DNA fragment added to each sample in known concentration) for detection of PCR inhibition (Evans et al. 2007). We quantified inhibition in terms of the number of cycles required for amplification of the IPC to a predetermined threshold concentration minus the number of cycles required for amplification of the IPC to the same threshold concentration in standards containing no inhibitors; specifically, we used the average value among 12 standards. We incorporated negative controls into all procedures, including extraction, PCR amplification, sequencing, and genotyping steps. Importantly, our technique quantified canine genomic DNA only, whereas previous studies (Rutledge et al. 2009) quantified total genomic DNA, which includes up to 20Â as much nontarget (e.g., from intestinal microorganisms) as target DNA (Ball et al. 2007).
For each fecal extraction protocol, we calculated success rates in terms of species identification, genotyping success, and both processes combined. We compared methods with respect to numbers of mitochondrial DNA amplifications and failures and microsatellite successes and failures using Fisher's exact tests (Zar 1999). We compared microsatellite genotyping success across species using a x 2 test of independence (Zar 1999). Because the cutoff for genotyping success was necessarily arbitrary, we also used a 2-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) to evaluate the effects of method and species on numbers of loci amplified (including zeros) in the canid scats. We used paired t-tests to compare DNA concentrations and inhibition between the direct and swab methods. We log-transformed the DNA concentration estimates prior to analysis to normalize residuals. To estimate 95% confidence intervals for proportions (or percentages), we employed a method based on the F-distribution (Zar 1999). Statistical tests were run using SYSTAT (version 9.0, SPSS Incorporated, Chicago, IL) and significance was assessed at alpha ¼ 0.05.

FILE: puechmaille2014.grobid.tei.xml
====================================================================================================
[SECTION] (no title)
The International Union for Conservation of Nature's Red List has become an increasingly powerful tool for conservation planning, management, monitoring, and decision making ( Rodrigues et al. 2006 ). At a regional level, a species can be classified as Regionally Extinct (RE) " when there is no reasonable doubt that the last individual potentially capable of reproduction within the region has died or disappeared from the region or, in the case of a former visiting taxon, individuals no longer visit the region. This will depend on how much effort has been devoted to searches for the taxon, which in turn will vary, both with organism and region " . One could be fairly confident in saying that a large mammal is RE if it has not been observed over the last few decades; however, this might be rather difficult with small elusive mammals such as bats. Further difficulties arise when the species of interest is morphologically very similar to another more common species ( Boston et al. 2010, Puechmaille et al. 2012 ).
Non-invasive genetic techniques, using biological material left behind by animals as a source of DNA, are becoming routinely used in conservation biology and monitoring programs, particularly for threatened and protected species ( Luikart et al. 2010 ). The DNA obtained can be used to identify the species from which the sample originated, most commonly through sequencing of a short fragment of mitochondrial DNA ( Kohn and Wayne 1997 ). Potential difficulties associated with non-invasive genetics are the low quality and/or quantity of DNA recovered and the potential presence of PCR inhibitors ( Taberlet et al. 1999 ). Nevertheless, specific improvements in the techniques to extract and amplify DNA from non-invasive genetics have been developed to overcome these difficulties in a diverse range of taxonomic groups (e.g., Eggert et al. 2005, Puechmaille et al. 2007 ).
Mehely ' s horseshoe bat, Rhinolophus mehelyi Matschie 1901, is a medium-sized rhinolophid with a discontinuous distribution from North Africa (Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya, and Egypt) and southern Europe (Iberia, Sardinia, Sicily, and the Balkans) through Asia Minor, Anatolia, to Transcaucasia and Iran. The species is globally classified as " vulnerable " but is thought to have gone extinct in north-eastern Spain, Mallorca, Croatia, and Israel ( Flaquer et al. 2010 , Hamidovi ć pers. com., Levin pers. com.) and is near extinction in France, Romania, and Sicily ( Rombaut andHaquart 2002 , Dragu andBorissov 2011 , Mucedda pers. com.). Most observations in France are from the period 1908 -1965, during which this species was regularly observed at several sites in the Gard, H é rault, and Bouches-du-Rh ô ne d é partements in southern France ( Mottaz 1908, Hugues 1914, 1936, Gallocher 1958, K ö nig and K ö nig 1961, Jeantet and Gory 1997 , Jeantet pers. com.) and only once in Corsica ( Kahmann and Goerner 1956 ). Species identifications have been verified by examinations of voucher specimens previously collected in southern France and deposited in the Natural History Museum in Paris ( Rode 1939 , Masson andBesson 1988 , Puechmaille pers. obs.), the Natural History Museum of N î mes (Jeantet pers. com.), the Staatliches Museum fur Naturkunde Stuttgart ( K ö nig and K ö nig 1961 ), the Natural History Museum in Geneva ( Miller 1912 , Strinati andAellen 1958 ), and the Zoological Museum in Berlin (Lange pers. com.). In the last decade, sightings of hibernating bats similar to R. mehelyi have been reported, especially in the H é rault and Gard D é partements in southern France ( Ruffray 2011 , M é dard and Derivaz pers. com.). Nevertheless, R. mehelyi is morphologically very similar to Rhinolophus euryale Blasius, 1853, another medium-sized horseshoe bat regularly observed in these regions. These two species could easily be confused (discussed in detail in Puechmaille et al. 2012 ), especially when the animals are only observed from a distance, as during the hibernation period, when the bats should not be disturbed.
Here we report on a new strategy to identify bat species in hibernation through the genetic analysis of guano collected underneath the bats of interest. Pre vious studies have shown that it is possible to extract goodquality DNA from bat guano ( Vege and McCracken 2001, Zinck et al. 2004, Puechmaille et al. 2005, 2007, Puechmaille and Petit 2007 ), although it has never been tested with guano collected at hibernation sites. In this study, we used non-invasive genetics to confirm the species of a group of hibernating bats (Gardon gorges, Gard department, France) that were suspected to be Rhinolophus mehelyi based on visual observation.
On the 20th of February 2008, a plastic sheet covered with newspaper was placed in a cave underneath a group of 18 hibernating medium-sized Rhinolophus suspected to be Rhinolophus mehelyi based on visual identification. No droppings were present on the first visit (22nd February) 2 days later, whereas six droppings were collected on the second visit (27th February) 5 days later. Each dropping was individually placed in a tube with silica gel to absorb humidity and hence preserve DNA ( Puechmaille et al. 2007 ). Droppings were then sent to the laboratory where only non-invasive DNA samples are analyzed, hence minimizing potential contamination problems. For comparison, droppings collected in a cloth holding bag from captured Spanish R. mehelyi (colony Villuercas in Salsamendi et al. 2008 ) were also included. A total of eight droppings from France (n = 6) and Spain (n = 2) were extracted following the protocol detailed in Puechmaille et al. (2007) . Given that long DNA fragments have been amplified from guano ( Boston et al. 2012, Goodman et al. 2012, Ruedi et al. 2012, Dool et al. 2013 ), we amplified the full cytochrome b and partial D-loop in two overlapping fragments. The first fragment (885 bp) was amplified using primers mtDNA-R3-F and mtDNA-F3-R, and the second fragment (1025 bp) using primers mtDNA-R2-F and mtDNA-F2-R ( Puechmaille et al. 2011 ). PCR mix and PCR conditions were as described in Thong et al. (2012) . The amplified PCR products were then purified and directly sequenced by Macrogen Inc. (Seoul, South Korea) using the same primers as mentioned above. The forward and reverse sequences per fragment were edited and assembled for each individual using the program CodonCode Aligner 4.0.1 (CodonCode Corporation, Dedham, MA, USA).
Of the six French samples extracted, two did not amplify whereas four amplified for both fragments. We combined these six sequences obtained (GenBank accession number KF031265 -KF031268) with another five sequences retrieved from GenBank and belonging to Rhinolophus mehelyi (n = 1), R. euryale (n = 3), and R. ferrumequinum (n = 1, used as the outgroup) to perform a maximum likelihood tree reconstruction in PAUP* ( Swofford 2003 ) using HKY models as selected by the hierarchical likelihood ratio test in Modeltest 3.7 ( Posada and Crandall 1998 ).
The phylogenetic reconstruction clearly indicated the presence of two strongly supported clades (bootstrap supports of 100%), which could be identified as being Rhinolophus euryale and R. mehelyi based on the sequences of known identity from GenBank and the Spanish R. mehelyi samples ( Figure 1 ). Whereas the two non-invasive samples from Spain grouped with R. mehelyi , all the French sequences from the hibernation site grouped with R. euryale , and hence belong to this latter species.
These results highlight the limitations of visual identification of hibernating bats and advocate for the use of non-invasive genetics to confirm species identity for rare bats, especially for those that are difficult to identify on the basis of morphological criteria. Recently, Puechmaille et al. (2012) reviewed morphological criteria to differentiate both species and showed that some of these criteria vary geographically, further complicating the correct identification of these species. Although our study revealed unambiguously that the suspected animals in the gorges du Gardon were Rhinolophus euryale and not R. mehelyi ; these results on their own are not enough to confirm that the species is extinct in France. Further field surveys combined with non-invasive genetic analyses are urgently needed to clarify the status of the species in the sites where the species was present until the 1960s ( Jeantet andGory 1997 , Gory andJeantet 1999 ).
In terms of climatic conditions, hibernating sites generally have low temperatures and high humidity ( Webb et al. 1996, Vi š ň ovsk á et al. 2006 ). DNA degradation decreases at low temperatures but increases at higher humidity; therefore, equipment should be placed in the driest locations available where the subject bats are present. We also recommend that samples only a few days old should be preferentially collected. Previous work has demonstrated that ca. 90% of samples kept in dry conditions provide adequate quality and amount of DNA for species identification ( Puechmaille et al. 2007, Boston et al. 2012 ). In the present study, we amplified large fragments ( > 800 bp) to maximize the amount of information obtained from the sequences to gain information on population differentiation between the French and Spanish samples. If species identification is the only target, shorter fragments allowing species discrimination should be used (usually ca. 100 -200 bp), which would likely increase amplification success ( Broquet et al. 2007 ). DNA extraction protocols that efficiently remove PCR inhibitors should preferentially be used ( Puechmaille et al. 2007 ); however, if some inhibitors remain after extraction, more diluted DNA extracts should be used and/or amplified along with bovine serum albumin that binds to inhibitors during the PCR. As seen with the group of hibernating bats in the Gardon gorges, bats are unlikely to produce large numbers of droppings during their hibernation period but might produce a few droppings when they wake up from torpor, allowing their genetic identification based on mitochondrial DNA. Identification to the species level might not be possible if two species cannot be differentiated using mitochondrial DNA, either because of current or past hybridization (e.g., Myotis myotis/Myotis blythii ; Berthier et al. 2006 ). In such situations, species identification could be obtained through microsatellite genotyping using reference species datasets.
Studies based on droppings have demonstrated that individuals could be identified by their unique genetic multilocus genotype ( Puechmaille et al. 2007 , Puechmaille andPetit 2007 ) and although here we only used mitochondrial DNA, it should be possible to also amplify nuclear DNA from these droppings from hibernation sites. DNA fingerprints obtained at hibernation sites could then be compared with fingerprints obtained at maternity colonies and would allow the identification of connections between maternity colonies and hibernation sites, still a grand challenge in bat biology. These techniques, although probably very costly if used at large scale ( Boston et al. 2012 ), could nevertheless be used for smaller sample sizes to inform movements of rare and endangered species that cannot be marked with more conventional techniques (e.g., ringing or passive integrated transponder tagging). The genetic information obtained non-invasively can also be used to investigate the fidelity of individuals to a particular site or survival rates if the sampling is carried out in multiple years. Additionally, these data can also inform about population structure and genetic diversity.
With the increasing legal requirement of countries to monitor and preserve their biodiversity, new methods such as non-invasive genetic tools presented herein are necessary to study species, particularly those critically endangered and elusive.
