[SECTION] (no title)
Sperm quality is an important aspect of reproductive fitness and an indication of the integrity of male reproductive system physiology. Spermatozoa have been reported to be more important than ova regarding the potential to transmit DNA damage to the next generation (Lewis & Aitken, 2005), due in part because of the presence of damage repair systems in oocytes (Ashwood-Smith & Edwards, 1996) that are largely absent in sperm (Leal et al ., 2009). Although zebrafish Danio rerio (Hamilton 1822) are a prominent model organism and sperm can be sampled from D. rerio (Jing et al ., 2009), assessment of sperm is seldom included in D. rerio research projects. Measurement of DNA damage in D. rerio sperm by the comet (single-cell gel electrophoresis) assay has been conducted, but the method has been applied only to excised testes after euthanasia (Bony et al ., 2010;Uren-Webster et al ., 2010). Validating assessment of genotoxicity in sublethally extracted sperm and assessing §Author to whom correspondence should be addressed. Tel.: +44 1752 232 940; email: Ted.Henry@ plymouth.ac.uk #Present address: Bermuda Institute for Ocean Sciences, 17 Ferry Reach, St. George's, GE 01, Bermuda. effects of repeated sampling can reduce numbers of experimental animals, a key aim in animal research (Buchanan-Smith et al ., 2005). The objective of this study was to develop and validate methods for evaluation of DNA damage in sperm cells using the comet assay (Jha, 2008), and to evaluate the effect of the frequency of non-invasive sperm sampling on sperm number and presence of DNA damage in sperm.
Typically, D. rerio spawn at the beginning of the photoperiod (Lawrence, 2007), and, in this experiment, sperm from adult male fish (age c. 120 days, maintained under routine approved animal welfare protocols) were sampled within 1 h of the start of the photoperiod. Fish were lightly anaesthetized with MS-222 and held within a 1 cm deep groove cut in a sponge to enable access to the ventral surface and facilitate sperm collection during examination by stereomicroscope. Slight abdominal finger pressure was applied and expelled sperm was collected in a hand-pulled glass capillary tube (Na-hep micro-haematocrit tubes, diameter 1•55 ± 0•05 mm, Fisher Scientific; www.fisher.co.uk), following the method of Wilson-Leedy & Ingermann (2007). Sperm collected in the tube was expelled onto a glass microscope slide that was kept on ice (to reduce evaporation from sperm sample drop). The mean volume of the sperm sample obtained was 2 μl (range 1-5 μl), and was consistent with other studies (Xu et al ., 2008). A 0•5 or 1•0 μl (depending on volume obtained from fish) aliquot of the sperm sample was pipetted from the glass slide into a tube and stored on ice for analysis within 6 h. Fish were allowed to recover in fresh water before they were returned to the system aquaria. The whole sampling process from anaesthesia to recovery took <5 min, and fish were held out of water for <1•5 min.
Validation of the comet assay in D. rerio sperm was conducted in three separate experiments. Sperm samples were exposed in vitro to hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2 ); unless otherwise specified, all chemicals were obtained from Sigma-Aldrich (Sigma-Aldrich Company Ltd; www.sigmaaldrich.com). Sperm samples (total volume collected) from three male fish were pooled, diluted in 100 μl Hank's buffered saline solution (HBSS) and triplicate aliquots of the sperm dilution were incubated at the following final H 2 O 2 concentrations: 0, 10, 25, 50, 100 and 200 μM [range selected on sensitivity of aquatic organisms (Cheung et al ., 2006)]. After 10 min incubation, cells were centrifuged (8000 g, 4 min) into a pellet, H 2 O 2 was removed and the cells were re-suspended in 10 μl HBSS to be processed for the comet assay.
The comet assay was adapted from a protocol developed for human sperm (Simon et al ., 2010). In brief, sperm cells (10 μl) were mixed with 180 μl low melting point agarose (0•5% agarose), pipetted onto a slide precoated with 1•5% normal melting point agarose (dried overnight) and covered with a glass cover slip. Gels were allowed to set for 1 h in a cold room (5 • C) before cover slips were removed, and slides were placed in lysis solution (2•5 M NaCl, 100 mM EDTA, 10 mM Tris and 1% Triton X-100, pH 10) for 1 h. The present procedure differed from that of Simon et al . (2010) in that decondensation steps were not used because they caused increased damage in control D. rerio sperm. After lysis, slides were placed in electrophoresis buffer (300 mM NaOH and 1 mM EDTA, pH 13) for 20 min (to unwind DNA), followed by electrophoresis (25 V, 280-350 mA) for 20 min. Slides were washed in neutralization buffer (0•4 M Tris-HCl, pH 7•5) and distilled water, allowed to dry overnight and scored for % tail DNA (100 cells per slide, Komet 5, Kinetic Imaging, Andor Technology; www.andor.com) following routine procedures (Collins, 2004). The effect of sampling frequency on DNA damage and sperm counts was investigated in experimental fish stocked into nine 10 l glass aquaria supplied with partial (10% exchange per day) recirculating water. Each aquarium was divided in half with a mesh and six reproductively active females (demonstrated by previous pair spawning producing >50 viable embryos) were placed on one side of the mesh. Three reproductively active male fish (mean ± s.e. total length, L T = 33•8 ± 0•3 mm, n = 27 fish) were placed into each tank on the opposite side of the mesh from females. Male fish were individually identifiable by their size within each aquarium and were allowed to acclimate to the aquarium for 7 days. The frequency of sperm sampling was the test variable with three tanks per treatment: fish were sampled every 2, 4 or 7 days (n = 3 tanks and n = 9 males per treatment). Fish in the twoday treatment were sampled (as described above) every other day for 14 days, the four-day treatment group were sampled on days 0, 4, 8 and 12 and the seven day treatment group were sampled on days 0, 7 and 14.
For sperm cell counts, a haemocytometer (Neubauer; www.marienfeldsuperior.com) was precoated with two applications of polyvinyl alcohol (Rain Repellent, Halfords PLC; www.halfordscompany.com) to prevent cells from sticking to the glass surface and allow free movement of sperm (Wilson-Leedy & Ingermann, 2007). Sperm was initially diluted 1:25 (HBSS 300), followed by a second dilution (1:50) in trypan blue to stain viable cells. Cells were viewed under a compound light microscope (×40 objective, ×400 magnification, Leitz Laborlus S; www.leica-microsystems.com), and the number of sperm cells in each sample was determined as the mean of five independent counts of a 1 μl volume (grid dimensions 1 mm × 1 mm × 0•1 mm, Neubauer haemocytometer). At the final sperm sampling event for each group of fish (day 14 for two-day and seven-day treatment fish, and day 12 for the four-day treatment group), a sub-sample of sperm from each individual male (c. 1 μl) was diluted (1:100) with HBSS and used for assessment of DNA damage (comet assay) as previously outlined.
Statistical analysis of results was conducted with STATGRAPHICS 5.1 (Statistical Graphics Corp.; http://statistical-graphics-corp.software.informer.com/). Concentration response in sperm DNA damage following in vitro exposure to H 2 O 2 was tested by logistic regression. DNA damage following sublethal sperm extraction was tested by general linear model (GLM) on arcsine-transformed % tail DNA data, and the independent variables were sampling frequency and individual fish. The effect of sampling frequency on sperm cell counts was tested by GLM with sampling day and sampling frequency as model factors (effects of individual fish or L T were not significant and removed from the model).
Levels of DNA damage in sperm increased with concentration of H 2 O 2 (in vitro incubation for 10 min) [Fig. 1(a)], and levels of DNA damage in unexposed sperm were 9-12% tail DNA, consistent with recommended controls (Collins, 2004). Two of the 27 males died during the experiment (both from the four-day treatment group apparently because of aggressive interactions between fish), but all other fish appeared normal and had no gross external lesions, abnormal behaviour or reduction in feeding rate. Of the 140 total attempts to collect sperm, 18 (13%) were unsuccessful, and, of these unsuccessful attempts, eight (5•7%) were attributed to two males that were consistently poor at producing sperm for sample collection. Evaluation of DNA damage in sperm from fish that were sampled repeatedly during the 14 day experiment indicated no significant differences in fish sampled every 2, 4 or 7 days [Fig. 1(b)], and low variance among treatments was observed (mean ± s.e. twoday fish = 18•5 ± 0•1, four-day fish = 16•7 ± 0•2 and seven-day fish = 15•8 ± 0•2% tail DNA, n = 7-9 fish per treatment). At time 0, before repeated sampling of sperm began, sperm counts were variable among aquaria in the treatment groups (mean = 2•8 × 10 6 μl -1 , minimum = 0•5 × 10 6 μl -1 and maximum = 6•0 × 10 6 μl -1 ), and time 0 sperm counts were excluded from analysis of the effect of repeated sampling over time. The number of sperm in fish sampled every 2 days decreased 57% after 14 days sampling (mean ± s.e. down from 1•7 ± 0•3 day 2 to 0•7 ± 0•1 day 14 cells × 10 6 , GLM P < 0•01). Fish sampled every 4 days produced 22% lower sperm counts (mean ± s.e. down from 1•8 ± 0•3 day 4 to 1•4 ± 0•1 day 12 cells × 10 6 ), but this decrease was not significant (GLM P > 0•05), and no change in the number of sperm was observed in fish sampled every 7 days (2% decline, mean ± s.e. down from 1•31 ± 0•1 day 7 to 1•28 ± 0•1 day 14 cells × 10 6 , GLM P > 0•05) (Fig. 2). The present results indicate that repeated sampling of sperm can be conducted in D. rerio, and assessment of sperm (including DNA damage) can be included among the endpoints that are tested in numerous investigations that use the D. rerio model. The repeated sperm sampling procedure did not appear to negatively affect fish (i.e. no lesions, abnormal behaviour or alteration in feeding were observed) and indicated that this non-invasive approach can be integrated into experiments with adult fish with minimal adverse effect.
Results indicate that H 2 O 2 -induced DNA damage in D. rerio sperm is similar to that observed in sperm of other organisms. In mammals, sperm exposed in vitro to 100 mM H 2 O 2 had similar levels of DNA damage as reported in D. rerio (this study), with up to 60-70% tail DNA observed in humans Homo sapiens, bulls Bos taurus and mice Mus musculus (Villani et al ., 2010). Integrity of DNA within but the observed decline in sperm count in fish sampled every 4 days was not significant (GLM P > 0•05) and sampling frequency did not affect sperm counts in fish sampled every 7 days (GLM P > 0•05). The curves were fitted by (a) y = -0
sperm is important, as DNA damage in sperm can affect subsequent reproductive success (Zhou et al ., 2006;Lewis & Galloway, 2009), but studies of DNA damage in D. rerio sperm are limited (Uren-Webster et al ., 2010). In this investigation, repeated sampling of sperm from D. rerio did not induce DNA damage regardless of the frequency of sampling, indicating that the sampling procedure did not induce appreciable DNA damage in sperm. The level of in vivo DNA damage in sperm in this study was similar to levels of damage in D. rerio sperm reported in the study of Uren-Webster et al . (2010), in which adult D. rerio sperm had up to 12% tail DNA by comet assay in sperm obtained by crushing testes after euthanasia, slightly higher than control levels reported in Bony et al . (2010) following a similar technique with excised testes. The repeated method for non-invasive sperm sampling is preferable to obtaining sperm via crushing testes because the comet assay can be conducted on a more homogeneous cell type (i.e. mature spermatozoa) with similar sensitivities rather than a mixture of gonad cells of differing sensitivities. Furthermore, the fish do not need to be euthanized. The frequency of sperm sampling affected the sperm concentration, indicating that use of a sampling frequency that does not affect sperm concentration is important. It is possible that the decrease in sperm counts in fish sampled every 2 days, and the non-significant trend of reduced sperm counts in the four-day sampled fish, will become more pronounced over longer sampling periods. Repeated sampling of sperm has been reported to reduce or eliminate sperm present in samples obtained from birds (Lombardo et al ., 2004), however little information is available on the impact of sperm sampling frequency on sperm characteristics in other organisms including important laboratory models.
Sperm production in D. rerio follows a pattern of cystic spermatogenesis over a six-day cycle from early spermatid formation to production of mature spermatozoa (Leal et al ., 2009). The method of sampling in this study is expected to enable assessment of mature spermatozoa only, and the observed decrease in sperm counts in fish sampled every 2 or 4 days is consistent with limitations in capabilities of fish to produce sperm. The effect of repeated sampling on numbers of sperm produced has not been investigated previously in D. rerio. Previous studies with D. rerio have reported large differences in sperm counts ranging from 250 cells μl -1 (Njiwa et al ., 2004), 8•8 × 10 4 cells μl -1 (Tan et al ., 2010) and 8 × 10 6 cells μl -1 (Xu et al ., 2008), but accurate sperm concentration is often not the focus of studies directed at cryopreservation of sperm and preserving sperm quality characteristics (Jing et al ., 2009;Wilson-Leedy et al ., 2009). Lower proportions of spermatozoa and higher proportions of spermatocytes have been reported after histological examination of adult male D. rerio following toxicant exposure (Uren-Webster et al ., 2010); however, assessment of sperm concentration has not been included in any other study that investigated the effects of experimental treatments in D. rerio. Sperm concentration can affect sperm motility (Jing et al ., 2009), an important characteristic for sperm quality, and sperm motility characteristics have been positively correlated to fertilization success in a number of teleost species, including D. rerio (Paull et al ., 2008).
Results of this study indicate that repeated sampling of sperm can be done with minimal effect on adult D. rerio and produce samples that are useful for assessment of sperm quantity and quality measurements. If sperm is sampled too frequently, the number of sperm that are obtained decreases over time, which is probably related to the time required for spermatogenesis to generate mature spermatozoa. The comet assay can be effectively applied to assess DNA damage in D. rerio sperm, as has been done in sperm from other organisms, and repeated sperm sampling from D. rerio does not lead to elevated DNA damage in sperm. Integration of assessments to determine the quantity and quality of sperm into experiments with D. rerio could be applied readily to add information on the effects of different types of experimental treatments on an important component of male reproductive success.

FILE: Methods Ecol Evol - 2016 - Bylemans - An environmental DNA‐based method for monitoring spawning activity  a case study .grobid.tei.xml

[SECTION] materials and methods

[SECTION] p r i m e r d e s i g n a n d t e s t i n g
Primers amplifying fragments of c. 150 bp of Macquarie perch mitochondrial (12S) and nuclear (ITS1) DNA were designed, using GEN-  EIOUS v. 7.1.7 (Kearse et al. 2012). Target regions were selected on the basis that they are present in multiple copies within a cell and they are highly variable between species (Long & Dawid 1980;Foran 2006;Hardy et al. 2011). Both primer pairs were tested in silico for undesirable primer interactions and specificity. The best performing primer pairs were tested in vitro by running quantitative PCR

[SECTION] noninvasive
Monitoring methods that do not affect the physical integrity of the organism, but may affect fitness or behavior (qPCR) reactions on a three point, ten-fold dilution series of genomic DNA from Macquarie perch and closely related co-occurring species. For all positive amplifications PCR products were purified, using the MinElute Ò PCR purification kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) and Sanger sequenced to confirm the absence of nonspecific amplification (for full details on primer development and testing see Appendix S1, Supporting Information).
Prior to the experimental set-up, all equipment was soaked for approximately 20 min in a 10% (v/v) bleach solution and thoroughly rinsed with UV-sterilized tap water to destroy any potential contaminating DNA. Experimental fish, 18 one-year old Macquarie perch, were sourced from the Narrandera Fisheries Centre (NFC) (NSW Department of Primary Industries) and used in two tank configurations. Due to the limited number of individuals, configurations were set-up at different times (October 2014 and December 2014) (Fig. 1). Each set-up consisted of six experimental tanks (three replicates per treatment) and a single Negative Control Tank (NCT), which contained no fish to evaluate potential cross-contamination. The first set-up, containing low (one fish/50 L) and high (five fish/50 L) density Experimental Spawning Tanks (EST), was used to simulate spawning for solitary (i.e., the release of gametes by a single male and female) and broadcast (i.e., the release of gametes by multiple males and females) spawning species, respectively. The second configurations consisted of low and high-density Experimental Control Tanks (ECT) to evaluate the potential impact of the sampling strategy on eDNA concentrations. Water samples (50 mL) were collected prior to stocking tanks with experimental animals to confirm the absence of Macquarie perch eDNA. After introducing experimental animals to the tanks, five samples were collected over a 14-day period for each tank (Fig. 1). After collecting samples at day 14 (336 h), EST were supplemented with a 10 mL mixture of Macquarie perch milt (fish seminal fluid obtained from NFC) and UV-sterilized tap water to replicate a single spawning event.
Appropriate milt volumes for low and high density treatments were calculated based on the milt production of single ripe male (10 mL/700 g body weight) (Asmus M., pers. comm.) and the mean body weight of the experimental animals (17Á2 AE 7Á5 g). An equivalent volume of UV-sterilized tap water was added to all the control tanks (NCT and ECT). Water samples were collected from all tanks for an additional 8 days (Fig. 1). After each sampling event, 50 mL of UV-sterilized tap water was added to each tank to keep water volumes constant.
In order to confirm the applicability of our method in the field, a smallscale field survey was conducted targeting known spawning grounds for Macquarie perch within the Upper Murrumbidgee River (UMR) (NSW, Australia). Over a period of 3 years (2012-2015), acoustic telemetry methods were used to track the spawning movements of adult Macquarie perch in the UMR (P. McGuffie, unpubl. data). Six potential spawning riffles, located within a remote section of the UMR, were identified based on this previous research and monitored, using egg collections and eDNA sampling during the spring of 2015 (Fig. 2). Over three sampling events (October 20, Environmental DNA of all collected samples was captured by filtering water samples immediately (experimental samples) or within 24 h (field samples) through a 1Á2 lm glass fiber filter. Before and between filtering samples, all equipment was soaked for 10 min in a 10% (v/v) bleach solution and thoroughly rinsed with UV-sterilized tap water. After sterilization of the filtering equipment, a Negative Equipment Control (NEC) was obtained by filtering 500 mL of UV-sterilized water before loading experimental or field samples. All filters were placed in a 5 mL tube, using sterilized forceps and stored at À20 °C.
Environmental DNA extractions, using the PowerWater DNA Extraction Kit (MoBio Laboratories, Carlsbad, CA, USA), and further analyses were conducted in the trace DNA laboratory at the University of Canberra (Australia). Concentrations of nu-and mt-eDNA in all samples were determined by performing three qPCR replicates per sample for each target fragment, using the SYBR Ò Select Master Mix (ThermoFisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). All qPCR analyses were performed in a final volume of 20 lL on a 96-well plate, using the Viia7 Real-Time PCR System (ThermoFisher Scientific). For each plate a five point standard curve with three qPCR replicates for each DNA concentration (5 9 10 6 -5 9 10 2 ) was used to infer absolute eDNA abundance. Cycling conditions consisted of an initial activation step of 2 min at 95 °C, 55 2-step cycles of 15 s at 95 °C and 1 min at 60°C, and a melting curve step with a continuous increase of 0Á05 °C s À1 from 60 °C to 95 °C. Amplification curves and melt curves were visually inspected and replicates were omitted if the amplification curve did not show a clear exponential phase or the observed melt curves deviated from those observed in the standard curve samples. Additionally, positive PCR replicates obtained from negative control samples (NCT and BFC) and a random subset (≥10%) of experimental and field samples were purified and sequenced. All obtained sequence reads matched the Macquarie perch target sequence. More detailed information for the sample analysis protocol can be found in the Appendix S2.
From the eDNA copies per reaction we calculated the number of eDNA copies per litre of water collected. A correction for the dilution effect was incorporated for all experimental samples and qPCR replicates showing no amplification were assigned a concentration of zero eDNA copies per litre. The obtained eDNA concentrations were subsequently log transformed, using eqn 1. The relative abundance of nu-and mt-eDNA fragments was determined on a per sample basis by calculating the ratios of [nu-eDNA] to [mt-eDNA] across all independent qPCR replicates. All graphs used to visualize changes in the log transformed eDNA concentrations and the ratios of [nu-eDNA] to [mt-eDNA] were constructed, using the packages GGPLOT2, GRIDEXTRA and COWPLOT in R v.3.1.3 (R Development Core Team 2010).

[SECTION] p r i m e r d e s i g n a n d t e s t i n g
After in silico and in vitro testing of the potential primer pairs, the best performing primer combinations were selected for further analyses. Final primer combinations amplified a 148 bp and 157 bp fragment of the 12S and ITS1 region of Macquarie perch, respectively (Table 2). Both primer pairs were considered highly specific as no amplification was observed in closely related co-occurring species (Appendix S1).

[SECTION] e x p e r i m e n t a l r e s u l t s
The ECTs showed a rapid increase in nu-and mt-eDNA within the first 24 h after stocking the tanks with Macquarie perch (Fig. 3). After this initial build-up phase, eDNA concentrations reached a plateau at which equilibrium between eDNA production and degradation was achieved. The observed equilibrium concentrations were generally higher in the high-density treatments and this trend was observed for both nu-and mt-eDNA. When evaluating the relative abundance of nu-and mt-eDNA, the results indicate that both target fragments are equally abundant since the calculated ratios do not deviate strongly from one (Fig. 4). Although a small increase in nu-eDNA concentrations can be observed in the low density ECT at 384 h (Fig. 3), a closer inspection of the raw data revealed that this was due to an increase in a single tank. As the ECT were set-up a month after the EST and immature experimental animals were used, this increase in nu-eDNA is unlikely to be caused by the presence of spermatozoa. A more likely explanation for this pattern is the higher natural variation in eDNA concentrations when species densities are low or increased stress levels experienced by individual fish due to the increased temporal sampling between 336 and 384 h.
Within the EST, the nu-and mt-eDNA concentrations generally follow the same trend as in the ECT for the first part of the experiment. After supplementing the tanks with Macquarie perch milt, however, the abundance of both target fragments increases (Fig. 3). Samples collected one hour after milt supplementation had the highest concentrations of both target fragments. While there is no obvious difference in these peak concentrations between density treatments, there is a clear difference in concentrations between target fragments. In both density treatments, milt supplementation resulted in an approximately 100-fold increase in nu-eDNA relative to mt-eDNA. This relative difference in eDNA concentrations remains detectable in the high and low density treatments for approximately 40 to 60 h, respectively (Fig. 4). Additionally, the results indicate that the degradation profiles for eDNA originating from spermatozoa are dependent on the fish density and the target fragment. A comparison between density treatments reveals that spermatozoa eDNA, both nu-and mt-eDNA, degrades faster in the high density tanks. When comparing the nu-and mt-eDNA degradation curves after milt supplementation for both density treatments, the results indicate that the mt-eDNA follows a typical exponential degradation curve while the nu-eDNA degradation curve follows an inverse logistic function (Fig. 3). This trend can also be observed in Fig. 4 where the calculated ratios show a peak 24 h after milt supplementation.
All NEC and the samples from the NCT associated with the ECT showed no signs of contamination. In contrast, contamination was observed in the NCT which was run simultaneously with the EST (Appendix S3). Analyses of all the samples collected from this tank showed low levels of nu-eDNA shortly before and after EST were supplemented with milt while no mt-eDNA was detected. The most likely source of contamination is thus the handling of Macquarie perch milt prior to collecting the 336 h samples which has caused the transfer of few spermatozoa into the associated NCT. Given that only low levels of nu-eDNA were detected in the NCT (i.e., average log transformed nu-eDNA concentration across all positive samples is 2Á94 AE 2Á32) and no increase in eDNA concentrations was observed in the EST samples collected at 336 h, the observed contamination levels are unlikely to affect the general trends observed.
Through the conventional monitoring methods we were able to confirm the absence of spawning migration during the first day of eDNA sampling (October 8, 2015). In addition, egg collections indicated that Macquarie perch were reproductively active at two spawning riffles (UMR04 and UMR06) during October 21st, 24th, and 27th (Table 3). The eDNA analyses clearly show that outside of the reproductive period (October 8, 2015) the ratios between nu-and mt-eDNA concentrations do not deviate from one (Fig. 5). In contrast to the conventional monitoring, eDNA monitoring did not show evidence of spawning activity during October 24th but all samples collected during October 27th showed an increase in ratios between nu-and mt-eDNA (Fig. 5).
The eDNA analyses performed on both BFC's and NEC's yielded one positive amplification for the 12S gene fragment in the BFC associated with the samples collected from UMR04 on October 27th. Given that all other controls tested negative for Macquarie perch DNA and high concentrations were obtained from a single qPCR replicate (1201 DNA copies/ reaction), it is highly likely that contamination occurred during the PCR set-up. This was further supported by performed an additional six qPCR replicates for both target fragments for this BFC, which did not produce a positive amplification. As such, contamination due to improper sample handling or DNA extractions can be excluded and the results obtained from all associated samples were not omitted from the analyses.

FILE: Diversity and Distributions - 2013 - Dutta - Fine‐scale population genetic structure in a wide‐ranging carnivore  the.grobid.tei.xml
====================================================================================================
[SECTION] methods

[SECTION] study area
We conducted our study in a landscape of approximately 45,000 km 2 in the Satpura-Maikal landscape of Central India (21.15 N -76.50 E, 22.80 N -81.05 E). Narmada and Tapti are the major rivers in this landscape, the catchment of which is formed by the Satpura Range in the north and Maikal Range to the east (Krishnan, 1982). The Vindhyachal Range runs parallel and north of the Satpura Range, separated by the Narmada floodplain. Altitude varies from 320 to 1352 msl and topography ranges from plains, undulating plateaus and grasslands to precipitous cliffs. Temperature ranges from 2 °C in the winter to 48 °C in the summer, marked by an intervening monsoon season (June-August) when the area receives 1000-2200 mm of rainfall. Forest types vary from dry deciduous mixed forest, dry deciduous teak (Tectona grandis) forests, to moist peninsular sal (Shorea robusta) forest.
We sampled four leopard populations in five Tiger Reserves (TRs) in two central Indian states: Madhya Pradesh (MP) and Maharashtra (Mh) (Fig. 1). These TRs are Satpura (1428 km 2 , MP), Melghat (1677 km 2 , Mh), Pench (758 km 2 , MP; 258 km 2 , Mh) and Kanha (2059 km 2 , MP). Although Pench TR is physically present in two states (MP and Mh), the leopard population is contiguous between the two states, and we treated it as one unit in this study to make it biologically meaningful. Satpura and Melghat are located on the western edge and Kanha and Pench on the eastern edge of this landscape, and these two pairs of TRs are each inter-connected by a forest corridor (Fig. 1). Satpura is also connected by a corridor to Pench, while there is patchy connectivity between Melghat and Pench. Leopards and their prey species were reported from these corridors (Jhala et al., 2011). The matrix between the eastern and western pair of TRs has some tracts of forests but is highly populated and contains numerous small cities, towns and villages along with dams, mines and other industries. The soil is agriculturally very productive, and large areas of forest have been converted into cultivation.

[SECTION] field methods
Because direct sighting and sampling from wild leopards are very difficult, we used non-invasive faecal sampling as a source for DNA. During April-June 2009 and Nov 2009-May 2010, we (the first and second author, with the assistance of forest staff) sampled along existing forest trails and roads on foot and by vehicles, collecting felid (leopard and tiger) scats from the TRs and the corridors. We used systematic sampling inside the TRs using a 10 km 2 grid as the sampling unit. We sampled all the grids inside the TRs at least once except those that were completely occupied by dense human populations, barren-land, inaccessible terrain or water bodies. We used stratified random sampling in corridors. Each corridor was stratified based on previous information about leopard occupancy (Jhala et al., 2008); grids with known occupancy were searched preferentially. Our sampling covered 15,000 km of trails and represented c. 8000 km 2 of the total area of 45,000 km 2 . In the field, we identified felid scats by their morphology and associated signs such as scrapes and pugmarks. The GPS location of each scat was recorded. Samples were stored in absolute ethanol until DNA extraction.

[SECTION] genetic methods
We extracted genomic DNA using the QIAamp mini-stool kit (Qiagen Inc., Valencia, CA, USA) following the manufacturer's instructions. DNA samples were first screened for species identification using a leopard-specific FAM-labelled NADH4 marker (Mondol et al., 2009) that amplifies a 130 bp fragment and a tiger-specific TET-labelled NADH5 marker (Mukherjee et al., 2007) that amplifies a 160 bp fragment. Samples that were confirmed as leopards in duplicate runs along with a positive and negative control were then screened with a panel of seven microsatellite loci. Details of individual identification, error rates and characteristics of the microsatellites are described in Dutta et al. (2012) and available in Table S1.
All PCRs were carried out in 5 ll reactions, containing 2 ll Qiagen multiplex PCR buffer mix (Qiagen Inc), 0.2 lm labelled forward (Applied Biosystems, Carlsbad, CA, USA) and 0.2 lm unlabelled reverse primer, 0.5 ll of 109 BSA (New England Biolabs, Ipswich, MA, USA) and 1.5 ll DNA template. PCR conditions for microsatellites were as follows: initial denaturation (94 °C for 15 min), 45 cycles of denaturation (94 °C for 30 s), annealing (Ta for 45 s) and extension (72 °C for 45 s), and a final extension (72 °C for 30 min). PCR conditions for species identification followed protocols and conditions outlined in Mondol et al. (2009) and Mukherjee et al. (2007). All PCR products were separated using capillary electrophoresis on an ABI 3730xl sequencer, using GeneScan -500 LIZ ® size standard (Applied Biosystems) and alleles were scored on GENEMAPPER-4.1 (Applied Biosystems).
We carried out all pre-PCR procedures in sterile conditions in a separate room using aerosol barrier tips to minimize cross-contamination. Negative controls were included in all extractions and PCR to detect the presence of any exogenous DNA or reagent contamination. To account for error rates such as false alleles (FA) and allelic dropouts (ADO), we followed a modified multi-tube approach of Taberlet et al. (1996) and repeated each PCR four times for microsatellite analysis and accepted an allele score only if it amplified at least three times.

[SECTION] data analysis
Because faecal DNA samples are more prone to error, we used the methods outlined in Dutta et al. (2012) to assess the reliability of our markers. We used MICRO-CHECKER 2.2.3 (van Oosterhout et al., 2004) to detect loci containing errors due to scoring or stuttering and estimated FA, ADO and calculated the cumulative P ID (probability of identity) and P ID (sibs) value (Waits et al., 2001) using GIMLET (Vali ere, 2002). Cumulative P ID values provide a measure of power of our panel of selected markers to distinguish individuals. Once we confirmed the reliability of our microsatellite scores, the variability of the microsatellite panel, and the power to distinguish between individuals, we used the program CONVERT (Glaubitz, 2004) for file conversions and enumeration of private alleles.
We measured genetic diversity using estimates of the number of alleles per locus (A), allelic richness (A R ), private allelic richness (P R ), observed (Ho) and expected (He) heterozygosity. We used CERVUS 2.0 (Marshall et al., 1998) to measure A, Ho and He and for individual identification. We used a stringent criterion of five out of seven matching loci to compare each multilocus genotype and identify unique individuals. We used HP-Rare (Kalinowski, 2004(Kalinowski, , 2005)), which uses a rarefaction method to compensate for unequal sample sizes, to compute A R and P R for each population.
We conducted tests for global and population-level deviations from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (HWE) and linkage disequilibrium (LD) using GENEPOP 4.0.10 (Rousset, 2008) with a Bonferroni correction (Rice, 1989) applied for multiple comparisons. We used ARLEQUIN with 10,000 permutations to test the statistical significance of pairwise F ST values (Weir & Cockerham, 1984) as a measure of genetic differentiation among the four TRs.
We measured D EST (Jost, 2008), an improved measure of genetic distance, using the web-based program SMOGD (Crawford, 2010). Gaggiotti et al. (1999) suggested that F ST is well suited when sample size and number of loci are relatively low, whereas D EST appears to be a more accurate and unbiased estimator of differentiation, and outperforms F ST for highly polymorphic markers like microsatellites and when sample sizes are large. We used 1000 bootstrap replicates, and the overall value for each population was calculated as the harmonic mean of D EST across loci, as executed by the software. In addition, we examined whether inter-population genetic differences could be explained by isolation by distance by conducting Mantel tests in ISOLDE (Rousset, 2008) within GENEPOP 4.0. We performed this test for both F ST and D EST . As the straight line Euclidian distance between TRs is not a true representation of their connectivity, we used a modified measure of geographic distance to better represent connectivity through forest cover. We measured the geographic distance between the TRs as the distance through forest cover on GOOGLE EARTH (Ver.6.0.3.2197, Mountain View, CA, USA).
As distance-based measures of population differentiation better reflect evolutionary and historic averages rather than current migration rates, we used individual-based Bayesian approaches to address contemporary genetic processes. We used two individual-based Bayesian clustering methods, STRUCTURE 2.3.3 (Pritchard et al., 2000) and TESS 2.3 (Chen et al., 2007). STRUCTURE is a non-spatial Bayesian clustering analysis that uses a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) procedure to estimate the posterior probability that the data fit the hypothesis of K clusters [(Pr (X|K)]. We allowed the value of K to vary between 1 and 10 and performed 10 independent runs for each value of K. We used the admixture model with correlated allele frequencies (Falush et al., 2003) Diversity and Distributions, 19, 760-771, ª 2012 John Wiley & Sons Ltd without any additional population information using a burnin of 100,000 MCMC steps followed by an additional 100,000 iterations. The mean and standard deviation of Pr (X|K) from the 10 replicate runs were used to find the most likely value of K. We also used the ΔK method of Evanno et al. (2005) based on the second-order rate of change in log Pr (X|K) as implemented by the program STRUCTURE HAR- VESTER (Earl & von Holdt, 2011).
TESS (Chen et al., 2007) is a spatially explicit clustering program that builds individual neighbourhood networks using the Voronoi tessellation. In addition to multilocus genotypic data from individuals, TESS uses spatial information to define population structure without using predefined population information. We ran the TESS analysis for 10,000 burn-ins followed by 50,000 run-in sweeps for K (2-10) with 10 independent runs of each K. We used admixture models with the Dirichlet model of allelic frequencies and the interaction parameter (w) at the default value of 0.6, as suggested by the authors (Chen et al., 2007). We used the Deviance Information Criterion (DIC) and standard deviation to estimate the number of genetic clusters and to compare the performance of various models used in the analysis (Durand et al., 2009). To account for difference between runs and label switching, wherein replicate runs may switch labels for individual runs, we used the large K greedy algorithm in CLUMPP 1.1 (Jakobsson & Rosenberg, 2007) to align the 10 runs with the selected K.
To examine whether individuals originated from the TR in which their scats were collected, we used GENECLASS2 (Piry et al., 2004) with the assignment/exclusion of individuals option. We used a Bayesian approach (Rannala & Mountain, 1997) in combination with the resampling method of Paetkau et al. (2004), wherein we simulated 10,000 individuals at an alpha of 0.01. We also performed a second set of analyses with STRUCTURE, incorporating geographical sampling as prior population information (LOCPRIOR model) with all other parameters being identical to the other STRUCTURE analysis. We used a threshold of q ! 0.8 to assign individuals as residents of that subpopulation and those with q between 0.2 and 0.8 as individuals of admixed ancestry.
We selected the 'detect migrants' function in GENECLASS 2.0 because it is explicitly designed to identify first-generation migrants (Paetkau et al., 2004;Piry et al., 2004), that is, individuals born in a population other than the one in which they were sampled. We computed a likelihood ratio test to compare the population where the individual was sampled over the highest likelihood value among all available populations (L = L_home/L_max), while all other criteria were the same as above. We also used the 'detect migrants' function in STRUCTURE to identify migrants.

[SECTION] genetic variability and summary statistics
We collected a total of 1411 felid scat samples, from which we identified 463 tiger and 287 leopard scats. The break-up of these 287 leopard positive samples from each sampling area was as follows: Melghat (42), Satpura (101), Pench (44), Kanha (95) and Corridor (5). We optimized a set of seven highly polymorphic loci to identify 217 individual leopards (geographic location of each individual is shown in Fig. S1) with a cumulative P ID of 1.44EÀ10 and P ID (sibs) of 5.24EÀ04. These microsatellites have been previously validated on blood and/ or tissue samples and have been found to perform well on faecal samples (Uphyrkina et al., 2001;Mondol et al., 2009). Details of microsatellite characteristics, success and error rates, and individual identification were previously described in Dutta et al. (2012) and are provided in Table S1. Eighteen individuals were recaptured twice, three individuals three times, two individuals four times and one individual seven times.
When samples from all reserves were pooled, six of the seven loci showed significant deviation from HWE. When reserves were tested separately, zero-four loci were in disequilibrium (Table 1), and no locus was consistently out of HWE. Six pairs of loci of 84 pairwise comparisons (four pairs in Pench and two in Satpura) were in significant LD after Bonferroni corrections, and these pairs were not consistent across the populations.
All loci were polymorphic in all populations, and genotypic data revealed high levels of genetic diversity at the seven microsatellite loci across TRs. In the global sample, the mean number of alleles was 13.29 with a range from 10 (FCA008) to 18 alleles (FCA304) and the mean observed (Ho) and expected (He) heterozygosity was 0.74 and 0.84, respectively. All individual reserves had high and comparable levels of polymorphism (number of alleles in all loci > 7) and average allelic richness (8.4-9.9, Table 1). The frequency of private alleles was highest in Satpura, followed by Melghat (Table S2).
Overall average F ST value for this landscape was 0.041 (SD 0.009). All pairwise comparisons of genetic differentiation using F ST and D EST were significant at P < 0.05 (Table 2). F ST and D EST values were highest between Kanha and Satpura. Mantel tests as implemented in ISOLDE in program GENE- POP suggested no significant correlation between geographic and genetic distance measures: F ST (r = 0.5, P = 0.67) or D EST (r = 0.6, P = 0.5).

[SECTION] population structure
In the STRUCTURE analysis, the probability of the data, Pr (X| K), was highest for K = 5 (Fig. S2), beyond which the standard deviation of Pr (X|K) began to increase substantially. The ΔK approach, on the other hand, indicated the presence of two distinct genetic clusters with a smaller peak at K = 4 (Fig. S2a). In cases where the STRUCTURE program finds clustering solutions with similar probabilities at different values of K, the lowest value is typically the most accurate (Pritchard et al., 2000;Pritchard & Wen, 2004). Thus, although there is evidence for population subdivision at both K = 2 and K = 4, we consider K = 2 to be the optimal value in our study. At K = 2, Satpura TR forms one genetic cluster and the three other TRs form another cluster (Fig. 1). K = 4 shows a more fine-scale population structure, wherein each genetic cluster corresponds to each sampled TR.
In TESS, the DIC method infers a K of 4-5 (Fig. S2 (b)). However, in all runs where K > 2, the results were inconsistent between runs and individuals assigned to populations lacked any spatial coherency. At K = 2, all 10 independent runs produced consistent patterns and made geographic sense, wherein Satpura forms one cluster and the other three reserves form another genetic cluster (Fig. 1) and corresponds to the results from STRUCTURE. At K = 3 and K = 4, individual runs were inconsistent. At K = 3 (results not shown), seven of the 10 runs produced results similar to K = 2 (one cluster comprising Satpura, and the other cluster composed of the other TRs), whereas the third cluster contained only 4-7 individuals. At K = 4, three different kind of clustering patterns were observed in TESS, making its interpretation difficult (Fig. S3). Thus, we selected K = 2 as the most parsimonious answer.
We observed that in all of the runs at all values of K using both the programs, Satpura always clustered independently of the other populations. To test whether Satpura was driving the substructuring patterns observed, we ran STRUC- TURE excluding Satpura, using all the same parameters. In this analysis, STRUCTURE detected three genetic clusters that were highly admixed but corresponded to the three reserves (Fig. S4).
The rate at which individuals correctly assign to their sampled locality can be used as an assessment of population genetic structure (Manel et al., 2005). Using the GENECLASS assignment/exclusion test, 164 of the 217 individual leopards (75%) were assigned with the highest probability to the location from which they had been sampled. Many of the individuals that were 'misassigned' were subsequently identified as being of admixed ancestry and/or first-generation migrants. When we used the location prior model in STRUC- TURE, 84% (183 ⁄ 217) of the individuals had high probability of being residents (q > 0.8).

[SECTION] identification of migrants
We identified nine migrants in this landscape. STRUCTURE and GENECLASS produced similar results and identified several of the same individuals (Table 3). STRUCTURE detected six  migrants and GENECLASS detected eight migrants when the two genetic clusters were used as prior population information.
We also ran the analysis with the four TRs and used this analysis to identify which reserve was the source of the putative migrants. We found that six individuals were common to both outcomes, and all three migrants in Satpura TR were assigned to Melghat TR as their source population. STRUCTURE identified 26 individuals of admixed ancestry (Satpura-1, Melghat-13, Pench-7, and Kanha-5), which had q values between 0.2 and 0.8. These individuals could not be definitely identified as either migrants or residents.

[SECTION] genetic variability in leopards
Leopards in central India showed high levels of genetic diversity. The observed and expected heterozygosity (0.74 and 0.84, respectively) were higher than those reported in the only other published study on Indian leopards (Mondol et al., 2009; Ho = 0.57, He = 0.68). All the TRs had similar values of Ho, He, A R and mean number of alleles, but the private allele richness for Satpura and Melghat was higher than for Kanha and Pench. Melghat and Satpura had five private alleles each, while Satpura had the highest frequency of private alleles (Table S2). Among the other subspecies, P. p. pardus has been reported to have the highest observed heterozygosity values of 0.803 (Uphyrkina et al., 2001) and 0.77 (Spong et al., 2000). Heterozygosity was slightly lower in P. p. fusca (0.696) and in P. p. saxicolor (0.616), much lower in P. p. kotiya (0.485) and P. p. japonensis (0.478) and lowest in P. p. orientalis (0.356) (Uphyrkina et al., 2001). P. p. nimr was genetically impoverished (Perez et al., 2006).

[SECTION] population structure of leopards
The significant deviation from HWE for the global test indicated population substructuring, which was further confirmed by the low, but significant F ST values across all comparisons. When comparing pairwise differentiation measures (F ST and D EST ), it is important to note that the highest levels of differentiation observed are between Kanha and Satpura, populations that are not connected by corridors (Fig. 1); and the lowest values are between Kanha and Pench, populations that are connected by a corridor. The appropriate choice of the number of subpopulations, K, was not straightforward for this dataset as we found indications of K = 2 and K = 4. We selected K = 2 as the most parsimonious choice for our dataset based on higher q values, greater geographical concordance, support from spatial and non-spatial approaches, and recommendation from previous studies to choose the smallest value of K that captures the most structure in the data (Pritchard et al., 2000;Pritchard & Wen, 2004). Both STRUCTURE and TESS consistently identified one cluster that consisted of individuals almost exclusively from Satpura, whereas the other cluster consisted of individuals from the other three reserves. However, there is also evidence of ongoing differentiation, based on the second peak for second-order rate of change at K = 4, combined with the high frequency of accurate assignments. The further subdivision of the larger genetic cluster (Kanha-Pench-Melghat) into populations corresponding to geographic locations (Fig. S4) suggests that genetic subdivision is ongoing among leopards in this landscape. Leopards in the entire landscape are admixed, but the Satpura population is genetically more distinct from the other three reserves. Because Satpura is closest to the Narmada River, it could be genetically connected to protected areas across the river that are known to have good leopard populations (Jhala et al., 2011). Leopards could use the several riverine tributaries to move across the river (Athreya, 2006). Alternatively, there could be something specific to the corridor between Melghat and Satpura that prevents higher levels of gene flow. A fine-scale GIS analysis comparing factors such as forest cover, prey availability, road density, human population, land-use patterns and disturbances such as mines and dams is needed to determine which factors are responsible for the patterns that we observe. Although corridors in this landscape have several open-cast coal mines that have existed since as early as 1904 (Gee, 1940) and continue to exist all along the corridor (Singh & Shukla, 2004), we cannot conclusively determine how the Melghat-Satpura corridor differs from the other corridor in this landscape based on our study. The relationship between geographic and genetic distances (F ST and D EST ) among populations was not significant, suggesting absence of isolation by distance in leopard meta-population in our study area and that the observed subdivision cannot be explained by geographic distance between the TRs. Our analysis confirms that the results are not an artefact of sampling scale, nor are they driven by one population. Considering that leopards are habitat generalists (Bailey, 1993) and can disperse over long distances, these results are rather surprising and indicate the role of habitat fragmentation in increasing genetic isolation.
Leopards and predator-occupied forests were abundant in the 19th century in central India, when rewards were given for killing predators (Rangarajan, 1998). Conversion of forest lands into agricultural areas and demand for wood to construct railroads in India escalated the denudation of these Central Highland forests in the 19-20th century, leading to the degree of habitat fragmentation that we observe today (Rangarajan, 1998). Although leopards are often found in disturbed and degraded forests habitats, in close proximity to human habitation, and can survive on small prey like domestic dogs, cats, sheep and goats (Seidensticker et al., 1990;Edgaonkar & Chellam, 2002), given ample medium to large prey and some cover, leopards prefer undisturbed areas distant from human settlements (Ngoprasert et al., 2007;Gavashelishvili & Lukarevskiy, 2008). Leopards tend to avoid areas where tigers live at high densities because tigers are known to kill and out-compete leopards (Schaller, 1967(Schaller, , 1972;;Seidensticker, 1976;McDougal, 1988;Odden et al., 2010); and opportunistically steal their prey (Seidensticker, 1976). For example, in Sariska TR in western India, leopard densities have substantially increased since tigers were extirpated in 2004 (Chauhan et al., 2005;Mondal et al., 2012). Because tigers avoid human-dominated areas, these areas create a potential competition-free refuge for leopards (Odden et al., 2010). However, ecological escape from competition with other carnivores may lead to leopards coming into direct conflict with humans (Athreya, 2006).
Previous studies show that many other large carnivore species can be genetically differentiated at different levels due to habitat fragmentation. In a concurrent study in this same landscape, Sharma et al. (2012) reported low genetic substructuring of tigers, with lower F ST values, indicating higher gene flow than in leopards. In Tanzania (Spong et al., 2000), leopards had high gene flow and very low genetic differentiation. Pumas in Wyoming (Anderson et al., 2004) and Brazil (Miotto et al., 2011) did not have significant population substructuring, whereas Ernest et al. (2003) found significant genetic structure in California where urbanization has severely reduced and isolated natural habitats for the species. Jaguars were found to have high genetic structure and very low migration rates in the Upper Parana Atlantic forest due to severe habitat fragmentation over the past 30 years (Haag et al., 2010). Ultimately, even in highly vagile species, it appears that genetic differentiation varies by the landscape configuration, intensity of the habitat change and species life-history traits, ecology and behaviour.
Dispersal in the Central Indian leopard metapopulation Wright (1931) and Franklin (1980) projected that one successful migrant per generation would be sufficient to prevent population differentiation caused by genetic drift. More recent work suggests that 1-10 migrants per generation may be necessary (Mills & Allendorf, 1996) or even more than 10 migrants per generation (Vucetich & Waite, 2000). Our assignment tests allowed us to identify at least nine-first-generation migrants in our landscape. We identified three migrants in Satpura, one in Melghat, four in Pench and one in Kanha. Because six of the individuals identified with the four TRs as reference in the analysis were the same as those identified with two genetic clusters, we use the results from the former analysis to assign these migrant individuals to source TRs. Four of these six individuals were assigned to TRs connected by corridors. All three migrants in Satpura were assigned to Melghat, and one migrant in Pench was assigned to Satpura TR. These are pairs of TRs that have interconnecting corridors. Two individuals in Pench had the highest probability of having originated from Melghat, and one migrant in Kanha was assigned with highest probability to Satpura. Eleven per cent of all sampled individuals had admixed ancestry. The presence of a substantial number of admixed individuals in these areas suggests that leopards have been able to move across the landscape and reproduce, at least in the recent past.

FILE: Optimization of DNA extraction in the spiny spider crab Maja brachydactyla determining the best extr.grobid.tei.xml

[SECTION] (no title)
stage of the eggs. We consider the three macroscopically distinguishable stages described by González-Gurriarán et al. (1998): A (orange eggs, much yolk), B (brown eggs, visible eyes) and C (dark eggs, many cromatophores, hardly yolk).
We tested several DNA extraction methodologies in fresh and stored in ethanol eggs of ten females from Golfo Ártabro and Ría de Arousa (Galicia, NW Spain). These methods included incubation in 10% bleach, heat shock, mechanical methods (cutting, puncture or homogenization), extraction with Chelex 100 (Bio-Rad), hypotonic shock and extraction with the NucleoSpin Tissue kit (Macherey-Nagel). DNA was quantified using the Nan-oDrop 1000 Spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and we amplified the 16S gene to check its quality. We used the primers 16L29-F and 16HLeu-R (Schubart 2009), and the PCR was performed with the NZYTaq 2× Green Master Mix kit, separate MgCl 2 (Real Laboratory) in a volume of 25 μL. Each reaction contained 25 ng of DNA, 12.5 μL of Green Master Mix, 4 mM of MgCl 2 and a concentration of 0.5 μM for every primer. The PCR consisted in a denaturalization of 5 min at 95 °C, 35 cycles of 30 s at 95 °C, 30 s at 53.1 °C and 45 s at 72 °C, and a final extension of 5 min at 72 °C. The amplification success was tested by electrophoresis and a gel of genomic DNA was performed to corroborate the data obtained by spectrophotometry. We only achieve to amplify the target gene with the DNA obtained by mechanical homogenization and using the commercial kit, as well as with some combinations of these methods with the others. However, the kit had the highest success rate.
We also tested the best developmental stage of eggs and sampled conservation method for DNA extraction in six M. brachydactyla females from the Ría de Arousa. We took two ovigerous females for each egg stage and, for each Abstract Methodological studies are an important previous step in molecular research. We optimize a method for DNA extraction from eggs and a noninvasive extraction method for adult tissues of Maja brachydactyla. Our results show that lyophilized eggs in B developmental stage are the most suitable for DNA extraction. Regarding adult tissues, we propose setae as an alternative tissue for DNA extraction, since prevents mutilation of specimens, which avoids infections and fitness reduction. That is especially relevant in studies with endangered species of crustaceans.

[SECTION] keyword crab • maja • dna extraction method • egg developmental stage • sample conservation • sampling without death
Methological studies focused on improving DNA extraction and sample storage (Bitencourt et al. 2007;Palero et al. 2010) are an important previous step in multiple molecular studies. In the present study we optimized the DNA extraction process from embryonic and adult tissues of Maja brachydactyla (Balss 1922), a decapod crustacean present in the northeastern Atlantic (Neumann 1998;Sotelo et al. 2009). We analyzed different extraction methods, sample conservation, type of adult tissue, and the developmental spawn, we analyzed two replicas of frozen eggs, two of lyophilized eggs and two of eggs conserved in absolute ethanol. The DNA of these eggs was extracted using the Nucle-oSpin Tissue kit. Concentration and quality were tested by spectrophotometry and electrophoresis. The statistical analysis showed that B stage eggs provide the higher DNA concentration. However, the ANOVA only detected statistically significant differences between the amount of DNA obtained from lyophilized and frozen eggs, being lyophilized eggs which provided more DNA.
We also took samples of pleopod setae, pereiopod setae and an endite of nine females from Golfo Ártabro. The DNA of these samples was extracted using the Nucle-oSpin Tissue kit, and the DNA concentration and quality was checked as in the test of the conservation method. The ANOVA showed that endites and pleopod setae provide a higher DNA concentration than pereiopod setae. However, we achieved to amplify the target gene from the three tissues.
Although we expected C stage to be the best developmental stage for DNA extraction, we found B stage to provide more DNA. A possible reason is the presence of substances that interfere in the extraction or hard structures that obstruct the access to the DNA in C stage eggs.
We expected freezing to be the most suitable conservation method for the posterior DNA extraction. Nevertheless, we got a higher quantity of DNA from lyophilized eggs and eggs in ethanol. One possible reason is that part of the DNA was lost during egg handling. Lyophilization and conservation in ethanol induce tissue hardening which facilitate handling. Another advantage is that storage in ethanol does not require special equipment, and DNA quality is similar that in the case of lyophilized eggs.
The most used tissue for DNA extraction in crustaceans is the muscle (McKeown and Shaw 2008;Baggio et al. 2011). However, this study aims to find alternative tissues which avoid the specimen death. This enables to continue researching with the same specimens or even the specimens' liberation after the sampling. Moreover, DNA extraction from structures that prevent the specimens' mutilation, reduces the probability of infections caused by the sampling and avoid fitness decrease. Therefore, we propose setae as an alternative tissue for DNA extraction. In females, the best tissue is indisputably the pleopod setae. Nevertheless, males pleopods are transformed into copulatory appendages, so DNA cannot be extracted from pleopod setae. Furthermore, the extraction of endites from a live specimen is complicated. So, pereiopod setae seem to be a good alternative for DNA extraction in males. From these structures we obtained enough DNA to amplify and sequence the 16S gene of M. brachydactyla, which indicates a good quality of the DNA. These setae have a sensorial function (Laverack 1988) and play a role in the camouflage (Fürböck and Patzner 2005). Nevertheless, sampling would involve such a small area that hardly affects crabs life. Thereby, the utilization of setae for DNA extraction enables to return the specimens to the marine environment. This is especially relevant for sampling in endangered species of crustaceans, since it allows obtaining genetic information without affecting natural populations.
