FILE: WR13073_Berry_SlowRecruitment.grobid.tei.xml
====================================================================================================
[SECTION] materials and methods

[SECTION] study site
Details on the study site have been presented elsewhere (see Berry et al. 2012), and a brief summary is presented here. The study was carried out at Karara and Lochada pastoral stations, Western Australia (28 58 0 05 00 S, 116 40 0 51 00 E), which are adjacent reclaimed pastoral leases. The landscape is semiarid (rainfall 320 mm annually) and is dominated by mixed Acacia shrublands and sparse York gum (Eucalyptus loxophleba) woodlands. Minimal predator control had been conducted on the pastoral leases and the surrounding area before the present study and mostly by neighbouring pastoral leases in an ad hoc manner, to control wild dogs (Canis familiaris).

[SECTION] sampling
We employed eight transects, each containing 11 'sticky wicket' hair-snares spaced at 1-km intervals. The 'sticky wicket' trapped hair as foxes passed between three vertical sticks covered in double-sided tape to enter a monitoring plot containing scent and audio lures (Berry et al. 2012). We employed a mixture of linear and irregularly shaped transects that encompassed 90degree bends. By necessity, transects ran along dirt tracks and hair-snares were placed adjacent and running perpendicular to the tracks within the shrubland vegetation. Although the tracks were predominantly cleared of vegetation, in general, the dominant shrubland vegetation at Karara-Lochada is open enough that foxes can travel unimpeded. We, therefore, assumed that the placement of hair-snares in the vicinity of the tracks minimally biased our analysis. Furthermore, the even density of tracks throughout Karara-Lochada (Fig. 1) should mean that our analysis was representative of the study area. The present study incorporated capture information from the final two sessions reported previously (Berry et al. 2012), namely June and August 2008, here identified as Sessions 1 and 2, and extended an identical sampling regime of ~45-day intervals between sampling sessions that each consisted of four consecutive sampling days (occasions) for a further 12 months until July 2009 (six further sessions). The final sampling session in July 2009 occurred 20 days after deployment from an aircraft of 1080 poison baits at 50 baits km -2 , which was identical to the deployment implemented in August 2008 (Berry et al. 2012), and covered the entire Karara-Lochada study site and a further 5-km buffer from the property boundary. Fifty baits km -2 is the operational rate for feral-cat control (Algar and Burrows 2004). A large rainfall event followed several days after the September 2008 baiting, making it unlikely that baits remained viable for long after. In total, eight sampling sessions took place; however, samples were not obtained for three of these sessions because foxes were absent or at extremely low densities and hairs were not collected on hair-snares.
Sticky wickets were checked daily and hairs were removed from the tape with sterilised forceps, placed in a sealed paper envelope, labelled, frozen at À20 C and transported to the DNA laboratory within 2 weeks of collection. To limit any effect of time on the quality and quantity of DNA in each follicle, DNA extraction was carried out within 2 weeks of the receipt of the samples. Laboratory analyses were conducted under strict protocols and guidelines, to minimise poor-quality samples and reduce genotyping errors (see Berry et al. (2012). DNA was extracted from a maximum of 10 hairs per sample (minimum 1; mean 3.8 AE 0.2) by using the Qiagen DNeasy Blood and Tissue Kit (Cat. 69504; Hilden, Germany).

[SECTION] genotyping and individual identification
Following DNA extraction, samples were genotyped with eight microsatellite DNA loci and the gender of each fox was determined with a male-specific sry product (Berry et al. 2012). Three PCR replicates of each locus were made for each sample. Results of the fragment analysis were analysed using GENEMARKER (SoftGenetics, State College, PA, USA) and all allele calling was checked by eye. The male-specific marker amplified only in the presence of male fox DNA. Therefore, to distinguish between a female and failed amplification, each sample without sry amplification was cross-referenced, with the amplification success of two microsatellite loci coamplified in the PCR multiplex (Berry et al. 2012).
Consensus genotypes were calculated according to the criterion of Frantz et al. (2003) where a homozygous genotype was accepted if the same single allele was present in all three replicates, and a heterozygous genotype was accepted if two different alleles were present in each of two or more replicates. Consensus genotypes for each sample were input into the Excel macro GENECAP (Wilberg and Dreher 2004), which identified genotypes differing by one or two alleles, generated capture histories, provided allele frequencies and probability of identity (PID) statistics (Waits et al. 2001). On the basis of PID results presented in Berry et al. (2012), samples that produced consensus genotypes at five or more loci were sufficiently informative to distinguish individuals and were used to create capture histories. Samples that did not meet the criteria were re-amplified and re-genotyped to obtain more complete genotypes (one example in each of Sessions 1 and 2). Allelic dropout (ADO) and false alleles (FA) were computed from the data with the program GIMLET (Valiere 2002). Identifying individual foxes in this manner is analogous to direct capture for the purposes of capture-recapture analysis.

[SECTION] density estimation using spatially explicit capture-recapture (secr) models
Spatially explicit capture-recapture (SECR) models generated in the program DENSITY were used to estimate the density of foxes within Sessions 1, 6 and 7 (Efford 2004;Efford et al. 2009). SECR uses the locations that each animal is captured to fit a model of the detection process and to provide an estimate of density that is unbiased by incomplete detection and edge effects (Efford 2004). We used the full maximum likelihood estimator (Borchers and Efford 2008) of density (D), and a halfnormal detection function incorporating g 0 (susceptibility to capture at the centre of a home range), and s (a measure of the spatial extent of susceptibility to capture). We identified our hair-snares as proximity detectors (allowing multiple withinoccasion captures per individual), and ran the analysis with a buffer of 10 000 m. Alternative buffer sizes and detection functions had a minimal effect on parameter estimates. Sixteen biologically plausible models were fitted to the capture data and their fit was evaluated with Akaike's information criterion corrected for a small sample size (AICc; Burnham and Anderson 2002). We tested models that maintained a constant density throughout the sampling period, D(.), or a change in density between sessions, D(session). Models that allowed for behavioural responses to capture (b), and individual heterogeneity (two-group mixture; h), in both g 0 and s, and all combinations of these variables, were also tested. Parameters were estimated with model averaging. Sessions 2, 3, 4, 5 and 8 were excluded from the SECR analyses because, at most, one sample was collected in any of those sessions. However, an approximate density was calculated for Sessions 2 and 5 when a single fox was captured by dividing one by the mean effective sampling area identified with SECR modelling during three pre-baiting sessions (Berry et al. 2012;293.3 km 2 ). Sex was not included in the models because of low sample sizes.

[SECTION] apparent survival and abundance
Open-population capture-recapture analysis, based on Pollock's robust design, was conducted with the program MARK (White and Burnham 1999). This analysis enabled estimation of apparent survival (s), capture probability (p), recapture probability (c), abundance ( N ) and temporary immigration (G). Four biologically plausible models were constructed that included behavioural responses to capture (probability of recapture = probability of capture) and individual heterogeneity in capture (two-group mixture). Models that incorporated change in survival and abundance between sessions were also considered, as were models that kept these parameters constant. This analysis was applied to all sessions where foxes were detected (i.e. excluding Sessions 3, 4 and 8). The support for competing models was ranked with AICc, and parameters were estimated with model averaging.

[SECTION] movement between recaptures
The mean distance moved by individual foxes between recaptures was calculated as the cumulative distance moved between trapping locations in order of recapture date within a session, divided by the number of recaptures. Individuals never recaptured were not included in these analyses. For this analysis, we included movement information from foxes collected under comparable experimental conditions during pre-baiting Sessions 1-3 described in Berry et al. (2012). Data were checked for homogeneity of variances with Cochran's C test. Data with heterogeneous variances were log-transformed. A Student's t-test comparing the log10 mean distance moved before and after 1080 baiting (Sessions 2-7) was conducted with the software package JMP (version 5.0; SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC, USA).

[SECTION] species identification, genotyping and error rates
Thirty-five hair samples were collected during Sessions 3-8. These were added to the 52 samples collected from Sessions 1 and 2 that represented 24 individual foxes (Berry et al. 2012).
Thirty-four of the 35 samples were identified as fox, and of these, 33 (97%) provided more than five locus microsatellite genotypes (6 locus n = 2, 8 locus n = 31; Table S1, available as Supplementary Material for this paper). Including the samples from Sessions 1 and 2, 60, 21 and four samples provided eight, seven and six locus genotypes, respectively (no five locus genotypes). No samples contained more than two alleles at any loci, indicating that there were no instances of mixed samples.
Comparisons of genotypes revealed no cases of one-and twoallele mismatches. The average per locus, per replicate rate of allelic dropout (ADO) was 0.016, and the average per locus, per replicate rate of false alleles (FA) was 0.014. The probability of identity (sibling) for the most variable five loci was 0.006, and for the five least variable loci was 0.012, indicating that the fivelocus criterion for accepting genotypes was acceptable. The probability of identity (unrelated) for both the most and least variable five loci was <0.001. Among samples identified as recaptures, the mean probability that any pair of samples were full siblings rather than true recaptures (PIDsib) was 0.003 (AE0.0002 s.e.) and the maximum PIDsib between any pair of samples was 0.012, with only one instance of >0.01

[SECTION] fox capture histories
Five samples (15%) collected during Sessions 3-8 yielded unique genotypes, and thus represented individual foxes. Twenty-eight samples (85%) yielded genotypes that were present at least twice in the dataset and represented six different individuals. In total, 11 individual foxes (seven males and four females) were identified during Sessions 2-7. The initial pre-baiting (Session 1) sex ratio of male:female was 1 : 1.3 (n = 23) and post-baiting (Sessions 2-8) was 1.75 : 1 (n = 11).
The sex ratio pre and post-baiting was not significantly different (c 2 with Yates correction = 0.54, P = 0.46). None of the 23 foxes caught in the session before baiting was recaptured in any of the seven sessions following baiting.

[SECTION] density
Density was estimated directly for Sessions 1, 6 and 7, when multiple individual foxes were detected. All well supported models incorporated a session effect on density and the spatial extent of susceptibility to capture (s) (Table 1). The best supported model also included a behavioural response to capture (probability of capture = probability of recapture), and heterogeneity in response to capture g 0 (b + h). Models ranked 2 and 3 also included heterogeneity in s. The parameter estimates for Session 1 differ slightly from those from the same session (labelled Session 3) in Berry et al. (2012) because of differences in the models selected by AICc and the incorporation of data from different sessions.
Fox density decreased substantially following the initial 1080 baiting, from an estimate of 0.51 foxes km -2 (AE0.17 s.e.) to 0.003 foxes km -2 . Over the following 12 months (7 sessions) density remained very low and not estimatable by SECR, until Sessions 6 and 7 when it increased to a maximum of 0.11 foxes km -2 AE 0.04 s.e. just before the second episode of aerial baiting (Fig. 2), after which no foxes were detected in Session 8. The probability of capture at the centre of a home range g 0 was 0.160 (AE0.092 s.e.) and 0.007 (AE0.014 s.e.) for the 'trap happy' and 'trap shy' groups, respectively.

[SECTION] abundance and apparent survival
The best supported model incorporated change in abundance and apparent survival between sessions and assumed unequal probability of capture and recapture (Table 2). Temporary emigration was constant in these models. Model averaging indicated that there were 30.75 trappable foxes (AE6.83 s.e.) present at Karara-Lochada during Session 1 before the initial baiting and 3.23 (AE0.079 s.e.) in Session 2 immediately after baiting and also in Session 5 (Fig. 3). Ten months after baiting, the number of trappable foxes present in the study area had risen to 12.94 (AE4.09 s.e.) by Session 7. The model-averaged probability of capture was 0.20 (AE0.07 s.e.), and probability of recapture was 0.23 (AE0.04 s.e.). Apparent survival following the initial 1080 baiting (between Sessions 1 and 2) was effectively zero, and remained zero (inestimable) for ~7 months because of zero or sparse captures until the period between Sessions 6 and 7, where it rose to 0.68, which is similar to that before baiting (Berry et al. 2012), although the analysis could not resolve standard error for this estimate because of limited sample size.

[SECTION] changes in the extent of movement between recaptures
Foxes moved significantly further between recaptures after baiting than they did before baiting (Fig. 4; t = 3.41, d.f. = 18, Table 1. Models fitted for spatially explicit capture-recapture analysis of fox density at Karara-Lochada Station, Western Australia, during three sampling sessions, namely Session 1 (prebait), Session 6 and Session 7 (post-bait) Models are defined in terms of whether density was constant (.) or varied between sessions (session), and the effects of behaviour (b) and individual heterogeneity (h) on g 0 and s, and whether s differed between sessions (session).  P < 0.001). Individual foxes did not move between transects in the pre-baiting session, but three foxes moved between transects following baiting, with two of these foxes (both male) moving over 10 km in one day. The parameter s, which describes the spatial extent in susceptibility of capture, and thus indexes home-range size (Efford 2004), was 629.01 m (AE119.52 s.e.) in Session 1 before baiting. During Sessions 6 and 7 (when captures were sufficient to estimate s), it increased to 5174.74 m (AE1078.26 s.e.) and 2600.64 m (AE834.62 s.e.), respectively (values from the best supported model).



====================================================================================================
FILE: HIGH TURNOVER RATE REVEALED BY NON-INVASIVE GENETIC ANALYSES IN AN EXPANDING EASTERN IMPERIAL EAGLE .grobid.tei (1).xml
====================================================================================================
[SECTION] materials and methods

[SECTION] study area
The 21,600 km 2 study area covers the north-eastern part of the Hungarian Plain and nearby the mountains of Mátra, Bükk, and Zemplén (46°35'-48°30'N 19°35'-21°50'E), a region holding more than 90% of the Hungarian, and more than 60% of the EU population of Imperial Eagles. The lowland plain habitats (90-120 m a.s.l.) are mainly intensive agricultural fields with small pastures and groups of poplar (Populus spp.) and black locust trees (Robinia pseudoacacia). The mountain habitats (200-700 m a.s.l.) are mainly forested by native oak (Quercus petrea, Q. cerris) and beech (Fagus sylvatica) or by introduced pine trees (Pinus silvestris, P. nigra, Larix decidua).

[SECTION] sample collection and dna extraction
Altogether 3771 shed feathers of adult breeding eagles were collected under nests and roost sites in Eastern Hungary between 1997 and 2006 (Fig. 1). Most nests and nearby roosting trees were visited twice per year, first in June, when nestlings were ringed as part of the population monitoring protocol (Horváth et al. 2011) and between July and September after fledging, in order to reduce disturbance. As at this time chicks' flight feathers are only growing and the breeding pair is extremely territorial all feathers can be assumed to belong to the resident pair. Also it is unlikely that feathers from the year before sampling could remain in a condition good enough to be suitable for DNA analyses (Vili et al. 2013).
For DNA extraction we used feathers with minor or no sign of degradation (Hogan et al. 2008), most probably shed less than 1-3 weeks prior to the collection. Feathers were stored in a dry, cool and dark place to minimize further degradation of the DNA. The superior umbilicus part of the feather shaft was separated as described by Horváth et al. (2005).
Altogether 46 territories, where at least three years of consecutive breeding was observed were selected. As we found strong bias toward females in a previous study of Imperial Eagles where all available feathers were submitted to molecular sexing (Vili et al. 2009b) we primarily searched for the most suitable female samples. Because of this, one to three of best quality feathers of a given territory in a given year were selected for DNA extraction and molecular sexing. DNA was extracted according to the standard salting out method as described by Gemmell and Akiyama (1996). To facilitate the digestion process by reducing disulphide bonds in the keratin tissue, 10 μl 1M Dithiothreitol (DTT) was added to each sample (Weigmann 1968). The efficiency of the purification procedure and the degradation of DNA were checked before further analyses by agarose gel electrophoresis (3μl on 0.8% gel).

[SECTION] molecular sexing
Each individual feather was sexed by amplifying introns of the sex chromosomelinked CHD1 gene, using the primers (2550F and 2718R) and PCR conditions published by Fridolfsson and Ellegren (1999). In Imperial Eagles, these primers amplify a larger sequence (CHD1Z, 700bp) in both sexes and a smaller one (CHD1W, 450bp) in females only (Horváth et al. 2005, Vili et al. 2009a). To identify the sex of the sampled specimen 5μl of the PCR product was visualized by ethidium-bromide on 2.5% agarose gel.

[SECTION] microsatellite fragment analysis
Sequences of nine dinucleotide repeats (Martinez-Cruz et al. 2002) and eight tetranucleotide repeats (Busch et al. 2005) have been published for Spanish and Eastern Imperial Eagles. To identify individual DNA-profiles of breeding eagles, two dinucleotide (Aa02 and Aa39) and six tetranucleotide loci (IEAAAG04, IEAAAG12, IEAAAG11, IEAAAG15, IEAAAG09 and IEAAAG14) were selected and amplified with the use of fluorescently labelled primers. A modified version of the PCR protocol described by Martinez-Cruz et al. (2002) was used in the amplification procedure in which a touchdown PCR was performed in all loci. For loci Aa39, Aa02, IEAAAG09 and IEAAAG14 the annealing temperature was decreased from 66 to 50°C and for IEAAAG04, IEAAAG12, IEAAAG11 and IEAAAG15 from 60 to 50°C. The exact fragment lengths of the amplified PCR products were determined by capillary electrophoresis (ABI PRISM® 310 Genetic Analyzer, Applied Biosystems) with GeneScan 3.7 and PeakScanner 1.0 softwares (Applied Biosystems), using the ILS600 (Promega) internal lane standard. Each sample was scored three times independently and genotypes were assigned without the knowledge of the sample's origin. Allele frequencies and probability of identity (PI, the probability that two randomly chosen individuals in a population will have the same genotype at multiple loci, Waits et al. 2001) were calculated with GenAlEx 6.4 (Peakall & Smouse 2006), deviation from the Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium and the probability of null alleles were calculated with Micro-checker 2.2.3 (Van Oosterhout et al. 2004).

[SECTION] turnover rate
Genetic tagging allowed us to estimate the turnover rate of only females in the population. As we could not obtain DNA sample at every studied nest in each year, minimum and maximum turnover rates were estimated. According to the data from nest site ranges where suitable samples were available from each studied year, when a female was identified in any two years at a certain nest site no other female was found between those dates at the same site. Any female lost from a nest site range did not reappear later in the same range. These data suggest that when one individual was identified at least twice as a resident female (first at the start of the studied period and second after the years without samples), the same individual was using the nest site range in the missing years as well (Table 1, rows a-b).
When data was missing between different individual residents, the minimum turnover rate was estimated by assuming a single change that was actually detected by genotyping, and the maximum rate was estimated by assuming changes for every missing year in addition to the one detected (Table 1, rows c-f). Both minimum and maximum rates were determined by averaging the number of turnover events in each territory, in order to avoid Table 1. Observed patterns of re-identification and replacement events of females with incomplete sampling. A and B represent the different genotypes, question marks represent the years without suitable samples for individual identification. When a different female was found after the missing years, minimum and maximum number of changes was calculated. E.g. in rows a and b no change was assumed, because the same female resided at the nest site both times; in row d the minimum is one that was detected by the genetic tagging and the maximum is three, because there were two years without data. pseudo-replication, which could happen if using the data of the same individuals or the same territories as independent.
Differences between the turnover rates in mountain and lowland territories were tested with Brunner-Munzel test using the "lawstat" package (Hui et al. 2008) implemented in the R statistical computing environment (version 2.12.1; R Development Core Team 2011).

[SECTION] sampling success
Altogether 497 selected feathers were sexed of which 450 (90.5%) derived from females and only 47 (9.5%) from males. Therefore, due to their low sample size males were excluded from the present analysis.
For the fragment analyses we selected the best quality female feather of a given breeding attempt. Out of these 166 samples 153 (92.1%) amplifications were successful, determining altogether 77 different female genotypes in 46 territories. Therefore indicating that 28.8% of all breeding attempts (530) and 51.1% of all territories (90) was successfully sampled in the study area during the 10 year period.

[SECTION] individual identification
Two of the eight loci were assumed to contain null alleles (Aa39 and IEAAAG09). In order to avoid the genotyping bias all homozygous genotypes were excluded from the analyses on these loci. On the other six loci there was no significant difference from the Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium and there was no evidence for linkage disequilibrium (Table 2). The PI value of the marker set was 3.7×10 -6 . Genotyping errors were calculated as described by Rudnick et al. (2005) because of the similarity of the sampling and processing methods. The 153 analysed female feathers represented 1224 genotyped loci out of which 25 (2.04%) were missing after multiple PCRs (1.22%) or could not be clearly identified (0.82%) and hence were treated as missing data.
In the first sampled year of all the 46 territories we identified 46 different females. In the subsequent years 107 individuals were identified, out of which 74 (69.2%) were the same as in the previous year, meaning they were re-found in the territory. In 31 cases (28.9%) new residents were found and only two birds (1.9%) were detected in a different territory as before (see details below).
Out of the 31 replacement events, we had data on the age category of the new and replaced females in 20 cases based on their plumage identified in the field. In the majority (14) of these, adults were replaced by adult birds. In four cases females in immature plumage were replaced by immature ones and in only two cases were immature birds replaced by adults.

[SECTION] high turnover rate in expanding eastern imperial eagle population

[SECTION] birds re-identified in different territories
Birds were re-identified in different territories in two cases. In the first one, a breeding female was found again three years later in a nest which was assigned to another territory (Fig. 2). In the other case, according to field observation, two breeding pairs were assumed to have changed their territory boundaries several times in a three year period. This was later partly confirmed by genetic data (Fig. 3).

[SECTION] turnover rate
Turnovers were calculated in each territory then averaged to obtain the minimum and maximum average turnover rates. Minimum average yearly turnover rate of female resident eagles (replacement of a genetically tagged resident by a genetically tagged new female) was 27.7%, while maximum rate (interpreting all missing years between two different females on the same territory as replacement events) was 35.5 % (see Materials and methods and Table 1).
Turnover rate tends to be smaller in the mountain territories than in the lowlands (21.2-28.3% vs. 29.3-38.0% respectively, Table 3a and b) although the difference was not statistically significant (minimum rate: Brunner-Munzel Test Statistic = -0.8035, df = 24.409, p = 0.429; maximum rate: Brunner-Munzel Test Statistic = -0.764, df = 24.237, p = 0.452).

[SECTION] table 3a.
Turnover events in the sampled lowland territories. Capital letters (A-C) represents genetically identified female individuals in the given territory in alphabetic order, while lower cases (a-c) are the probable individuals, which were not genetically identified in the given year but according to our observations the double replacement (e.g. A -B -A) is unlikely. FILE: URSUS-D-13-00001.1.grobid.tei.xml
====================================================================================================
[SECTION] (no title)
Sloth bears (Melursus ursinus) are endemic to the Indian subcontinent and are evolutionarily distinct from other bear species of the world (Servheen et al. 1999). It is a medium-sized bear (adult males 75-140 kg; females 55-95 kg) with a suite of adaptations for feeding on ants and termites. Sloth bears are listed as vulnerable on the International Union for Conservation of Nature red list of threatened species (Garshelis et al. 2008) and in Appendix I of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (http://www.cites. org). They are also protected under Schedule I of the Indian Wildlife Protection Act, 1972 (http://envfor. nic.in/legis/wildlife/wildlife1.html). Sloth bears are found in a variety of habitats, including wet or dry tropical forests, savannas, scrublands, and grasslands (Joshi et al. 1995, Sreekumar and Balakrishnan 2002, Akhtar et al. 2004, Ratnayeke et al. 2007). As a result of continued habitat destruction and degradation, sloth bear populations have declined or become fragmented. Habitat has been lost, degraded, and fragmented by over-harvesting of forest products (timber, fuel wood, fodder, fruits, and honey), establishment of monoculture plantations, and expansion of agricultural areas, human settlements, and roads (Santiapillai and Santiapillai 1990).
Non-invasive genetic sampling has been used to study most of the extant bear species (Paetkau and Strobeck 1998), but to our knowledge these methods have not been developed to monitor populations of the sloth bear. Here we describe a non-invasive genetic method for individual identification that can be used for population monitoring and genetic studies of sloth bears.

[SECTION] methods
During November 2009-May 2010, we collected fecal and hair samples from wild sloth bears in four tiger reserves (TR) in Central India: Kanha, Satpura, Pench (in Madhya Pradesh), and Melghat (in Maharashtra). We sampled along forest trails and collected bear scats identified by their morphology (size, shape, and diameter) and the presence of ants, termites, or seeds. We stored these samples in 100% ethanol until DNA isolation in the lab.
We isolated genomic DNA using the QIAamp mini-stool kit (Qiagen, Venlo, Netherlands) following the manufacturer's protocol for isolation of DNA from stool for human DNA analysis. We carried out all pre-PCR procedures with aerosol barrier tips in a separate room to minimize cross-contamination.
To select a panel of microsatellite loci, we used 21 geographically isolated non-invasive samples (2 hair samples from known captive individuals, and 3 hair and 16 scat samples from geographically isolated sloth bear positive samples; Fig. 1). We used these slothbear-positive samples to screen 18 microsatellites developed on American black bear (Ursus americanus; Paetkau and Strobeck 1994, Paetkau et al. 1995, 1998), brown bear (U. arctos; Taberlet et al. 1997, Bellemain andTaberlet 2004), polar bear (U. maritimus; Poissant and Davis 2011), and domestic dogs (Ostrander et al. 1993, Cronin et al. 2009).
Because these primers were developed on other bear species and dogs, we screened them on known sloth bear samples using gradient PCR from 48uC to 60uC to optimize the annealing temperature. We used a multiplex pre-amplification method to increase the success rate of amplification of each locus and the quality of the amplified DNA fragments (Poissant and Davis 2011). We conducted preamplification PCR in 25 mL reactions containing 0.5 U Ampli Taq Gold DNA Polymerase (Applied Biosystems, Carlsbad, California, USA), 0.01 mM each fluorescently-labeled forward primer, 0.01 mM each unlabeled reverse primer, 2 mM MgCl 2 , 1X Gold buffer, 0.1 mM of each dNTP, 2 mL 10X BSA, and 4-5 mL of the DNA extract. We performed a second round of PCR amplification for each locus as described above except the final reaction volume was 10 mL, and we added 0.2 mM of both forward and reverse primer and 1.5 mL of pre-amplified product as the DNA template. PCR conditions were: initial denaturation step (95uC for 10 min), 45 cycles of denaturation (95uC for 30 sec), annealing temperature (Ta, for 30 sec) and extension (72uC for 1 min), and a final extension step (72uC for 7 min).
Conditions for PCR pre-amplification were the same except the Ta (60uC for brown bear primers and 50uC for the remaining primers) and 25 cycles of amplification. We ran all PCR products on an ABI 3730xl sequencer, using GeneScan TM -500 LIZ (Applied Biosystems) size standard. We scored alleles using GeneMapper-4.1 (Applied Biosystems). We included negative controls in all PCR reactions to detect any contamination. To minimize genotyping errors, we followed a modified multitube approach (Taberlet et al. 1996) and repeated each PCR 4 times for each sample and for each microsatellite locus.
We used CERVUS-3.0.3 (Kalinowski et al. 2007) for individual identification. We used GIMLET-1.3.3 (Valie `re 2002) to obtain measures of genetic variation such as mean number of alleles per locus, observed (H o ) and expected (H e ) heterozygosities, and P ID (probability of identity) and P ID(sibs) value (Waits et al. 2001). We used MICRO-CHECKER-2.2.3 (van Oosterhout et al. 2004) to detect loci containing errors due to scoring or stuttering and large allele dropout. We estimated PCR success and genotyping error rates (false alleles [FA], and allelic drop out [ADO]) using GIMLET. We conducted tests for deviations from Hardy Weinberg equilibrium (HWE) and tests for linkage disequilibrium (LD) in GENEPOP-3.4 (Raymond andRousset 1995, Rousset 2008) with a Bonferroni correction (Rice 1989).

FILE: Estimating fish abundance and biomass from eDNA concentrations variability among capture methods and.grobid.tei.xml
====================================================================================================
[SECTION] materials and methods

[SECTION] target species
Brook Charr is a sportfish highly valued for anglers and susceptible to overfishing (Johnston & Post 2009), with a well-known ecology. In Qu ebec in particular, Brook Charr supports the most important freshwater angling fishery involving 500 000 fishermen and 4 000 000 angling days per year (Department of Fisheries and Oceans Canada (DFO) 2012 and unpublished provincial government statistics 2013). Despite such a high fishing pressure, little data exist to determine the current status of Brook Charr populations and their temporal dynamics, and there is no standardized method to compare population data. Brook Charr live in clear and well-oxygenated rivers, lakes and ponds and prefer water temperatures between 11 °C and 13 °C, but the annual range of temperature the species is exposed to spans approximately 0-20 °C (Power 1980). As for other fish species, increased water temperature has been documented to result in higher metabolic rate in Brook Charr (Selong et al. 2001;Gale et al. 2013).

[SECTION] experimental design
The relationship between Brook Charr abundance/biomass and eDNA concentration was evaluated at two different temperatures by collecting water from aquaria and then comparing results among eDNA capture methods. Brook Charr fingerlings (age 0+) were obtained from a fish hatchery (Pisciculture de la Jacques-Cartier Inc, Cap-Sant e (Qc), Canada). Brook Charr fingerlings were placed in aquaria at two different temperatures whereby 15 aquaria (plastic 20-L containers filled with 15 L of water) were kept at 7 °C and 15 others at 14 °C (Fig. 1). These water temperatures roughly correspond to limits most likely to be encountered by Brook Charr during their growing season corresponding also to the period when eDNA monitoring would most likely be performed for management purposes. For each temperature, 0, 5, 10, 15 and 20 fish were placed in each aquarium with triplicate for each fish abundance (30 aquaria in total). The aquaria without fish (abundance: 0; Fig. 1) were used as negative controls (i.e. three aquaria were used as negative controls for each temperature). The total biomass for each aquarium was measured using the difference in weight between a water bucket with and without fish. Fish were acclimated to the experimental temperature for at least 5 days prior to the onset of the experiment to reduce changes in the rates of various physiological processes associated with stress due to abrupt alteration in temperature (Jobling 1994). Fish were then transferred to aquaria with sterilized instruments and left in aquaria in the dark and without stimulus for 48 h. They were then removed prior to water collection using sterile instruments, and the water has been rapidly collected to limit the effect of eDNA degradation. To ensure stable temperature among aquaria, the 20-L containers were placed in a larger pool with controlled water temperature. All fish were held in accordance with Laval University's Institutional Animal Care (CPAUL; protocol number: 2013033-1).

[SECTION] edna collection and capture
For each of the 30 aquaria, five separate 1-L samples of water (i.e. 1 L for each filter; Fig. 1) were collected in sterilized bottles after the water was well mixed using a sterilized stick. The water bottle was kept on ice and in the dark until filtration, which was performed 1-2 h after the water collection. Water samples were filtered using five different types of filters: mixed cellulose ester filters (MCE, a combination of cellulose nitrate and cellulose acetate; Advantec) with a nominal pore size of 0.2 lm or 0.45 lm and glass microfibre filters (GF, borosilicate glass) with a nominal pore size of 0.7 lm (Whatman GF/F), 1.2 lm (Whatman GF/C) or 3 lm (PALL Type A/D). All filters were frozen at À20 °C immediately after DNA filtration. In addition to filtration material composition and pore size, the filter thickness also varied: 133 lm of thickness for the MCE 0.2 filter, 145 lm for the MCE 0.45 filter, 420 lm for the Whatman GF/F filter, 260 lm for the Whatman GF/C filter and 660 lm for the PALL Type A/ D filter. Filtration tools were sterilized after each filtration with a 10% bleach solution. Bottles of water were all collected at the same time for each temperature treatment and filtered in a random order by two simultaneous water pump systems.

[SECTION] extraction and amplification
DNA was extracted using the salt extraction method (Aljanabi & Martinez 1997). A 139-bp fragment of the cytochrome b gene (cyt b) was amplified using the BRK2 primers and probes designed by Wilcox et al. (2013): forward primer (5 0 -GCCAAGTAATATAGCTACAAAACCTAAT AGATC -3 0 ), reverse primer (5 0 -GCCAAGTAATATAG CTACAAAACCTAATAGATC -3 0 ), probe (5 0 -ACTCCGA CGCTGACAA -3 0 ). The eDNA concentration was quantified using real-time Taq-Man â PCR with a 7500 Fast Real-Time PCR system (Life Technologies). For each sample, the qPCR was performed six times on separate plates (3 replicates per plate). The final reaction volume was 20 lL, including 1.8 lL of each primer (10 lM), 0.5 lL probe (10 lM), 10 lL Environmental Master Mix 2.0 (Life Technologies), 3.9 lL diH 2 0 and 2 lL DNA. The qPCR amplification was performed under the following conditions: 2 min at 50 °C, 10 min at 95 °C, followed by 70 cycles of 15 s at 95 °C and 60 s at 60 °C. Each qPCR plate included three wells that contained all reagents, but no DNA template, to serve as a negative control (N total = 60 qPCR negative controls). Each qPCR plate also contained a 7-point qPCR standard curve ranging from 4.0-2.6 10 À4 ng/reaction. The R 2 values for the qPCR standard curve ranged from 0.99 to 1.00, and the efficiency ranged from 89 to 98%. Filtration, extraction, preparation of the qPCR plates and qPCR cycling were all performed in different rooms to avoid potential laboratory cross-contamination. TaqMan â Exogenous Internal Positive Control Reagents (Life Technologies) were also used to detect deviation of the amplification curves potentially caused by inhibitors (Pilliod et al. 2013a). The effect of inhibitors on the deviation of the Ct values was evaluated from the comparison of the Ct values between amplifications containing positive exogenous internal control in sterile nuclease-free water (i.e. inhibitor free). A Ct shift of ≥3 cycles beyond the water blank was considered inhibitory (Hartman et al. 2005).

[SECTION] statistical analyses
Mixed-design analysis of variance was performed with R 3.0.3 using the function Anova() of the CAR library to evaluate the differences in eDNA concentration captured using different types of filters, water temperatures and fish abundance/biomass per tank. The tank replicates were also included as a random variable. Because the normality and homoscedasticity assumptions were not satisfied, differences in eDNA concentration among filters for each fish abundance were assessed by the nonparametric Kruskal-Wallis one-way ANOVA followed by a Tukey's honest significant differences (HSD) test on ranks. To test for significant differences in the average eDNA concentration between 7 °C and 14 °C for each type of filter and fish abundance, Mann-Whitney test was performed. To evaluate the relationship between abundance/biomass and eDNA concentration, the quantification of the amount of eDNA was obtained by averaging amplification technical replicates (Ellison et al. 2006). The relationships between eDNA concentrations and fish abundance or biomass were initially examined in bivariate scatterplots. Linear and exponential regression models were plotted only for significant relationships (P ≤ 0.01 and R 2 > 0.40) when the necessary assumptions (normality and homoscedasticity) were satisfied. The Shapiro-Wilks test was used to verify the normality of distributions of the regression residuals, and the Levene's test was applied for assessing the equality of variances of the residuals. A Cook's distance test was used to detect outliers and influential points to increase the robustness of the relationship between abundance/ biomass and eDNA concentration. The latter statistical analyses were all performed using JUMP 9.0.0 (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC, USA), and the figures were drawn using SigmaPlot 10.0 (Systat Software Inc., CA, USA). The significance threshold used was P < 0.05. To inform about the dose response between fish density and the amount of eDNA released (e.g. activity increasing at high fish density (Gu enard et al. 2012)), the goodness of fit for models selection was conducted using the corrected Akaike's information criterion (AICc). AICc differences (ΔAICc) were obtained by the AIC of the exponential fits minus the AIC of the linear fits. Models with the smallest AICc values gave the most parsimonious description of the data. In general, ΔAICc >10 suggests strong evidence for a difference between models (Burnham & Anderson 2002). Regressions statistics and AICc values were calculated using R version 3.0.3.

[SECTION] effects of types of filters
The different types of filters differed in their efficiency in capturing eDNA. In general, higher levels of eDNA were captured with GF than were captured using MCE filters. At 7 °C, the filter GF of 0.7 lm yielded the highest eDNA concentrations for 10, 15 and 20 fish per tank (Fig. 2). At 14 °C, GF of 1.2 lm yielded the highest eDNA concentration at densities of 5, 10 and 15 fish per tank and GF of 3.0 lm at 20 fish per tank (Fig. 2). Overall, the GF of 1.2-lm filter had the highest eDNA collection efficiency (average of eDNA concentration for all fish densities and both temperatures = 115.28 ng/L, median = 38.55 ng/L), followed by GF of 0.7 lm (average = 81.12 ng/L, median = 4.57 ng/L) and GF of 3.0 lm (average = 67.16 ng/L, median = 22.49 ng/L). In contrast, MCE of 0.2 lm captured very low levels of eDNA (average = 9.04 ng/L, median = 3.74 ng/L) and, despite a larger pore size, MCE of 0.45 lm captured more eDNA than MCE of 0.2-lm filters (MCE 0.45 lm: average = 42.77 ng/L, median = 11.70 ng/L).

[SECTION] effect of temperature
A single aquarium exposed at 7 °C (10 fish) showed extremely high eDNA concentration (eDNA > 1500 ng/L). Therefore, the effect of temperature on eDNA concentration was assessed with (Fig. 3) and without this aquarium (Appendix S1). For both analyses, when considering each type of filter separately, water temperature significantly altered eDNA concentration except for the MCE of 0.2-lm and GF of 0.7-lm filters (Fig. 3 and Appendix S1). Filters with low levels of eDNA capture (i.e. MCE of 0.2 lm) did not detect the difference between the eDNA concentration at the two different water temperatures. Higher eDNA concentrations were found at 14 °C than at 7 °C at all levels of fish abundance, and the difference was consistently significant at all fish abundance for the GF of 3.0-lm filter (Fig. 3).

[SECTION] relationship between fish density and edna
Relationships were found between the eDNA concentration and fish density. Importantly, the predictive power of quantifying fish abundance/biomass varied between temperatures studies and among eDNA capture methods. The relationships between the eDNA concentration and fish abundance/biomass were stronger at 14 °C than at 7 °C (Table 2; Figs 4 and5; see Table S1 and Appendices S2 and S3 for results including outliers). Filter type and filter pore size also influenced the power of predict-ing fish abundance/biomass based on the eDNA captured, with strongest relationships observed with the GF of 0.7-and 3.0-lm filters (Table 1; Figs 4 and5). Except for the GF of 3.0-lm filter, which showed a significant evidence for a linear fit (fish biomass ΔAICc = 10.8; fish abundance ΔAICc = 6.9), no strong evidence was found for a difference between biomass/abundance and linear/exponential dose response (|ΔAICc| 4.9 for all other filter types; Table 1).

FILE: Isolation, characterization and multiplex PCR development of Bean Goose (Anser fabalis) microsatelli.grobid.tei (1).xml

[SECTION] (no title)
The global population appears to be decreasing, and the Bean Goose is currently listed as vulnerable on the Norwegian Red List (Henriksen and Hilmo 2015). As the Bean Goose is very shy and difficult to observe during the breeding season, DNA analyses of non-invasively collected molted feathers may be a valuable complement to traditional field-based approaches for counting and tracking Bean Geese. In this study we applied high-throughput sequencing to identify novel Bean Goose microsatellites. To facilitate genetic monitoring based on non-invasive sampling of molted feathers, we targeted microsatellite loci with short (\250 bp) amplicons, as amplification success and allele-dropout are affected by amplicon size when genotyping DNA from non-invasively collected samples (Broquet et al. 2007). Furthermore, we developed two multiplex PCR assays for 12 loci and evaluated these assays in a Taiga Bean Goose (A. fabalis fabalis) population in central Norway. Finally, these two assays were applied to test for cross-species amplification success in four other Anser species.
Samples collected in central and northern Norway from seven Bean Geese were sent as blood stored in lysis buffer and DNA (extracted from feathers) eluted in tris-EDTA buffer to Ecogenics GmbH (Balgach, Switzerland) to produce an enriched microsatellite library and to test for polymorphism. In brief, size-selected fragments from genomic DNA were enriched for simple sequence repeat (SSR) content using magnetic streptavidin beads and biotin-labeled CT and GT repeat oligonucleotides. The SSRenriched library was analysed on a MiSeq platform (Illumina, Inc., San Diego, CA, USA) using the Nano 29250 v2 format. After assembly, 5307 contigs or singlets contained a microsatellite insert with a tetra-or a trinucleotide of at least six repeat units or a dinucleotide of at least ten repeat units. Suitable primer design was possible in 2305 microsatellite candidates, of which 36 were tested for polymorphism. These 36 loci were selected because they yielded amplicons of fewer than 250 base pairs, which facilitates analysis of non-invasively collected samples. Selection was then performed based on genetic variation, single-PCR performance, and peak interpretation, and multiplex PCR was developed through tests of different combinations of markers and adjustments of primer concentrations for the final subsets. Microsatellite loci were PCR-amplified with fluorescent-labeled forward primers. Single PCRs were performed in a final volume of 10 lL, with a protocol consisting of 95 °C for 15 min, 35 cycles of 95 °C for 30 s, 57 °C for 45 s, 72 °C for 45 s, and a final extension step of 72 °C for 30 min. Multiplexing was performed with a Multiplex PCR Plus Kit (QIAGEN, Hilden, Germany), following the manufacturer's protocol but using an 8.4-lL reaction volume. PCR products (0.8 lL) were mixed with GeneScan 500 LIZ (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA, USA) size standard (0.14 lL) and Hi-Di formamide (6.16 lL). Alleles were separated using capillary electrophoresis on an ABI 3130xl Genetic Analyzer and sizes assigned using GeneMapper software (Applied Biosystems).
For genotyping, we used sample types relevant for genetic monitoring and conservation genetics, i.e. blood from two individuals, plucked feathers from two individuals, and molted feathers from 27 individuals, all collected in the years 1990-2014 in central Norway. Cross-species amplification of the markers was tested by including samples (blood or tissue) from four other Anser species. Genomic DNA was extracted from blood using a manual commercial kit (QIAGEN DNeasy Blood & Tissue Kit), following the manufacturer's protocol. DNA from feathers and tissue was extracted using an automated system (Maxwell Ò 16 Research Instrument; Promega Corp., Madison, WI, USA) and the Maxwell 16 tissue DNA purification kit, following the manufacturer's protocol.
The mean number of alleles, observed and expected heterozygosities, deviation from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, and linkage disequilibrium were estimated using Arlequin version 3.5.1.2 (Excoffier and Lischer 2010). A Bonferroni correction for multiple statistical tests (Rice 1989) was applied to linkage disequilibrium p values. Nullallele frequencies were estimated with Micro-Checker ver. 2.2.3 (van Oosterhout et al. 2004), and the probability of identity was calculated using GenAlEx 6.501 (Peakall and Smouse 2012).
PCR analysis of three to seven individuals was conducted for the 36 microsatellite loci, and allelic variation was detected in 34 of those (Table 1). Scoring both PCR performance and allele interpretation (results not shown), we selected 12 loci for multiplex PCR development. The two final multiplex PCR assays were typed in 31 presumably unrelated Bean Geese [17 females and 14 males; sex determined with the Z-002A marker (Dawson 2007)]. The  2). Heterozygotes were present in both sexes for all loci, indicating that none are sex-linked. The mean expected heterozygosity was 0.75 (range 0.54-0.85) and mean observed heterozygosity was 0.74 (range 0.58-0.87; Table 1). After correcting for multiple tests, no pairs of loci displayed significant linkage disequilibrium. There was no indication of null-alleles in any locus, but one locus (Afa18) deviated significantly from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (Table 2). The combined probability of identity for the 12 loci was 6.5 9 10 -13 . Cross-species application of the two multiplex PCR assays revealed that all 12 loci amplified successfully in four other Anser species and all loci were polymorphic in the Greater White-fronted Goose (A. albifrons), Lesser White-fronted Goose (A. erythropus), and Pink-footed Goose (A. brachyrhynchus), while three loci were monomorphic in the Greylag Goose (A. anser; Table 3). The lower proportion of polymorphic loci in the Greylag Goose is in line with previous studies showing that microsatellite performance decreases with genetic distance (e.g. Primmer et al. 1996), as the Greylag Goose is most distantly related to the Bean Goose among the four Anser species tested (Ruokonen et al. 2000). In conclusion, these novel microsatellite loci and their multiplex PCR assays will be useful for family analysis, genetic monitoring, and population genetic analyses of the Bean Goose, as well as for other Anser species.

FILE: 2013AProtocolforDNAExtractionfromFecesoftheWildPygmyLorisesNycticebuspygmaeus.grobid.tei.xml

[SECTION] materials and methods

[SECTION] fecal samples
Fecal samples from seven individuals of pygmy loris were collected from the Daweishan Nature Reserve of Pingbian, Yunnan Province, China. Samples of fresh fecal material were transported to the laboratory in an icebox, and stored at -70 º C. The procedure in this study followed protocols approved by China Wildlife Conservation Association, American Society of Primatologists Principles for the Ethical Treatment of Non-Human Primates, and also legal requirements of China.

[SECTION] total dna isolation
DNA was extracted by three different methods viz., alcohol extraction method (Zhang et al., 2004), PBS extraction (Sambrook and Russell, 2002) and acetone extraction method (Zhong et al., 2003). The method ultimately developed is described below: 1)
The fecal sample (0.05-0.10 g) was placed in a 2.0 ml centrifuge tube, to which double distilled water was added. The sample was mixed thoroughly and then kept at room temperature for 2 min.

[SECTION] 2)
The supernatant was poured in a 2.0 ml centrifuge tube, and centrifuged at 4,500x g at 4°C for 4 min; 3)
The supernatant solution was once again poured in another 2.0 ml centrifuge tube, and centrifuged at 5,040 g at 4°C for 6 min to pellet down the cells. 4) Supernatant was discarded and 500µl precooled (at -20°C) acetone was added in the cells, swirled and then after one minute centrifuged at 5,040 g at 4°C for 5 min. The cell pellet was washed with acetone, twice or three times.

[SECTION] 5)
The acetone was poured out and then the cells were treated with 500µl lytic buffer (200 mM NaCl, 100 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 2.0% SDS, 50 mM EDTA, 1.0% Triton X-100) at 55°C for 3 h or 24 h. Then added 1.25 µl RNase (10mg/ml) at 37 °C for 30 min.

[SECTION] 6)
To the above lysate equal volume of mixture of phenol: chloroform: isoamyl alcohol (25:24:1 volume), was added then mixed and kept for 1 min, and centrifuged at 16,000 g at 4°C for 10 min, The supernatant was collected and the pellet was wash by phenol: chloroform: isoamyl alcohol (25:24:1) 2 to 3 times.

[SECTION] 7)
The above supernatant containing DNA was treated with equal volume of isoamyl alcohol at -20°C for 12 h 8)
The DNA was centrifuged at 16,000 g at 4°C for 2 min. The supernatant was discarded while the pellet was washed with 70% ethanol and then with 20µl double distilled water twice. The DNA was stored at -20 º C.
Conventional electrophoresis was then performed to verify that DNA had remained intact (0.8% agarose gel, 100 volts, 0.5X TBE buffer) (Suau et al., 1999).

[SECTION] pcr
Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplification of Cyt b and D-loop was performed using primers shown below. Reactions were performed in 50 µl volume containing 1.0 µl DNA template, 5.0 µl 10  PCR buffer (containing 25 mmol/l Mg 2+ ), 1.0 µl of dNTPs (10 10 -3 mmol/ml), 2.0 µl primer (10  10 -6 mmol/ml), 0.5µl Taq DNA polymerase, and 40.5 µl ddH 2 O. Amplification conditions were as follows: 94°C initial denaturation for 5min; 30 cycles each of 94°C for 1min, 48 to 55°C for 1min, and 72°C for 1min; 72°C extension for 10min. PCR products were visualized on an agarose gel electrophoresis.

[SECTION] cyt b
sense antisense AGA CTC ATG ACT AAC ATT CGA TAG GGC TGT GTC TTC ATT TGA G D-loop (Chen et al., 2006) sense antisense CCT GAA GTA GGA ACC AGA TG CTC CAC CAT GAG TAG CAC CCA AAG C
Sequencing and sequence analysis PCR product was sequenced at the Beijing Genomics Institute (BGI). All the sequences was compared with the sequences in the Gen-Bank database using BLAST program available for the NCBI internet website (http://www.ncbi.nlm. nih.gov.).

[SECTION] nucleotide sequence accession numbers
The DNA sequences from this study were submitted to GenBank under accession numbers: Cyt b HQ842857-HQ842862 and D-loop HQ842864-HQ842879.

[SECTION] faecal dna quality
There was the tailing phenomenon in DNA by the different extract methods; all were different degree of degradation (Fig. 1); especially, the alcohol extract method and the PBS extract method; the products of the alcohol extract method and the PBS extract method were more segments, which were less than 100bp; however, the product of the acetone extract method were long fragments more than 2000bp and less degradation. The A260/A280 was about 1.8-2.0 of the fecal DNA.

[SECTION] amplificative quality from faecal dna
The PCR products of D-loop and Cyt b with pygmy loris' fecal DNA extracted by different extract methods, the D-loop was about 400 bp (Fig. 2A), and the Cyt b was near 1140 bp (Fig. 2B).
The amplification success rates of Cyt b with fecal DNA obtained by alcohol extraction method, PBS extraction method and acetone extraction method, were 20.98±0.83%, 22.94±0.72% and 32.51±0.55%, respectively. (Fig. 3A). The amplification success rates of D-loop with fecal DNA obtained by alcohol extraction method, PBS extraction method and acetone extraction method were 20.47±0.81%, 25.17±0.53% and 40.06±0.62%, respectively (Fig. 3B). The amplification success rates of Cyt b or D-loop with fecal DNA obtained by acetone extraction method was higher than that by alcohol extraction method and PBS extraction method. It is suggested that we can obtain high quality and quantity of fecal DNA by acetone extraction method.

[SECTION] materials and methods

[SECTION] sample collection
We sampled eight populations at cave locations known to house major gray bat hibernacula (Fig. 1 and Table 1) from throughout the species' geographic range. Geo graph ic distance between cave locations ranged from 0.5 km (Coach Cave and Jesse James Cave in Kentucky, thought to house a single interbreeding population and treated as such in this study;  and Barratt, 1996). Tissue samples were stored in microcentrifuge tubes containing 95% ethanol and kept at room temperature for short-term storage, followed by long-term storage at -20°C.
To ensure guano samples were from gray bats and not from other species, a species-specific diagnostic DNA marker was sequenced and identified prior to further analyses (methods described below). We collected between 30-100 guano samples per cave. We assumed, considering the very large populations (tens to hundreds of thousands of bats) at each cave, that any two guano samples were highly unlikely to correspond to the same individual. Tissue samples were limited to a maximum of 50 samples per cave, per our federal permit.
We also sampled a single maternity colony, Salt Peter No. 3 Cave on Fort Leonard Wood, MO (Fig. 1 and Table 1). Maternity colony bats were captured via harp traps placed at the cave entrance and sampled following wing tissue procedures described for the other sampling locales. Trapping at the maternity colony was conducted in mid-July of 2006, after parturition and prior to juvenile emergence, to minimize negative impacts on pregnant and juvenile bats.

[SECTION] dna extraction and sample identification
For those sampling locales where only guano was collected, we randomly selected 30-40 samples for inclusion in the study. DNA was extracted from guano samples using the Qiagen DNeasy Kit (Qiagen Inc., Germantown, MD) and from tissue samples using QuickExtract Solution (Epicentre, Madison, WI). Genomic DNA concentrations (ng/µL) were calculated using the NanoDrop® ND-1000 UV-Vis Spectrophotometer (Nanodrop Technologies, Wilmington, DE) and DNA quality was assessed using the 260:280 ratio, which is the primary measure of DNA purity, with a ratio of 1.80 being considered pure (Nano Drop Spectrophotometers Technical Bulletin T042). PROC GLM (SAS, 2005) was used to compare differences in DNA quantity and quality, as well as genotyping success, among sample types (fresh and age-unknown guano, and wing tissue).
In order to confirm species identity for each sample (guano and wing tissue alike) we generated mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) sequences (GenBank accession numbers KP986448-KP986462) for a species-level barcode marker described by Zinck et al. (2004). The marker sequence consists of 190 bp and partially overlaps (3'-5') the Valine tRNA and 16S rRNA (3') genes. As noted by Zinck et al. (2004), this same mtDNA marker region contains intraspecific sequence variation that could be informative for population genetic studies. We therefore applied the sequence data we generated for these markers to our study of gray bat population structure.
Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) was conducted with 1X PCR buffer, 1.5 mM MgCl 2 , 0.2 mM dNTPs, 10 pmol primers, 0.02 µg/uL T4, 2.5 units of Platinum Taq DNA polymerase (Life Technologies, Grand Island, NY), and 20 ng of DNA via 40 cycles of 95°C for 1 min, 55°C for 1 min, and 72°C for 1.5 min, with an initial denaturation cycle of 95°C for 2 min and a final incubation of 72°C for 7 min. PCR products were purified with the Montage PCR Cleanup Kit (EMD Millipore, Billerica, MA) and sequenced on a 3130 Genetic Analyzer (Perkin Elmer, Bridgeville, PA) using the Big Dye Terminator Reaction and subsequent cleanup. Sequence data were aligned using SeqMan 1.4.1 (Kleywegt, 2005) and CodonCode Aligner 3.5 (Codon -Code Corporation, Centerville, MA) software. Mitochondrial haplotypes were identified for each individual. All sequences were compared to reference sequences amplified by the Mysp1/ Mysp2 primer set (J. Zinck, personal communication), as well as to sequences amplified from the wing tissue of individuals positively identified as M. grisescens during capture and sampling. We visually identified a 185 bp region of the target locus for which most of the samples exhibited quality sequence data and used DNAcollapser in the FaBox (Villesen, 2007) online software toolbox to identify all unique haplotypes in the dataset and the samples belonging to each haplotype. To be conservative, we eliminated any sample associated with a haplotype that failed to exhibit a minimum of 95% nucleotide sequence identity to the most common confirmed haplotype (BLAST2seq; http://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/). Of the other bats that might co-occur in caves with gray bats, sequence matches were no higher than 88% identity (other Myotis spp.). CLUSTALW2 (Larkin et al., 2007;Goujon et al., 2010) was used to align all gray bat haplotypes that met our criteria for inclusion in the dataset.
In the course of compiling haplotype data for our sampled populations, we noted the presence of several nucleotide sites within the marker region that had the potential to be informative for population genetic analysis. This region included a short microsatellite-type domain in the 5' region of the 16S rDNA. One drawback of using this atypical VAL/16S marker for population genetic assessment is that there is a lack of comparative population data from other bat studies. Nonetheless, the benefit of adding a marker that would provide a different perspective, relative to conventional microsatellite DNA markers, to our overall analysis of gray bat populations argued for the inclusion of these data to the study.

[SECTION] genotype characterization
Using DNA extracted from a set of gray bat tissue samples (muscle and viscera, obtained through L. Muller, University of Tennessee, Knoxville), we evaluated 36 microsatellite loci previously developed for the greater mouse-eared bat (Myotis myotis - Castella and Ruedi, 2000) and four microsatellite loci pre viously developed for the Indiana bat (Myotis sodalis - Trujillo and Amelon, 2009). Of these 40 loci, eight loci successfully amplified gray bat DNA and were found to be polymorphic, including A2, C112, D9, E24, F14, and G9 from the M. myotis set, and MS4C09 and MS3D02 from the M. sodalis set. All loci contained dinucleotide repeat motifs. Primers were redesigned for the A2 and C112 loci and are henceforth referred to as A2L (forward primer CCAAAGTCCTGTCCACCTGT, reverse primer GATCCGTTGTCTCCCTCTCC) and C112L (forward primer AGGTGTGTGCCTGTGCG, reverse primer GTCAGCATGAAGAGAAA).
We conducted PCR following Zinck et al. (2004) with 10 pmol primer concentrations, 20 ng of DNA, and puReTaq TM Ready-To-Go TM PCR Beads (GE Healthcare, Pittsburgh, PA) for the M. myotis primers, and following Trujillo and Amelon (2009) for the M. sodalis primers, modified to add 0.02 µg/µL T4 protein. Amplification with msDNA primers was conducted using the same cycling conditions as for sequencing, except with annealing temperatures optimized for gray bats, at 52°C for D9, 54°C for A2L, E24, F14 and G9, 58°C for MS4C09 and MS3D02, and 63°C for C112L. Negative controls were included in all amplifications and reactions were prepared in a laminar flow PCR hood in a separate room from the extractions.
Fragment analysis was carried out on a 3100 Genetic Analyzer with GENEMAPPER software (Applied Biosystems, Grand Island, NY) and ROX 500 size standard. Fragment analysis reactions consisted of 2 μL PCR product, 0.5 μL size standard, and 10 μL HiDi Formamide (Applied Biosystems). All guano samples and putative homozygotes, and a subset of wing tissue samples, were amplified and genotyped at each locus a minimum of three times to confirm their status. MICRO -CHECKER (van Oosterhout et al., 2004) was used to estimate null allele frequencies and large allele dropout.

[SECTION] msdna genetic diversity
We characterized multilocus microsatellite genotypes by calculating the mean number of alleles per locus, and expected and observed heterozygosity in MSA 4.05 (Dieringer and Schlotterer, 2003), and F IS values in GENEPOP 4.0.10 (Raymond and Rousset, 1995). We then calculated rarefactioncorrected allelic richness in MSA 4.05 (Dieringer and Schlotterer, 2003). We conducted an analysis of variance using PROC GLM (SAS Institute, 2005) to determine whether differences in observed heterozygosity or allelic richness existed among populations, treating each locus as a randomized block to control for interlocus variation (Leberg, 1992). We also used PROC GLM to test for differences between sample types (guano versus wing tissue). Probability tests for Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium (HWE) and linkage disequilibrium were conducted in GENEPOP, then corrected for multiple comparisons using the sequential Bon ferroni method (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995).
To evaluate whether individuals from sampled sites were from a population that had experienced a recent bottleneck, we used 1,000 replicates of the two-phased model (TPM) with 70% of the mutations following a step-wise mutation model (SMM) and 30% following an infinite alleles model (IAM) in the program BOTTLENECK (Cornuet and Luikart, 1996). The Wilcoxon sign-rank test was used to determine whether the number of loci with heterozygote excess was significantly different than expected if no bottleneck had occurred.

[SECTION] mtdna genetic diversity
The mean number of mtDNA haplotypes and mean gene diversity (Nei, 1987) were calculated from intrapopulation genetic diversity measures output by ARLEQUIN 3.5.1.3 (Excoffier and Lischer, 2010). The mean number of pairwise nucleotide differences among haplotypes was also calculated from ARLE-QUIN outputs. A minimum spanning network among haplotypes, with equal weightings for transitions, transversions, and deletions, was calculated in ARLEQUIN and converted to a haplotype network using HAPSTAR 0.6 (Teacher and Griffiths, 2011).

[SECTION] msdna population genetic structure
Overall F ST and G' ST were calculated in MSA. We used GENEPOP to calculate an overall R ST , which is an F ST analog that takes into account evolutionary distances between alleles, and based the estimate on a simple stepping stone model of microsatellite mutation. We evaluated population structure within the msDNA dataset using several approaches. We estimated pairwise F ST (Weir and Cockerham, 1984) among hibernacula and assessed allele frequency differentiation using GENEPOP. We also incorporated estimates of pairwise R ST as implemented in ARLEQUIN ('R ST -like' option -Slatkin, 1995;Excoffier and Lischer, 2010). In both cases, the critical value used for determining statistical significance was adjusted using a Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons (Jaccard and Wan, 1996). The Bayesian clustering method of STRUCTURE 2.3.1 (Prit chard et al., 2000;Hubisz et al., 2009) was used to estimate the number of genetically divergent groups. Based on recommendations from Hubisz et al. (2009) for data sets with relatively low genetic differentiation and sampling locations with allelic pools that were likely largely independent of each other (we assume that with 30 or so samples from very large populations that were separated by considerable geographic distances that the likelihood of even a small number of recent immigrants in our samples would be very low), we analyzed our data using a no admixture model with correlated alleles and informative population priors. STRUCTURE run parameters included a 50,000 step burn-in stage and 50,000 Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) steps for each of 100 iterative runs for each K model within the range of K = 1-8. STRUCTURE results were processed using STRUCTURE HARVESTER (Web v0.6.93 -Earl and vonHoldt, 2012) and assessed following Evanno et al. (2005). Data from STRUCTURE HARVESTER relative to the optimal number of clusters (K) was entered into CLUMPP v1.1.2 (Jakobsson and Rosenberg, 2007) in order to optimize the assignment of populations to clusters (CLUMPP parameters included DATATYPE = 1, R = 100, GREEDY_ OPTION = 2, M = 2 algorithm options, and REPEATS = 10,000). We then performed a series of analyses of molecular variance (AMOVA) using ARLEQUIN 3.5.1.3 (Excoffier and Lischer, 2010) with significance determined from five loci (A2L, C112L, E24, F14, and G9) with 10% or less missing data via 10,000 permutations of the msDNA genotypes under three different putative population groups: 1) no regional structure, 2) populations west of the Mississippi River Alluvial Plain vs. populations east of the Mississippi River Alluvial Plain, and 3) populations grouped according to the msDNA STRUCTURE results.
We used GENEPOP to evaluate the association of genetic and geographic distances among populations. We ran the Isolation by Distance suboption with 1,000 permutations and the Spearman Rank correlation coefficient, after converting genetic differentiation values to F ST /(1 -F ST ) (Rousset, 1997), and evaluated the relationship with both linear distance and the logarithm of distance, which has been shown to perform better when testing for IBD in 2-dimensional space (Rousset, 1997). Pair wise F ST /(1 -F ST ) data from GENEPOP was then plotted in Excel against both pairwise distance and logarithm distance, separately, to obtain r-values.

[SECTION] mtdna population genetic structure
ARLEQUIN was used to perform AMOVA (Excoffier et al., 1992;Michalakis and Excoffier, 1996) on the mtDNA haplotype data under the same conditions as for the msDNA data, including putative groupings of: 1) no structure, 2) populations west vs. east of the Mississippi River Alluvial Plain, and 3) populations grouped according to msDNA STRUCTURE analysis. We also used ARLEQUIN to perform analyses of pairwise population differentiation and exact tests of population structure (Raymond and Rousset, 1995;Goudet et al., 1996), with statistical significance set at P ≤ 0.011 as described by Narum (2006). ARLEQUIN was also employed in testing for IBD via partial MANTEL correlations (Mantel, 1967;Smouse et al., 1986) among matrices of pairwise Φ ST , geographic distance, and region al association. A matrix of geographic distances (km) between colonies was generated with Geographic Distance Matrix Gen erator version 1.2.3 (Ersts, 2011). A second approach, iterative simulated annealing of populations into clusters to identify a structure maximizing the proportion of total genetic variation associated with intercluster genetic differentiation, was employed using the program SAMOVA 2.0 (Dupanloup et al., 2002). The program was used to assess structure, including K = 2, K = 3, and K = 4 clusters of populations, with and without constraints associated with geographic proximity between populations, and incorporated percent sequence divergence as a measure of between-haplotype genetic distance. For each K, 1,000 iterations of simulated annealing with randomized starting partitions were used. All other run parameters were set at default values.

[SECTION] multilocus assignment tests
In order to assess the potential utility of msDNA-based individual assignment tests in determining associations between summer colonies and winter hibernacula, we conducted assignment tests with the eight hibernacula populations and for the maternity colony on Fort Leonard Wood, MO (FLW-MO). For these tests we utilized conventional likelihood-based and k-nearest neighbors (k = 1, 3, 5, 10) assignment approaches, with 'pessim istic' cross-validation (leave-one-out; L1O) of accuracy rates, in the program MLC 1.0 (Topchy et al., 2004). Also, an exhaustive genetic algorithm search, employing L1O accuracy estimates, was implemented in the program GAFS 1.1 (default parameters - Guinand et al., 2004;Topchy et al., 2004) to determine the suite of available microsatellite markers (n = 1-8) that maximizes accurate reassignment of individuals to populations of origin.

[SECTION] animal care and use guidelines
All field methodologies followed the guidelines approved by the American Society of Mammalogists (Sikes et al., 2011).
Sample collection was permitted by the United States Fish and Wildlife Service (Permit # TE108962-0), The Nature Conser vancy, Arkansas Game and Fish Commission, Missouri Depart ment of Conservation, and Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency.

[SECTION] genetic diversity
DNA used in our analyses (positively identified as gray bat) was extracted from 96 age-unknown guano samples (average yield 21.95 ng/µL ± 16.51; average 260:280 ratio 1.65 ± 0.44), 92 fresh guano samples (average yield 15.57 ng/µL ± 16.10; average 260:280 ratio 1.61 ± 0.54), and 150 wing tissue samples (average yield 11.83 ng/µL ± 12.75; average 260:280 ratio 1.90 ± 1.20). Less than 5% of sample extractions provided > 100 ng/ µL DNA; those that did were considered outliers and not representative of typical sample yields.
Success of msDNA genotyping among samples ranged from three to eight loci (0 = 6.94 ± 1.06); any sample for which at least three loci were not resolved was discarded from the study. Genotyping success differed by sample type (F 2, 335 = 72.51, P < 0.001), with wing tissue samples having a higher average number of successfully amplified loci (7.88 ± 0.36) than guano samples (6.59 ± 1.38 for age-unknown and 6.35 ± 1.43 for fresh samples). Significant evidence for null alleles was identified for locus D9, with an Oosterhout frequency of 0.245. Because removal of D9 from our suite of microsatellites resulted in negligible differences in F ST , we concluded that any bias associated with this locus would be conservative and, therefore, included it in all subsequent analyses. Additionally, because using genotypes corrected for null alleles did not change the outcome of our analyses, we have reported data from the uncorrected genotypes.
Tests for linkage disequilibrium were not significant when the false discovery rate was adjusted for multiple comparisons. With the exception of CMC-AR, allele frequencies in hibernacula populations did not meet HWE expectations. There was signif icant variation in observed heterozygosity (F 7, 49 = 2.96, P = 0.011), but not allelic richness (F 7, 49 = 0.43, P = 0.880) among hibernacula (Fig. 2), and no population had significant heterozygote excess under mutation-drift equilibrium. Levels of We sequenced 307 samples for the target mtDNA locus. The target locus was comprised of 178 nucleotides, with 13 polymorphic positions, including six transitions and nine insertions/deletions (Table 2). Much of the haplotypic divergence (Fig. 3) was associated with a dinucleotide microsatellite (AT n ) located near the 5' origin of the 16S rDNA gene. Thirteen haplotypes (MG01-08, MG11-15) were identified within the hibernacula populations (Table 2), with a mean number of pairwise nucleotide differences among haplotypes of 4.2 (SD = 2.1). An additional two haplotypes (MG09-10) were identified from the maternity colony (FLW-MO), which also shared several haplotypes (MG01, MG04, MG06) with the hibernacula populations. The mean number of haplotypes within hibernacula was 3.875 (SD = 1.727) and the mean gene diversity was 0.241 (SD = 0.172). In terms of relative frequencies of haplotypes within hibernacula (Table 3 and Fig. 4), haplotype MG01 was dominant with a mean relative frequency of 0.865 (SD = 0.106). The next most common haplotypes, MG04 and MG03, had frequencies of 0.036 (SD = 0.068) and 0.029 (SD = 0.039), respectively. Haplotype MG01 also comprised 84.8% of the haplotypes found in the FLW-MO population (with the next most common haplotype, MG04, at 6.5%). In the minimum spanning network of all haplotypes (Fig. 3) MG01 is a central node for the radiation of several other haplotypes.

[SECTION] population genetic structure
With the nuclear msDNA loci, we found statistically significant overall genetic differentiation among hibernacula (F ST = 0.024, P < 0.001; G' ST = 0.121, P < 0.001; R ST = 0.060) and significant pairwise differentiation among a majority of populations (Table 4). No test for a pattern of IBD was statistically significant (P < 0.05), regardless of whether pairwise F ST or R ST estimates were used, or whether untransformed or log-transformed geographic distances were used.
For population clustering results from STRUC-TURE, K = 2 had the highest value of ΔK (= 95.067) by a wide-margin (the next highest value was for K = 3, ΔK = 3.164). The Evanno et al. (2005) method for selecting the most likely cluster model cannot identify the correct model when K = 1 is the best fit. In our case, the K = 1 model did not exhibit the highest mean LnP(K) as would be expected if K = 1 were the best fit, so we accepted K = 2 as the most probable population genetic structuring. Six of the eight hibernacula exhibited strong associations to one or the other putative genetic clusters (Fig. 4), but the associations of CC-MO and FC-AL were fairly weak. Cluster 1 included BSC-AR, CMC-AR, HC-TN, and PC-TN, and Cluster 2 included BC/ MPC-MO and CC/JJC-KY. AMOVA of the groupings derived from the msDNA structural analyses identified significant genetic structure among the K = 2 groups (Φ CT = 0.063, P < 0.001), as well as between three groups (Φ CT = 0.044, P < 0.001; when CC-MO and FC-AL were included as a separate group), accounting for 6.3% and 4.4% of the variation, respectively. There was no significant interregional differentiation between the two putative clusters of populations east and west of the Mississippi River Alluvial Plain (Φ CT = 0.000, P = 0.850), AMOVA of mtDNA haplotype data exhibited statistically significant genetic differentiation among all hibernacula (Φ ST = 0.061, P < 0.001; 6% of overall genetic variance). Differences between eastern vs. western hibernacula groups were likewise statistically significant (Φ CT = 0.086, P = 0.027; 9% of overall genetic variance). No significant interpopulation genetic differentiation was found within eastern and western clusters (Φ SC = 0.010, P = 0.250). The exact test of population structure within the mtDNA data also found significant overall differentiation (P < 0.001), with the same population pairings showing significant differentiation as with the pairwise Φ ST test (Table 5). AMOVA of the population clusters suggested by STRUCTURE analysis of the msDNA data did not yield statistically significant regional differentiation. SAMOVA also failed to detect statistically significant differentiation between clusters of populations, though PC-TN clustered away from all other populations in nearly all simulated cases.
IBD among all hibernacula was weak to mod erate, explaining 23% of the interpopulation differentiation (r = 0.486, P < 0.05). The extent of IBD was largely unchanged (r = 0.477, P < 0.05) by taking into account regional groupings of populations east and west of the Mississippi River Alluvial Plain.

[SECTION] multilocus assignment tests
The best accuracy level for correct reassignment of individuals to a regional autumn breeding site using our suite of eight microsatellite loci was only 31.4%. An optimized suite of five loci (A2L, C112L, D9, G9, and 4C09) was found to be only mar ginally superior (36.4%) to using all loci.
